United States 1920–45 Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on American history from the aftermath of the First World War through the end of the Second World War — normalcy and the 1920s boom, Prohibition and mass culture, the Great Depression, the New Deal, industrial and labor change, neutrality and rearmament, wartime mobilization, and the Manhattan Project through 1945.
Total pages: 26
Sources will be added as texts are processed. Entity, event, and concept pages will be built from those sources under a contemporary lens, without modern editorial framing.
Entities
People, places, and institutions of the United States, 1920–45.
(none yet)
Events
Elections, wars, strikes, legislation, crises, and other key occurrences.
(none yet)
Concepts
Broad themes, institutions, systems, and ideas.
(none yet)
Sources
The foundation of the wiki. Source pages summarize the primary and secondary texts used throughout.

allen-only-yesterday — [source] Only Yesterday: An Informal History of the 1920s (Allen, 1931) — Frederick Lewis Allen’s near-contemporary informal history of the United States from the Armistice of 1918 through the stock-market panic of 1929 and its immediate aftermath in 1930–31, emphasizing public mind, manners, politics, Prohibition, ballyhoo, Florida and Wall Street speculation, and Coolidge–Hoover prosperity. Read source page
allen-since-yesterday — [source] Since Yesterday: The 1930s in America (Allen, 1939/1940) — Frederick Lewis Allen’s near-contemporary informal history from the crest of the Big Bull Market (3 September 1929) through the British and French declarations of war on Germany (3 September 1939), emphasizing Depression collapse, Hoover to Roosevelt, New Deal politics and culture, Dust Bowl, labor and recession, and the approach of war. Read source page
groves-now-it-can-be-told — [source] Now It Can Be Told: The Story of the Manhattan Project (Groves, 1962) — Leslie R. Groves’s first-person administrative and operational history of the Manhattan Engineer District from his September 1942 appointment through the 1945 bombings and the December 1946 transfer to the Atomic Energy Commission. Read source page
roosevelt-as-he-saw-it — [source] As He Saw It (Elliott Roosevelt, 1946) — Elliott Roosevelt’s aide-son memoir of wartime conferences from Argentia through Cairo and Teheran (Yalta reconstructed), framed as a 1946 plea to restore Franklin Roosevelt’s Big Three peace architecture after Fulton and early Cold War friction. Read source page
conant-tuxedo-park — [source] Tuxedo Park: A Wall Street Tycoon and the Secret Palace of Science (Conant, 2002) — Jennet Conant’s biography of Alfred Lee Loomis—Wall Street financier, Tuxedo Park private laboratory founder, MIT Radiation Laboratory organizer, and Stimson-linked broker of radar and early atomic work—from Richards family frame through Tizard Mission, Rad Lab, and postwar seclusion. Read source page
lindbergh-economic-pinch — [source] The Economic Pinch (Lindbergh, 1923) — Charles A. Lindbergh Sr.’s 1923 Dorrance tract on postwar deflation, Federal Reserve and Esch-Cummins policy, profiteer control of banks and Congress, and a Book II program of farmer–labor–business federation against special privilege. Read source page
nevins-hill-ford-expansion-1915-1933 — [source] Ford: Expansion and Challenge, 1915–1933 (Nevins & Hill, 1957) — Second volume of the Columbia–Ford trilogy: Peace Ship and war production, Dodge suit and minority buy-out, Rouge vertical integration, Dearborn Independent anti-Semitism, Model T’s end, Model A and early Depression through the V-8. Read source page
nevins-hill-ford-decline-1933-1962 — [source] Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962 (Nevins & Hill, 1962/1963) — Third volume: NRA clash, UAW and Battle of the Overpass, Willow Run, Bennett vs. Henry Ford II, Breech/Whiz Kids rebuild, Ferguson suit, Ford Foundation public stock, and the post-autocrat corporation. Read source page
chernow-house-of-morgan — [source] The House of Morgan (Chernow, 1990/2010) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: Part Two Diplomatic Age through Crash, Depression, New Deal banking reform, Glass-Steagall, and Morgan Stanley. Read source page
paxson-recent-history-united-states — [source] Recent History of the United States, 1865–1927 (Paxson, 1928/1929) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: postwar / normalcy chapters (XXV–XXVII) as near-contemporary spine beside Only Yesterday. Read source page
gates-dupont-family — [source] The du Pont Family (Gates, 1979) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: interwar company, Pierre S. du Pont / GM, Christiana Securities, and family-control arc. Read source page
bird-sherwin-american-prometheus — [source] American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (Bird and Sherwin, 2005/2006) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Berkeley school, 1930s left politics, Los Alamos, Trinity, and 1945 bomb use (Parts One–Three); postwar hearing chapters period-gated. Read source page
sloan-my-years-with-general-motors — [source] My Years with General Motors (Sloan, 1964) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Durant vs. Ford, 1920 crisis, decentralized GM, 1920s market triumph, annual model/GMAC, and WWII defense through the 1945–46 strike; 1960s retrospectives period-gated. Read source page
gabler-walt-disney — [source] Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination (Gabler, 2006) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Kansas City/Hollywood animation, Mickey, Snow White, 1941 strike, and WWII studio through 1945; postwar Disneyland/EPCOT period-gated. Read source page
barlett-steele-empire-howard-hughes — [source] Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness (Barlett & Steele, 1979) — Investigative Hughes biography: Tool Co. inheritance, Hollywood, 1930s aviation records, WWII contracting, and 1947 Senate/Spruce Goose hinge; postwar RKO–Las Vegas–Watergate chapters period-gated to 1946–89. Read source page
bonadio-ap-giannini-banker-of-america — [source] A. P. Giannini: Banker of America (Bonadio, 1994) — Bank of Italy → Bank of America: 1920s branch wars, 1926 Octopus, Morgan/Wall Street, Crash/Transamerica, Walker/Monnet proxy war, New Deal/Morgenthau fights, WWII lending; founding-era Chs. 1–6 also copied to 1866–1919. Read source page
foster-henry-j-kaiser — [source] Henry J. Kaiser: Builder in the Modern American West (Foster, 1989) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: 1920s roads, Six Companies Hoover/Grand Coulee dams, WWII Liberty ships, Fontana steel, wartime image, Hughes cargo-plane strand, Permanente origins through 1945; Kaiser-Frazer/Hawaii period-gated. Read source page
nasaw-the-chief-hearst — [source] The Chief: The Life of William Randolph Hearst (Nasaw, 2000) — Copied from United States 1946–89: 1920s Hollywood/San Simeon, Depression, New Deal break, Hitler contacts, fall, and Citizen Kane; yellow-press origins and 1946–51 coda period-gated. Read source page
lyons-david-sarnoff — [source] David Sarnoff: A Biography (Lyons, 1966) — Copied from United States 1946–89: RCA birth, radio networks, Depression R&D, television struggle, and WWII electronics (Chs. 6–19); immigrant/Titanic origins and postwar color period-gated. Read source page
duncan-rickover-struggle-for-excellence — [source] Rickover: The Struggle for Excellence (Duncan, 2001) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Academy through BuShips Electrical Section and WWII (Chs. 1–5); Oak Ridge / nuclear-Navy chapters period-gated. Read source page
kroc-grinding-it-out — [source] Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s (Kroc with Anderson, 1977) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Lily Tulip paper cups, Florida boom, and Multimixer years (Chs. 3–5); 1954 McDonald’s empire period-gated. Read source page
schroeder-snowball-warren-buffett — [source] The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life (Schroeder, 2008) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Omaha/Washington youth and Philadelphia college (Chs. 5–14); partnership/Berkshire chapters period-gated. Read source page
trimble-overnight-success-federal-express — [source] Overnight Success: Federal Express and Frederick Smith (Trimble, 1993) — Copied from United States 1946–89: Dixie Greyhound/Toddle House fortune and Memphis childhood; FedEx founding period-gated. Read source page
mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky — [source] Vision: A Saga of the Sky (Mansfield, 1956) — Boeing company saga: mail planes and pursuits through all-metal 247, Flying Fortress, and WWII B-17/B-29 production (Battle of Kansas, Pacific Superfortress); founding and postwar jet/707 chapters also copied to sister period wikis. Read source page
cooper-barriers-down — [source] Barriers Down: The Story of the News Agency Epoch (Cooper, 1942) — Kent Cooper’s AP insider history of breaking the Reuters–Havas–Wolff cartel: South America, Japan/Rengo, Geneva press experts, 1934 emancipation, wartime truth-as-propaganda frame. Read source page
lansing-peace-negotiations — [source] The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative (Lansing, 1921) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: Wilson’s February 1920 demand for Lansing’s resignation, 1921 publication, Article 10 / Senate inheritance, Shantung, and the unratified French assistance treaty. Read source page

Only Yesterday: An Informal History of the 1920s
Author: Frederick Lewis Allen
Published: Harper & Brothers, 1931 (copyright Frederick Lewis Allen 1931; Agnes Rogers Allen 1959)
Working text: Open Road Integrated Media ebook edition, 2015 (ISBN 978-1-5040-1137-2; AA hash fbdb17eb865de244038dd09b1e3b3f4e)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/allen-only-yesterday.txt
Extract stats: 4,234 lines · ~118,806 words · 720,430 bytes (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Completeness Assessment
The clean digital EPUB extract is complete for wiki use. After modern Open Road marketing front matter and a machine table of contents, the body runs Preface → Chapters I–XIV → Appendix (“Sources and Obligations”) → Index. Modern Open Road author-promo trailer follows the copyright block at the tail and is not part of Allen’s 1931 text. Chapter structure matches the imprint contents list.
Overview
Allen frames the eleven years from the Armistice of 11 November 1918 to the stock-market panic culminating on 13 November 1929 as a distinct era—“the Post-war Decade”—whose destruction of Coolidge (and Hoover) Prosperity the crash hastened and dramatized. Writing in 1931 while recollection was still fresh, he deliberately emphasizes the changing state of the public mind, fads, fashions, and follies that touched daily life, and leaves much foreign policy to later historians. He acknowledges debt to Mark Sullivan’s method in Our Own Times and lists principal sources in an appendix rather than footnotes.
For this wiki the book is the natural 1920s narrative spine: demobilization and the League fight, the Big Red Scare, convalescence into mass amusements, the revolution in manners and morals, Harding and the oil scandals, Coolidge Prosperity and business culture, ballyhoo and Lindbergh, highbrow revolt, Prohibition and Capone, the Florida boom, the Big Bull Market, Crash, and the bitter 1930–31 aftermath. It pairs with Allen’s sequel Since Yesterday (1930s) once that source page is built, and later with Groves, Conant, Elliott Roosevelt, and the Nevins & Hill Ford volumes for wartime and industrial threads.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 69–82. ~560 words.
This book is an attempt to tell, and in some measure to interpret, the story of what in the future may be considered a distinct era in American history: the eleven years between the end of the war with Germany (November 11, 1918) and the stock-market panic which culminated on November 13, 1929, hastening and dramatizing the destruction of what had been known as Coolidge (and Hoover) Prosperity. Writing so soon after the event means breaking new ground; many events of those years, Allen notes, have never been chronicled in full—including a continuous narrative of the Harding scandals and of the Big Bull Market as economic and social phenomenon. A contemporary history is bound to be anything but definitive, yet half the enjoyment of writing it has lain in reducing to order a mass of material untouched by previous historians. Emphasis on the public mind and on sometimes trivial preoccupations is deliberate: the close-range writer has a special chance to record fads, fashions, and follies while recollection is fresh, and may leave foreign affairs whose full effect is not yet measurable to subsequent historians. Allen credits Mark Sullivan’s Our Own Times for developing this method, and adds an appendix of principal sources in place of footnotes.
Chapter I — Prelude: May, 1919
Lines 83–146. ~4,560 words.
If time were suddenly to turn back to the earliest days of the Post-war Decade, what would seem strange? Allen follows a moderately well-to-do young couple—Mr. and Mrs. Smith of any large city—through an ordinary day in May 1919, six months after the Armistice, when war ways have largely given way to peace but the decade’s profound alterations have hardly begun. Men’s fashions move glacially; Mrs. Smith’s skirt hangs six inches from the ground, stockings are black or tan not flesh-colored, powder is possible but paint still frowned on by the well-brought-up, hair is long, and short hair still smells of radicalism. Vitamins are unknown; tabloids are not yet born (the New York Daily News will appear 26 June 1919). Front-page news is the Navy seaplane NC-4’s Azores route, the Peace Conference, Victory Loan, returning transports, strikes, Mayor Ole Hanson against the I.W.W., woman suffrage, and Henry Ford’s libel suit. Babe Ruth is still obscure on the Red Sox; Dempsey–Willard is set for Toledo; golf has not yet become the business man’s weekly ritual.
High Cost of Living dominates breakfast talk—milk, steak, butter, eggs, and rents far above 1914. Mr. Smith’s open car (only about a tenth of 1919 production closed) may be a Ford Model T cranked by hand; registered passenger cars are under seven million versus over twenty-three million a decade later; speed limits average about twenty miles an hour. At the office, business is looking up after post-Armistice uncertainty; labor demands and Bolshevism and stock speculation are the clouds. Radio broadcasting does not yet exist for the Smiths. Allen closes the prelude by listing the decade’s coming furniture of mind—Coué, Dayton, cross-word puzzles, Teapot Dome, Coral Gables, Sacco and Vanzetti, speakeasies, Capone, Lindbergh—and leaves the Post-war Decade lying before them.
Chapter II — Back to Normalcy
Lines 147–276. ~9,660 words.
Early on the morning of 11 November 1918, Woodrow Wilson writes in pencil on White House stationery that the armistice is signed, everything America fought for is accomplished, and it will now be the country’s duty to assist by example, sober counsel, and material aid in establishing just democracy throughout the world. Allen reads the message as Puritan schoolmaster, moral idealist, and dogmatic prophet of democracy—Wilsonian and almost Lincolnian—yet notes that Lincoln did not live to see what happens to idealism in a post-war decade. The 11th of November is carnival in the streets; then come demobilization, cancellation of war contracts, the slow return of the A.E.F., and the bitter fight over the Treaty and the League.
Lodge, the Italian vote and Fiume, the secret memorandum entrusted to Henry White for Balfour, Clemenceau, and Nitti, Borah and the irreconcilables, and Wilson’s western tour and collapse fill the political center. Harding emerges as the available man of “normalcy”; Cox and Roosevelt lose in 1920. Allen ends with Wilson in S Street on Armistice Day five years after the war—supported so he will not fall—declaring that fools who resist Providence will meet utter destruction, and dying three months later.
Chapter III — The Big Red Scare
Lines 277–436. ~9,630 words.
If Americans turned a deaf ear to Wilson’s League in the early Post-war Decade, it was not only weariness of foreign entanglements. They were listening to rumors of radical conspiracy, cocked for bombs and Bolshevist armies, millions of otherwise reasonable citizens thinking Red revolution might begin next month or next week. Front pages shout strikes and anti-Bolshevist riots; radicals shoot Armistice Day paraders in Centralia and a white I.W.W. member is lynched from a bridge; Socialist assemblymen are expelled in New York; an Indiana jury acquits a man for killing an alien who shouted “To hell with the United States.”
Palmer’s raids, the Fighting Quaker, deportations, super-patriotic societies, blacklists that touch even charities and theatres and colleges (Frankfurter, Chafee, Dewey, Main Street), race riot in Chicago, and the Wall Street explosion of 16 September 1920 carry the narrative. By the time the explosion’s mystery is still unsolved years later, Allen judges that the country was already coming to its senses enough to see that no such plot could command more than a handful of fanatics—had it come a few months earlier, the indirect consequences might have been uglier still.
Chapter IV — America Convalescent
Lines 437–498. ~3,390 words.
The Big Red Scare dies slowly: insufficient cause for the panic; Communism localized in Europe; radicalism ebbing at home; Palmer’s methods scaring many Reds into “pale pinkness”; A. F. of L. leaders leaning over backward toward conservatism; wets acquiring a belated concern for personal liberty. More important, the temper of war’s aftermath gives way to the temper of peace—like an overworked business man beginning vacation, the country learns again to relax and amuse itself.
Mah-jongg, radio, confession magazines, Main Street, The Sheik, If Winter Comes, and above all the Hall–Mills murder of 16 September 1922 near New Brunswick feed a national appetite for diversion and sensation. Sacco and Vanzetti run as a recurring political and emotional storm; when the headlines finally scream execution, men shiver, wonder whether justice or hideous mistake, and turn to where Lindbergh is flying and what General Motors is doing.
Chapter V — The Revolution in Manners and Morals
Lines 499–634. ~11,210 words.
A first-class revolt against the accepted American order is under way in the early Post-war Decade, but Lenin has nothing to do with it. Shock troops are sons and daughters of well-to-do families; defiance is spoken across the breakfast table. While elders still shiver at the Red Menace they awake to the Problem of the Younger Generation. The old code—woman as guardian of morality, innocent waiting for the altar, a double standard for men—cracks under war, prosperity, the automobile, prohibition’s hypocrisies, Freudian talk, and freer manners.
Skirts rise, bobbed hair moves from radical stigma (1918) to boom business contested by hairdressers and barbers, cosmetics and cigarettes spread, petting and companionate-marriage talk alarm the pulpits, and divorce statistics and sex in fiction and film mark the change. Middletown evidence and fashion economics run through the chapter. Not until the decade nears its end do signs appear that the revolutionists are learning to be at home in the freer code, less obsessed with sex, and to discover among the ruins of the old dispensation a new set of enduring satisfactions.
Chapter VI — Harding and the Scandals
Lines 635–856. ~11,260 words.
Allen opens with Harry M. Daugherty’s 1926 refusal to testify before a federal grand jury—personal attorney to the Hardings, Attorney-General, relations “of the most confidential character,” answers that might tend to incriminate. On 4 March 1921 Wilson limps from the White House; Harding is sworn in; the reign of normalcy begins. The Ohio Gang, Daugherty, Jess Smith, Forbes and the Veterans’ Bureau, Fall, Doheny, Sinclair, Teapot Dome and Elk Hills, the Continental Trading Company Liberty-bond packages to Blackmer, O’Neil, Stewart, and Sinclair, Senate investigation, and the slow unraveling after Harding’s death in 1923 fill the narrative.
Coolidge inherits the mess; prosecutions and political embarrassment drag through the decade. When Hoover and Coolidge finally take part in dedicating Harding’s tomb in June 1931, Allen notes a certain restraint—it is not so easy as in 1923 to compose panegyrics on the good-natured man who had “taught us the power of brotherliness.”
Chapter VII — Coolidge Prosperity
Lines 857–987. ~8,520 words.
Business is booming when Harding dies; by kerosene lamp in a Vermont farmhouse Colonel John Coolidge administers the presidential oath to Calvin. The depression of 1921 has given way to improvement in 1922 and rushing revival in 1923. Stock prices on 2 August 1923 still suggest no unreasonable optimism—Steel 87, small volume—and the Big Bull Market is still far ahead, but the tide of prosperity is in full flood. Allen traces the jagged statistical path of the decade to the Everest of 1929 and the abyss of 1930–31.
Mass production, installment buying, the automobile and good roads, electrification, chain stores, advertising’s rise from business to self-styled profession to, among practitioners, a “racket,” service clubs, Rotary and boosters, the fusion of religion and business (The Man Nobody Knows), and Coolidge’s discreet obeisance before the great god business structure the chapter. Statesmanship of a sort Coolidge represents: encourage prosperity without hot water; accept the inevitable; do not try to be bolder than circumstances safely permit.
Chapter VIII — The Ballyhoo Years
Lines 988–1219. ~12,380 words.
One striking mark of Coolidge Prosperity is the unparalleled rapidity and unanimity with which millions fix attention on tremendous trifles—a heavyweight fight, a murder trial, a new car model, a transatlantic flight. Most causes célèbres are unimportant by traditional historical measure; that they could engage unprecedented numbers is not. Allen reviews Hall–Mills and the “pig woman,” Floyd Collins in the Kentucky cave, sports idols, beauty contests, cross-word puzzles, radio crazes, and above all Charles A. Lindbergh’s flight as the heroism of a stunt flyer who crossed the ocean for a money prize.
The Dayton Scopes trial is told at length: Bryan on the stand before reason as prosecutor, Raulston’s mercy, Scopes guilty and fined one hundred dollars, the law upheld on technicality but Fundamentalism losing in civilized opinion as the slow drift from certainty continues. By early 1928 ballyhoo’s bloom may be departing—Lindbergh has spoiled the public for lesser heroes; Sacco–Vanzetti and the 1928 campaign remind a well-fed people of public issues; and a ten-point gain in Radio common in a single day promises more immediate benefits than all the non-stop flyers and heavyweight champions in the world.
Chapter IX — The Revolt of the Highbrows
Lines 1220–1309. ~5,830 words.
Allen opens with Fitzgerald’s generation that found all Gods dead, all wars fought, all faiths in man shaken. Wartime social compulsion becomes peacetime habit—drives, quotas, canned publicity, the man who grips his pocketbook feeling mass opinion. Intellectuals revolt: against puritanism and censorship, against the exaltation of the business man, against the reformer (by 1925 a term of contempt among them), often in religious skepticism, united in scorn of the bourgeois majority held responsible for prohibition, Fundamentalism, and other repressions—Babbitts, Rotarians, the Klan, Service-with-a-Smile, boosters and super-salesmen, with Mencken as tone-setter.
Disillusionment and the lost generation’s meager pleasure in self-pity cannot find peace; Allen closes on groping for new values among those for whom the new day heralded in wartime had turned to night before it arrived.
Chapter X — Alcohol and Al Capone
Lines 1310–1431. ~7,770 words.
Had one told the average American in 1919 that prohibition would be the most violently explosive public issue of the nineteen-twenties, he would have thought the prophecy mad. Rum-ships outside the twelve-mile limit, hijacked beer trucks, stills by the carload, fashionable contraband cocktails, speakeasy grills, and Capone in an armor-plated car would have dropped his jaw. The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified to take effect 16 January 1920, had seemed to settle the issue.
Allen traces the ease of final dry victory after generations of uphill fighting, then the collapse of enforcement, wet and dry geography, corruption, Chicago gang war, Capone’s rise, rackets beyond liquor, and the Wickersham Commission’s paradoxical 1931 report—sorry inability to dry the country, individual commissioners split, corporate vote for further trial—satirized in Flaccus’s summary in F.P.A.’s column. As the decade bows out, prohibition, gangster, and racket problems remain unsolved for the nineteen-thirties; still the rum-running launch slips across the river and tabloid-readers find adventure in gangster killings.
Chapter XI — Home, Sweet Florida
Lines 1432–1547. ~5,960 words.
Allen quotes a bank vice-president’s unbuttoned 1925 rhetoric in the Miamian—palms, sun-kissed sky, Caribbean breeze—as the Florida boom hits its height amid Scopes aftermath, Red Grange, and The Man Nobody Knows. Miami becomes one frenzied real-estate exchange: thousands of offices and agents, binder boys, Coral Gables and the American tropics as sales religion, lot prices in a fever unmatched in ninety years.
The mayors’ “Fiesta of the American Tropics” at the turn of 1925–26 promises Love, Good Fellowship, and Sublime Beauty; by New Year’s the suspicion insinuates itself that new buyers are not appearing as they should. Collapse, bank strain, and the shift of speculative infection from Flagler Street to Broad and Wall follow. Florida house-lots a bad bet? Then, asks a public still enthralled by Coolidge Prosperity, what else is there to bet on? The Big Bull Market is getting under way.
Chapter XII — The Big Bull Market
Lines 1548–1738. ~9,540 words.
One day in February 1928 an investor asks an astute banker about common stocks; the banker thinks them dangerously high and would wait. By conservative canons he is right: Coolidge Prosperity confidence has already lifted prices far since 1924. Through 1927 speculation increases; brokers’ loans rise from about 2.82 billion to 3.56 billion; a record week of trading hits in December. After-dinner talk from New York to the lowliest village runs to the market.
Allen follows the 1928–29 advance: Radio and the new-era argument, investment trusts, rejection of “ten times earnings,” breaks in June and December 1928 that teach the lesson “when there is a break it is a good time to buy,” call money at 8 and 9 percent explained away, and the vision of an America set free from poverty and toil—cars, airplanes, high-tension wires, skyscrapers, and smartly dressed men and women spending with money won by being far-sighted enough, way back in 1929, to foresee what was going to happen.
Chapter XIII — Crash!
Lines 1739–1855. ~6,050 words.
Early in September the stock market breaks, recovers to a Times averages high on 19 September even above 3 September, then slips farther; by 4 October Steel, Can, General Electric, and Radio look like bargains to those trained by earlier breaks. Brokers’ loans still mount to a new high about $6.8 billion on 2 October—margin buyers undiminished. Then comes the cascade of mid-October and the panic days: 23 October’s Niagara of liquidation; Thursday the 24th’s forced selling as margins exhaust, the ticker lagging, the roar of panic on the floor; the midday bankers’ pool at Morgan’s—Mitchell, Wiggin, Potter, Prosser, Lamont, Baker—forty millions apiece to keep trading orderly, not to peg prices.
Black Tuesday and the weeks that follow shatter the price structure. Allen’s close: the Big Bull Market had been more than the climax of a business cycle; it had been the climax of a cycle in American mass thinking and mass emotion. With it gone and prosperity going, Americans face an altered world. The psychological climate is changing. The Post-war Decade has come to its close. An era has ended.
Chapter XIV — Aftermath: 1930–31
Lines 1856–1949. ~5,780 words.
Not without long and unhappy protest does the country accept the breakdown of Coolidge–Hoover Prosperity—bitter for a Republican party that had half forgotten the business cycle’s independence of political policies, bitterest for Hoover who had spoken of abolishing poverty. After the market goes over Niagara, the country turns to the President. He promises tax reduction, conferences against wage cuts, public works, and a campaign of reassurance that “conditions” are “fundamentally sound.” Mellon, Lamont, Barnes, and Hoover set dates for recovery; a Little Bull Market in early 1930 regains much ground, then sickens in April as the Coué formula fails against organic disease.
Allen lists diseases: overproduction of capital and goods; artificial commodity prices and pools; silver’s collapse; gold shifts to France and the United States; foreign unrest; the self-generating effect of depression; and the profound psychological reaction from 1929’s exuberance. Wheat crashes despite the Farm Board; industrial production sinks; banks fail including the Bank of the United States in New York; unemployment approaches some six million; apple salesmen stand on corners. Fashion and manners show armistice in the moral revolution—freedom kept, excited sense of smashing taboos gone. Allen ends: the stream of time often doubles on its course, but always makes for itself a new channel.
Appendix — Sources and Obligations
Lines 1950–1991. ~1,410 words.
Allen records principal debts: the Lynds’ Middletown; the Beards’ Rise of American Civilization (including the Washington Conference); William Allen White on Wilson, Harding, and Coolidge; Charles Merz on prohibition and related books; World Almanac, New York Times Index, and Times files. Chapter notes point to Baker on Wilson and the Peace Conference, Chafee on free speech and the Palmer raids, Nystrom on fashion, Lippmann and Krutch on morals and disillusion, Ravage and Bliven on oil and the Ohio Gang, Stuart Chase on prosperity, Silas Bent on ballyhoo, Pasley on Capone, Vanderblue on Florida, Whitney on the Exchange in the panic, and James Truslow Adams on “Presidential Prosperity.” Personal thanks close with Dorothy Penrose Allen. Dated Scarsdale, New York, June 1931.
Index
Lines 1992–4234. ~5,000 words of index entries.
Extensive subject and name index (A & P Gypsies through the alphabet) useful for locating persons, episodes, and themes across the narrative.
Coverage Guide
Mine first as the period’s popular-contemporary spine for 1919–1931. Chapters I–IV support demobilization, League and normalcy politics, Red Scare, and early-1920s cultural convalescence. Chapters V–X are strongest for manners, Harding scandals, Coolidge business culture, ballyhoo, intellectuals, and Prohibition/crime. Chapters XI–XIV are the core speculative cycle: Florida, Bull Market, Crash, and Hoover-era aftermath into 1931. Use the Appendix as a contemporary bibliography map, not as later historiography.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 69–82: Allen’s era definition (11 Nov 1918–13 Nov 1929) and method (public mind, fads, close range).
Lines 83–146: May 1919 baseline day (prices, cars, news, what the Smiths have never heard of).
Lines 277–436: Red Scare arc from Centralia and Palmer to Wall Street explosion.
Lines 499–634: revolution in manners and morals; bobbed hair, youth code, armistice at decade’s end.
Lines 635–856: Daugherty epigraph; Teapot Dome / Continental Trading Company bond chain.
Lines 988–1219: ballyhoo structure; Dayton trial; Lindbergh as age’s hero.
Lines 1432–1738: Florida boom to Bull Market new-era vision.
Lines 1739–1855: September–October 1929 breaks; 24 October; bankers’ pool; era’s end.
Lines 1856–1949: Hoover reassurance campaign; seven “diseases”; 1930–31 social mood.
Lines 1950–1991: Allen’s own source map for cross-checks.

Suggested Future Pages

Notes on Scope

sources/allen-since-yesterday.title: [source] Since Yesterday: The 1930s in America (Allen, 1939/1940)
sources/allen-since-yesterday.content:
Since Yesterday: The 1930s in America
Author: Frederick Lewis Allen
Published: Harper & Brothers, copyright 1939, 1940 (renewed Agnes Rogers Allen 1968)
Working text: Open Road Integrated Media ebook edition, 2015 (ISBN 978-1-5040-1138-9; AA hash 4a89b7cc41832b335854a1f2b02f4745)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/allen-since-yesterday.txt
Extract stats: 4,069 lines · ~113,787 words · 695,982 bytes (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Completeness Assessment
The clean digital EPUB extract is complete for wiki use. After modern Open Road marketing front matter and a machine table of contents, the body runs Preface → Chapters I–XII → Appendix (“Sources and Obligations”) → Index → About the Author. Modern Open Road author-promo trailer and copyright block sit at the tail and are not part of Allen’s 1939 text. Chapter structure matches the imprint contents list (twelve numbered chapters with internal § sections).
Overview
Allen’s sequel to Only Yesterday chronicles the decade from the peak of the Big Bull Market on 3 September 1929 to the British and French declarations of war on Germany on 3 September 1939—ten years to the day. He began serious work late in 1938, had the manuscript three-quarters done by late summer 1939 without knowing how the story would end, and took the European war as the natural close of an era, as the Panic of 1929 had closed the twenties. Overlap with Only Yesterday is deliberate: Chapter I revisits the crest day; Chapter II covers Panic through spring 1931 in abbreviated form so the thirties volume can show the height from which the country fell. Emphasis shifts from twenties fads and follies toward “the enormous economic and political transformation” of Depression and New Deal, though manners, radio, movies, sports, and popular culture remain thickly present.
For this wiki the book is the natural 1930s narrative spine: exit from prosperity, black depression, the Hoover–Roosevelt transfer and bank crisis, New Deal honeymoon and reform battles, Dust Bowl and rural change, 1936 landslide and Roosevelt hatred, cultural left and Hollywood, sit-downs and Court fight and Recession, and the shadow of European war. It pairs with Only Yesterday for 1919–31 atmosphere, and later with Groves, Conant, Elliott Roosevelt, and the Nevins & Hill Ford volumes for wartime science, diplomacy, and industry.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 223–232. ~510 words.
Ever since, in Only Yesterday, Allen tried to tell the story of life in the United States during the nineteen-twenties, he had it in mind to attempt something similar for the thirties. He began work late in 1938 and had the book three-quarters done by late summer 1939 without knowing how the story would end. The outbreak of war in Europe provided an obvious conclusion, ending an era as the Panic of 1929 had ended one. By an odd chance, the British and French declarations of war upon Germany fell ten years to the day after 3 September 1929, already chosen as the first chapter’s subject. Only Yesterday had run from the Armistice of 11 November 1918 to the Panic of October–November 1929, with a concluding chapter into spring 1931 (published December 1931). Some overlapping is necessary so the thirties story can start before the Panic and show the high place from which the country fell in 1929–32; the Panic itself is abbreviated because it was told at length in the earlier book. Selection and emphasis are harder close to the event: the heart of the thirties story is economic and political transformation, and the trivialities essential to the twenties are less significant here. Future events may date his appraisal; he hopes even miscalculations may show what pitfalls one readily fell into in 1939.
Chapter I — Prelude: September 3, 1929
Lines 233–346. ~6,540 words.
Do you remember what you were doing on September 3, 1929? Allen refreshes the recollection by re-living a single day when the Dow-Jones average made its all-time high and the wave of prosperity and speculation of the twenties attained its utmost height before it curled over and crashed. It is a very hot day from Maine to Nebraska. He walks the reader through streets, offices, brokers’ board rooms, newspapers, radio and talkies, sports, and household assumptions—margin speculation by well over a million people, brokers’ loans over eight billion dollars, call money at nine percent, Steel edging toward 261¾, Radio on a split basis looking absurdly high to later eyes but not to most men in the room.
A gallery of “a few people, 1929” and the decade’s furniture of mind closes the prelude: Shirley Temple is a baby less than five months old; the Dionne quintuplets are unborn; and so, for that matter, is the Depression. To be set down as the craziest of prophets one need only tell these men and women that within two months they will witness the greatest financial panic in American history and a prolonged economic crisis.
Chapter II — Exit Prosperity
Lines 347–484. ~6,990 words.
After September 3 the market drops, surges, drops again and does not surge back. At first there is little uneasiness—earlier breaks had been buying opportunities—and brokers’ loans rise to a final peak over eight and a half billion while prognosticators insist nothing is amiss. Foreign funds withdraw after Hatry’s collapse in England; industrial production slips. Then comes the October cascade and panic (abbreviated relative to Only Yesterday), followed by the afterglow of 1930: Hoover’s conferences and public works and “fundamentally sound” assurances, a Little Bull Market, then sickening relapse.
Bathtub gin, crime wave and racketeers, miniature golf and free wheeling, Wickersham’s confused Prohibition report, and Hoover’s political trouble fill the social middle. Allen’s close: traditional economic laws no longer seem to work; the learned are as baffled as anyone; Russia offers an alternative few embrace; the world enters bewilderment, mutual suspicion, and readiness for desperate measures—and the United States, falling from such a pinnacle, will not escape the confusion and dismay of readjustment.
Chapter III — Down, Down, Down
Lines 485–720. ~9,870 words.
June 1931: twenty months after the Panic. Eugenie hats, Wiley Post and Gatty’s Winnie Mae, Starr Faithfull, Cornell in The Barretts of Wimpole Street, The Green Pastures, Pearl Buck’s The Good Earth, and the fading twenties sports heroes set the cultural surface while the economy sinks. The Hoover Moratorium, the RFC as “a dole for corporations,” “Oh, Yeah?” skepticism, black depression statistics, freight-car hoppers too numerous for railroad police, servants discharged, golf clubs resigned, lunch counters instead of clubs—Allen inventories the descent.
The Lindbergh kidnap case becomes the decade’s absorbing crime drama. Stock tables from September 1929 highs through November 1929 panic lows to 1932 bottoms (Telephone, GE, Motors, Central, Radio, Steel) close the chapter: thus spoke the sensitive barometer; thus had departed the hopes of yesteryear. Was there no savior anywhere in sight?
Chapter IV — A Change of Government
Lines 721–882. ~8,120 words.
It begins to look as if saving the United States will fall into Franklin D. Roosevelt’s willing hands. The Republicans’ dull June 1932 convention renominates Hoover because it must. Democrats at Chicago—still reeling from a local bank panic—see Roosevelt’s long lead managed by Jim Farley (green-ink mass correspondence, six stenographers) and Louis Howe (asthmatic chief-of-staff on a Madison Avenue day bed). Nomination, the flight to Chicago, the platform, and the campaign against a doomed Hoover follow.
Bonus Army, rebellion and ferment, Technocracy’s brief national craze (Scott, Veblen, Soddy, energy survey, then December 1932 saturation), and the final banking collapse bring the curtain down. On the morning of 4 March 1933 a worn Hoover is told the banking system has stopped: “We are at the end of our string… There is nothing more we can do.” Allen’s judgment: for all Hoover’s asperities and political ineptitudes he had been a resourceful soldier of a doomed order and deserved no such personal humiliation—but the curtain was coming down.
Chapter V — New Deal Honeymoon
Lines 883–1064. ~8,050 words.
Saturday, 4 March 1933. Turn on the radio. Banks are shut; people read typewritten notices and walk away wondering how far five or ten dollars will go. The inaugural—“the only thing we have to fear is fear itself”—is what a huddled country wants to hear. Allen narrates the rush: bank holiday and Emergency Banking Act, fireside chat, beer and the road to Repeal, CCC, AAA, TVA, securities regulation, abandonment of gold, NRA and the Blue Eagle, public works, and the President’s intent to raise prices so debtors repay in dollars of the kind they borrowed (later progressive devaluation toward 59.06 cents gold).
Spring 1933 brings a shot-in-the-arm jump in prices, inventories, stocks, and the Reserve Board’s production index. All roads lead to Washington; the Hundred Days feel like multiple deals at once. Though the market looks ragged by late summer and indices slip from July’s peak, the prevailing public mood matches Disney’s three little pigs: America has learned to sing “Who’s Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?”
Chapter VI — A Change of Climate
Lines 1065–1234. ~10,170 words.
Social change is continuous, yet the climate alters. Most contrasts between twenties and thirties manners do not become clearly marked until about 1933—New Deal and Repeal—as if Americans had walked backward into Depression holding twenties customs, then turned face-forward into the new decade. The post-war revolution in manners (knee-length skirts, hip flasks, speakeasies, petting, Freudian talk, anti-Puritan defiance) cools into something less frantic; marriage and morals, fashion’s longer line, Repeal and the persistence of bootleg stills and rum-runners, sports and gambling (bingo, slot machines, Bank Night, softball), churches, and social-salvationist politics structure the chapter.
Fortune and revenue data suggest most Americans are glad Prohibition ended even while illicit liquor remains large. Underneath runs fear: old-age pensions, social security, the wish for rock-firm certainty. Except during the brief honeymoon when hope rode high, an undercurrent of fear persists—they want security under their feet and do not have it.
Chapter VII — Reform—and Recovery?
Lines 1235–1442. ~10,320 words.
The honeymoon ends in late 1933 not abruptly but in annoyances and discords. Industrial production’s spring leap from 59 to 100 collapses by November to 72—two-thirds of the gain lost while NRA accumulates momentum. Ford refuses the auto code; Hearst brands NRA “No Recovery Allowed.” Codes creak; price-fixing and little-business complaints multiply. Relief expands: CWA, then WPA with theatres, orchestras, murals; transient camps; NYA; surplus commodities; PWA and CCC as related giant works.
Dillinger, G-Men, and Dewey supply crime melodrama; Huey Long, Coughlin, Townsend, and other voices of discontent press from the flanks. The Supreme Court begins saying no to central New Deal statutes. Allen closes on the President’s long-horizon talk of what the people must decide in five or ten years—without yet a concrete path beyond eventual constitutional reckoning.
Chapter VIII — When the Farms Blew Away
Lines 1443–1542. ~5,770 words.
Armistice Day 1933: the first great dust storm sweeps South Dakota. Allen quotes R. D. Lusk’s Saturday Evening Post account of the Karnstrum farm in Beadle County—opaque black noon, handkerchiefs over faces, coughing black, fences and machinery buried—as type for storms from the Texas Panhandle to the Canadian border over the next two years. Black blizzards, ruined grasslands, and migrant tracks structure the disaster narrative.
Tenant mobility, “suitcase farmers,” tractors and larger-scale commercial farming, floods and dams, and the sense of a mature America that can no longer plunder and move on close the chapter. Durable development west of the Plains will require more disciplined pioneering than the old—even while the dispossessed still wander homeless through the land.
Chapter IX — The Voice with the Smile Wins
Lines 1543–1717. ~10,790 words.
Winter 1935–36 atmosphere: “The Music Goes ’Round and ’Round,” Major Bowes, Astaire and Rogers, Mr. Deeds, Shirley Temple, Life with Father, best sellers from It Can’t Happen Here toward Santayana’s The Last Puritan. Allen maps the changed world of 1936: pump-priming that works up to a point, streamlined trains and trailers, and the hatred of Roosevelt among eastern business and commuting classes—Mark Sullivan, club-car stories, “delusions of grandeur—He thinks He’s Franklin D. Roosevelt”—most intense on the Atlantic seaboard until exhaustion softens it around 1938.
Landon as “the Kansas Coolidge,” the campaign, and the landslide (“the voice with the smile wins”) return Roosevelt with something like a blank check. A coda on Edward VIII’s abdication broadcast lets Americans turn back to what their own chief of state will write upon that check.
Chapter X — With Pen and Camera Through Darkest America
Lines 1718–1897. ~9,450 words.
A 1925 New York cocktail party of writers and artists would have screamed over Martinis for sex freedom, fewer laws, scorn of Babbitts and business, debunking of Victorian heroes, and preference for Europe. A similar 1935 gathering has inverted the conversation: social salvation, economic justice, and American materials dominate; Queen Victoria and Longfellow return to favor via Hayes and Van Wyck Brooks. Tobacco Road, best sellers, proletarian and fellow-traveler writing, the Communist appeal and its limits, candid-camera documentary impulse, Benny Goodman and swing’s jitterbug vocabulary beside renewed Bach, censorship fights (“You Can’t Say That”), and Hollywood’s heaven of glamour and box office fill the tour.
Allen’s lesson from eighty-five million movie admissions: America is not—or not yet—proletarian-minded. Citizens will organize and use government to redress wrongs, yet still keep room for an Horatio Alger paradise where valour and glamour rise and live happily ever after.
Chapter XI — Friction and Recession
Lines 1898–2098. ~10,060 words.
In cold rain before the Capitol, Roosevelt takes the oath for a second term and speaks of one-third of a nation ill-housed, ill-clad, ill-nourished—the test of progress whether enough is provided for those who have too little. Listeners wait for something more specific. Sit-downs and the CIO, Taylor, Lewis, and Girdler, the Supreme Court battle (Wheeler’s Democratic opposition, Hughes’s letter, the Court’s spring 1937 prudence upholding railway labor, farm mortgage, minimum wages, Wagner Act), 1937 montage, and the sharp Recession follow.
By late 1937–38 prestige in Congress is weakened, economic policies look wanting, unemployment remains hateful. Was the New Deal played out? Perhaps—but if so the fact is being obscured by storm clouds rolling in from Europe that will make citizens look on country and government with new eyes.
Chapter XII — The Shadow of War
Lines 2099–2272. ~10,110 words.
Studio Nine: H. V. Kaltenborn at a CBS microphone through the September 1938 Czech crisis, millions listening while strapless evening dresses and local politics pause. “We take you now to Prague” becomes the sound of a world closing in. Isolation versus intervention, neutrality legislation, arms embargo debates, the Martian panic of Welles’s War of the Worlds beside real German advances, New York World’s Fair’s “World of Tomorrow,” a royal visit, and a summer lull structure the approach.
Liberals who once laughed at red scares now fear Nazi propaganda and German–Latin American trade; dinner tables talk of planes from South American bases and the Panama Canal. Then Chamberlain’s tired radio voice from London: no German undertaking to withdraw from Poland—this country is at war with Germany. With those sentences, spoken so quietly thousands of miles away, an era ends for America and another begins.
Appendix — Sources and Obligations
Lines 2273–2314. ~2,420 words.
Allen again places the Lynds first—Middletown in Transition (1937) as indispensable as Middletown had been for the twenties. For Hoover chapters: Myers and Newton’s documented narrative; Joslin’s Hoover Off the Record. For the New Deal: Roosevelt’s Public Papers and Addresses; the Beards’ America in Midpassage; Moley’s After Seven Years. Chapter notes point to Flynn and Mitchell on NRA and Johnson, Bromley and Britten and Fortune on youth, Harrison and Laine after Repeal, Lubell on nickels and slots, and many magazine pieces on sports, crime, and culture. Personal thanks close with Agnes Rogers Allen. Dated New York City, 10 November 1939.
Index
Lines 2315–~4026. Extensive subject and name index (AAA through the alphabet) for locating agencies, persons, and themes across the narrative.
Coverage Guide
Mine first as the period’s popular-contemporary spine for 1929–1939. Chapters I–III support the crash-to-trough economic and social descent and Hoover-era atmosphere. Chapters IV–V are strongest for the 1932–33 transfer, bank crisis, and Hundred Days. Chapters VI–X carry manners, reform battles, Dust Bowl, 1936 politics, and culture. Chapters XI–XII are core for labor/Court/Recession and the approach of war through 3 September 1939. Use the Appendix as a contemporary bibliography map. Panic mechanics remain fuller in Only Yesterday Chapter XIII.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 223–232: decade definition (3 Sept 1929–3 Sept 1939) and method (economics/politics over twenties trivia).
Lines 233–346: crest-day baseline (prices, brokers’ loans, what 1929 cannot imagine).
Lines 347–484: exit from prosperity; Wickersham; bewilderment close.
Lines 485–720: 1931–32 descent; Lindbergh case; 1929–32 stock table.
Lines 721–882: Farley/Howe machine; Technocracy; Hoover’s “end of our string.”
Lines 883–1064: inauguration radio scene; Hundred Days; “Big Bad Wolf.”
Lines 1065–1234: 1933 as climate turn; Repeal and residual bootleg; security-fear undercurrent.
Lines 1443–1542: Armistice Day 1933 dust storm; suitcase farmers; mature America.
Lines 1543–1717: Roosevelt hatred geography; 1936 landslide.
Lines 1718–1897: 1925 vs 1935 intellectuals; swing; Hollywood vs proletarian mind.
Lines 1898–2098: second inaugural; sit-downs; Court fight; Recession.
Lines 2099–2272: Kaltenborn/Munich; isolation debate; Chamberlain 3 Sept 1939 close.
Lines 2273–2314: Allen’s source map for cross-checks.

Suggested Future Pages

Great Depression (United States) — event/concept cluster from Panic through 1932–33 trough.
New Deal Honeymoon and Hundred Days — event page on March–June 1933 legislation and mood.
Dust Bowl — event page on Plains storms, migration, and soil politics.
Roosevelt Coalition and 1936 Landslide — event/concept page including anti-Roosevelt hatred.
Sit-Down Strikes and the CIO — event page (1936–37).
Supreme Court Fight (1937) — event page on packing plan, Hughes letter, and judicial shift.
American Isolation and the Approach of War (1935–39) — concept/event page through 3 Sept 1939.
Repeal and Post-Prohibition Drinking — concept page linking XXI Amendment, residual bootleg, and manners.

Related Sources

Only Yesterday — companion informal history of the 1920s and Panic (already in wiki).
Nevins & Hill Ford volumes (expansion; decline and rebirth) — industrial continuity across the same decades (to be added).
Groves, Now It Can Be Told; Conant, Tuxedo Park; Elliott Roosevelt, As He Saw It — wartime science and diplomacy bridge beyond Allen’s 1939 close (to be added).

Notes on Scope
Near-contemporary informal history (preface dated 10 November 1939), not archival monograph. Exceptionally strong on sequence of public mood from crash through New Deal to war’s edge; individual statute, market, and diplomatic details should be cross-checked against specialized sources when building detailed entity or event pages. Foreign affairs thicken only in the final chapter by design; the European crisis is seen primarily as it registers on American radio, opinion, and neutrality politics.

sources/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hug.title: [source] Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness (Barlett & Steele, 1979)
sources/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hug.content:
Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness
Authors: Donald L. Barlett and James B. Steele
Published: 1979 (W. W. Norton & Company; originally Empire: The Life, Legend, and Madness of Howard Hughes; Norton paperback reissue 2004 as Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash e52a0b470771df3e9e8152f929451816)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hughes.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 36,061 lines · ~315,387 words · 1,925,679 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This is the home wiki (United States 1920–45) source page; the same book will also be copied to United States 1946-89. Mine first for THIS wiki from Chs. 1–5: early years and Hughes Tool inheritance, Hollywood, 1930s aviation heroics, World War II contracts / flying boat / “Hate Hughes Club,” and the XF-11 crash plus 1947 Senate investigation as the period hinge. Period-gate to 1946–89: Chs. 6–25 (RKO, Culver City revolt, Mormon aides, TWA jets, Las Vegas, Air West, Watergate/Hughesgate, CIA Project Jennifer/Glomar, death/estate). Ch. 1 family/Hughes Tool founding (~1908–09 rock bit) is background only — NOT sufficient to copy the whole book into United States 1866–1919.
Overview
Empire (1979; Norton 2004 reissue Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness) is Barlett and Steele’s four-year investigative biography of Howard Robard Hughes, Jr. (1905–1976), built from more than a quarter-million pages of scattered government, corporate, and court records rather than Hughes-company cooperation. The authors treat Hughes as a figure whose public legend—record aviator, Hollywood producer, defense contractor, reclusive billionaire—was sustained by secrecy, public relations, and decades of distorted repetition. The narrative runs from colonial Hughes family roots and Howard Hughes Sr.’s rock-bit invention through young Howard’s inheritance fight, Hollywood films (Hell’s Angels, Scarface), speed records and the 1938 around-the-world flight, wartime plywood bomber and flying-boat programs, the 1947 Brewster Senate hearings, and then postwar RKO, Hughes Aircraft’s electronics boom, TWA jet financing, breakdown and seclusion, Las Vegas empire-building, political influence, Watergate-era money trails, the Romaine Street burglary, CIA’s Glomar Explorer, death in Acapulco, and the Mormon-will fortune battle.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers Hughes’s rise through inheritance, Hollywood, aviation fame, and wartime contracting to the 1946–47 Senate circus—core material beside defense-industry and Hollywood sources. Period-gate hard after Ch. 5 except where Ch. 5’s 1947 hearings complete stories already under way in the war years.
EPUB structure: Also-by list; title/copyright (1979 Empire / 2004 Norton reissue); Contents; Preface; Acknowledgments; Prologue; Chapters 1–25; Epilogue; Chronology; Appendices; Sources; Notes.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / TOC
Lines 1–315. Also-by Barlett/Steele titles; Norton 2004 reissue copyright and original 1979 Empire title; Library of Congress data; full Contents listing Preface through Notes with chapter subheads (Family, Rock Eater, Hate Hughes Club, Project Jennifer, etc.).
Preface
Lines 316–448. Frames Hughes as the most misunderstood figure of his era; recounts 1976 death fingerprint verification for Treasury/FBI; contrasts public legend with documented losses and secrecy; describes four years of research across fifty cities, fifty government offices, and a fifty-thousand-page document collection—the largest outside the Hughes organization.
Acknowledgments
Lines 449–538. Credits anonymous Hughes employees and associates, dozens of libraries and newspaper archives, court clerks, and research collaborators who supplied access to the scattered record on which the biography rests.
Prologue — Death in Mexico
Lines 539–876. Opens on Hughes’s final hours at the Acapulco Princess Hotel in April 1976—Waldron pouring water, erratic breathing, heart stopping at 1:27 P.M.—then flashes back through the reclusive endgame that preceded his last flight home to Texas.
Chapter 1 — The Early Years
Lines 877–2456. Traces the Hughes clan from colonial Virginia through Missouri law and Iowa respectability; Howard Hughes Sr.’s Spindletop-era oil-field work and 1909 two-cone rock-bit patent founding Hughes Tool; Allene Gano’s courtship and Houston life; young Howard’s mother-dominated childhood; parents’ deaths; and the teenage fight with relatives and executives for control of the tool company and his inheritance.
Chapter 2 — Hollywood
Lines 2457–3141. Hughes and Ella Rice move to Los Angeles in 1925; failed Swell Hogan and modest Everybody’s Acting; Caddo Film Company and Noah Dietrich as administrator; obsessive production of Hell’s Angels with real aerial combat footage; and the censorship battles over Scarface that established Hughes as a producer willing to fight the Hays Office.
Chapter 3 — Hero
Lines 3142–4549. Aviation supplants movies after 1932; Hughes streamlines the H-1 racer at Lockheed, founds Hughes Aircraft as a tool-company division, sets speed records, and in 1938 completes the around-the-world flight in a Lockheed 14—cementing the Lindbergh-era hero image while rarely visiting Houston kin again.
Chapter 4 — The War Years
Lines 4550–6051. Hughes seeks Wright Field contracts against the perceived “Hate Hughes Club”; wins wartime bomber and flying-boat programs using duramold plywood construction; navigates strange procurement bedfellows and cost overruns; and pushes the giant Hercules flying boat and XF-11 reconnaissance prototype even as management chaos grows at Culver City.
Chapter 5 — The Senate Investigation
Lines 6052–7328. After Chuck Perelle’s reforms fail against Hughes’s interference, the July 1946 XF-11 crash in Beverly Hills triggers Senator Owen Brewster’s hearings; Hughes testifies in Washington while the Spruce Goose remains unfinished; the committee’s political theater culminates in Hughes flying the Hercules at Long Beach in November 1947—the hinge between wartime contracting and postwar empire.
Chapter 6 — Movies, Missiles, and Communists
Lines 7329–8556. Post-hearing staff reorganization brings Frank Gay to Romaine Street; Hughes buys RKO in 1948 and runs it from seclusion; anti-Communist crusading and blacklist politics mesh with his need to purge troublesome stockholders and reshape the studio.
Chapter 7 — Revolt at Culver City
Lines 8557–9569. Hughes Aircraft’s 1950s electronics and Falcon-missile boom outgrows Culver City management; Tucson plant tax controversy; a 1953 executive revolt over charity fronts, political insurance, and Hughes’s remote control of a now-massive defense contractor.
Chapter 8 — Seeds of Disaster
Lines 9570–10441. Mormon aides rise in the inner circle; Hughes commits to a $400-million TWA jet fleet order without clear financing; Rockefeller and Zeckendorf are drawn into a secret sale that never closes—planting the seeds of the late-1950s financial crisis.
Chapter 9 — Breakdown
Lines 10442–11671. Secret 1957 Tonopah marriage to Jean Peters; deepening isolation, psychiatric crisis, and institutionalization rumors; showdown with Noah Dietrich and Wall Street lenders over TWA jet commitments and Hughes Tool collateral.
Chapter 10 — Retreat
Lines 11672–12984. December 1960 voting-trust agreement strips Hughes of TWA control; flight to Rancho Santa Fe with germ-phobia rituals; manhunt when he vanishes from the Beverly Hills Hotel; lenders take the airline while Hughes retreats from public business.
Chapter 11 — A New Career
Lines 12985–13954. Four-and-a-half-year seclusion ends with a train move to Boston’s Ritz-Carlton; medical-institute cover stories; transition planning through Bob Maheu toward a Nevada relocation and a new phase of hidden operations.
Chapter 12 — Lord of the Desert
Lines 13955–14963. 1967 Desert Inn purchase launches the Las Vegas casino-buying spree; public-relations blitz and masterplan for Strip dominance; Washington warnings about monopoly and hidden ownership as Hughes becomes “lord of the desert.”
Chapter 13 — Out of Control
Lines 14964–16515. Rival Kirk Kerkorian builds the International Hotel; Hughes lieutenants feud; conspiracy fears, press leaks, and the Boxcar nuclear-test shelter scheme expose how little Hughes actually controls his Nevada empire.
Chapter 14 — The $90-Million Mistake
Lines 16516–17308. Vietnam-era helicopter contract mispricing costs Hughes a fifth of his fortune; lobbying Lyndon Johnson; the “buy-in” and renegotiation fights that typify his postwar defense-industrial missteps.
Chapter 15 — The Billion-Dollar Deal
Lines 17309–18086. Hughes insists on “billionaire” press identity while secretly strapped; cornering TWA stock then selling out to become liquid—turning airline equity into cash for Las Vegas and Summa operations.
Chapter 16 — The Hijacking of Air West
Lines 18087–18918. 1970 hostile takeover of regional carrier Air West (Bonanza/Pacific/West Coast merger); squeeze tactics, overbooked holiday flights, and CAB/Washington rubber-stamping that Maheu and Raymond Cook botch—another Hughes airline adventure ending in federal scrutiny.
Chapter 17 — Gold Fever
Lines 18919–20196. 1967–68 precious-metals panic; Hughes buys hundreds of Nevada mining claims through Maheu; prospector parades, sting operations, and mining-stock swindles tied to the Hughes name and President’s brother subplot.
Chapter 18 — Turning Point
Lines 20197–21456. Jean Peters’s 1970 divorce announcement; Hughes ousted from effective control by Bill Gay, Chester Davis, and Nadine Henley; Summa Corporation hands change while Hughes remains a figurehead in exile.
Chapter 19 — The Political Connection
Lines 21457–22383. Two decades of IRS, CAB, Interior, and Pentagon favors; secret contributions and “I can buy any man” bravado; political machine that runs on the Hughes name regardless of who actually pulls levers.
Chapter 20 — Life in Exile
Lines 22384–23649. Clifford Irving hoax autobiography of 1971–72; Bahamas move; $350-million Howard Hughes Medical Institute giveaway; Hughes declared invalid as aides wall him off from the world.
Chapter 21 — Watergate
Lines 23650–24690. December 1973 flight to Freeport on Khashoggi’s plane; Hughes–Nixon money threads, Bebe Rebozo, and Larry O’Brien as “well-wired source”—connecting the reclusive billionaire to the scandal consuming Washington.
Chapter 22 — Hughesgate
Lines 24691–25540. June 1974 Romaine Street (“the Bastille”) burglary of Hughes archives; million-dollar ransom for stolen files linking Project Jennifer, Watergate, and Las Vegas operations.
Chapter 23 — The CIA’s Best-Kept Secret
Lines 25541–26252. Los Angeles Times leak of Hughes–CIA contract to raise Soviet submarine K-129; Glomar Explorer cover story; Mell Stewart problem and grand-jury aftermath of the stolen Romaine documents.
Chapter 24 — The Last Year
Lines 26253–27715. Hughes’s seventieth year contrasts profitable Hughes Aircraft with loss-ridden Summa; legacy reckoning; last fights among aides; Candyman and missing-will anxieties before the final move to Mexico.
Chapter 25 — The Fight for the Fortune
Lines 27716–29563. April 1976 body flown Houston to Methodist Hospital; autopsy and identity confirmation; cover-up of neglect; Mormon will surfaced in Las Vegas; fallout among heirs, executives, and courts over a billion-dollar estate.
Epilogue — A Summing Up
Lines 29564–30316. Argues Hughes’s legend outran his business acumen—passbook savings would have beat his empire-building; fame and control of image, not Midas touch, drove movies, aviation, and seclusion; public relations sustained the superman myth after repeated corporate failures.
Notes
Lines 30317–36061. Endnotes keyed to chapters; documentary citations from FBI, CIA, SEC, CAB, congressional hearings, court records, and newspaper archives supporting the narrative.
Coverage Guide
Early years, Tool Co., inheritance (wiki core — background-heavy)
Ch. 1: Hughes family, rock-bit invention, parents’ deaths, fight for company control—essential for Howard’s 1920s entry into wealth and autonomy; Sr.’s ~1908–09 founding is background, not 1866–1919 wiki material on its own.
Hollywood and celebrity culture (wiki core)
Ch. 2: Hell’s Angels, Scarface, Caddo/Dietrich administration, censorship fights—1925–32 Hollywood and Hughes’s producer persona.
Aviation records and Hughes Aircraft origins (wiki core)
Ch. 3: H-1 racer, speed records, 1938 around-the-world flight, founding of Hughes Aircraft—1930s hero narrative and defense-industry roots.
World War II contracting and flying boat (wiki core)
Ch. 4: Wright Field/Hate Hughes Club, duramold bomber, Hercules flying boat, XF-11 program—wartime procurement, cost overrun, and Culver City chaos.
1946–47 Senate hinge (wiki core / period close)
Ch. 5: XF-11 crash, Brewster committee, Spruce Goose flight—natural close for this wiki; treat Ch. 6 opening only as forward pointer unless completing a 1947 thread.
RKO through TWA crisis (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 6–10: studio takeover, aircraft revolt, Mormon aides, jet order, TWA voting trust—postwar empire and breakdown; full mining in United States 1946–89.
Las Vegas, airlines, mining, political machine (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 11–19: Boston exile, Desert Inn, Kerkorian rivalry, helicopters, TWA sale, Air West, gold claims, 1970 ouster, Washington influence.
Exile, Watergate, CIA, death, estate (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 20–25 plus Epilogue: Irving hoax, Nixon money, Romaine burglary, Glomar Explorer, 1976 death, will fight, summing-up on legend vs. losses.

sources/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.title: [source] American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (Bird and Sherwin, 2005/2006)
sources/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.content:
American Prometheus
Authors: Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin
Published: 2005 (Knopf); First Vintage Books edition, May 2006
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 422cbf640ccecea946b652ad85b730c8)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 35,044 lines · ~314,407 words · 1,953,744 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Parts One–Three (and the wartime close of Part Three) cover Oppenheimer’s Harvard–Göttingen–Berkeley formation, Popular Front / New Deal left politics, the Chevalier affair, Los Alamos directorship, Trinity, and the 1945 use of the bombs—core material beside Now It Can Be Told and Tuxedo Park. Mine first from Chs. 2–22 (roughly 1922–1945). Preface, Prologue, Parts Four–Five, and the Epilogue (AEC hearing, Super fight, St. John exile, family coda) remain primarily for the 1946–89 wiki; use them only as brief forward pointers when completing a wartime story.
Overview
American Prometheus is Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin’s biography of J. Robert Oppenheimer (1904–1967): theoretical physicist, builder of the Berkeley theoretical school, scientific director of Los Alamos, postwar government adviser and Institute for Advanced Study director, and the most prominent scientist destroyed by the McCarthy-era security system. Bird and Sherwin frame his life as triumph (quantum physics, wartime leadership, public intellectual stature) and tragedy (left associations, Chevalier episode, hydrogen-bomb opposition, Lewis Strauss’s vendetta, and the 1954 AEC hearing).
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book is a Manhattan Project and interwar-science spine: Harvard and European training into the Berkeley school, 1930s left politics and personal entanglements that later haunted security files, Coordinator of Rapid Rupture into Los Alamos, Bohr’s open-world vision, Interim Committee debates, Trinity, and Hiroshima/Nagasaki. Parts Four–Five (post-1945 AEC politics and 1954 hearing) are retained for continuity only; period-gate hard after 1945 except where needed to finish the wartime arc.
EPUB structure: Table of Contents; Title / Dedication / Praise; Preface; Prologue; Parts One–Five with Chapters One–Forty; Epilogue; Author’s Note and Acknowledgments (Sherwin); Notes; Bibliography; Illustration Credits; About the Authors / Also by; Vintage copyright block.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–208. TOC; title/dedication/praise; Knopf/Vintage front matter.
Preface
Lines 209–407. Opens on December 1953: Strauss hands Oppenheimer the AEC charges letter; the career-and-self-worth crisis that structures the biography’s tragic arc.
Prologue
Lines 408–551. Princeton funeral, 25 February 1967: six hundred mourners; “Oppie” as teacher, “father” of the bomb, national hero, then fallen figure—“Damn it, I happen to love this country.”
PART ONE
Lines 552–555. Part divider opening youth and scientific formation (Chs. 1–7).
Chapter One — “He Received Every New Idea as Perfectly Beautiful”
Lines 556–1427. Early-century science revolution; Oppenheimer childhood as “unctuous, repulsively good little boy”; Ethical Culture / New York Jewish milieu and first intellectual formation.
Chapter Two — “His Separate Prison”
Lines 1428–1933. Harvard 1922 enrollment; Standish Hall; extreme physique and social isolation; early adult “separate prison” temperament.
Chapter Three — “I Am Having a Pretty Bad Time”
Lines 1934–2580. Post-Harvard emotional crisis (1926 letter); Cambridge difficulties and near-disastrous psychological strain after the protective undergraduate shield falls away.
Chapter Four — “I Find the Work Hard, Thank God, & Almost Pleasant”
Lines 2581–3119. Move to Göttingen (1926); quantum mecca of Lower Saxony; hard, almost pleasant work and scientific maturation under Born’s circle.
Chapter Five — “I Am Oppenheimer”
Lines 3120–3649. End of Göttingen year; homesickness and American chauvinism (New Mexico deserts); self-assertion as Oppenheimer among European peers (Rabi contrast).
Chapter Six — “Oppie”
Lines 3650–4260. Zurich productivity; Perro Caliente rhythm—intense work then New Mexico horseback renewal; 1931 letter on a restless, uncompromising world.
Chapter Seven — “The Nim Nim Boys”
Lines 4261–4887. Parents’ 1930 Pasadena visit; Depression-era family fortune after Julius’s 1928 retirement; Berkeley/Caltech “Nim Nim Boys” circle and politics vs. truth/beauty question.
PART TWO
Lines 4888–4891. Part divider: politics, love, and wartime recruitment (Chs. 8–14).
Chapter Eight — “In 1936 My Interests Began to Change”
Lines 4892–5633. Meeting Jean Tatlock (spring 1936); courtship; political awakening tied to personal life (Serber: Jean as truest love).
Chapter Nine — “[Frank] Clipped It Out and Sent It In”
Lines 5634–6290. Julius’s death (20 Sept 1937); Chevalier friendship and ambiguous Communist Party membership claims; brother Frank’s Party card episode.
Chapter Ten — “More and More Surely”
Lines 6291–6711. Nazi–Soviet pact (24 Aug 1939) and Poland invasion; Weisskopf on a decisive weekend turning Oppenheimer away from the Party; letter to Willie Fowler.
Chapter Eleven — “I’m Going to Marry a Friend of Yours, Steve”
Lines 6712–7294. Break with Tatlock; engagement near-misses; courtship and marriage path to Kitty (Serber on her advancing Robert’s career).
Chapter Twelve — “We Were Pulling the New Deal to the Left”
Lines 7295–7869. Popular Front / New Deal left organizing; teachers’ union and related Bay Area political work pulling reform leftward.
Chapter Thirteen — “The Coordinator of Rapid Rupture”
Lines 7870–8532. Early fission program role—“Coordinator of Rapid Rupture”; recruitment into the wartime bomb project apparatus.
Chapter Fourteen — “The Chevalier Affair”
Lines 8533–8811. Haakon Chevalier approach and the security episode that will haunt every later clearance fight.
PART THREE
Lines 8812–8815. Part divider: Los Alamos and the gadget (Chs. 15–22).
Chapter Fifteen — “He’d Become Very Patriotic”
Lines 8816–9615. Wartime patriotism and lab leadership persona; building the Los Alamos community.
Chapter Sixteen — “Too Much Secrecy”
Lines 9616–10178. Secrecy regime, compartmentation tensions, and scientific communication under military control.
Chapter Seventeen — “Oppenheimer Is Telling the Truth …”
Lines 10179–10767. Security interrogations and truthfulness contests inside the project’s clearance culture.
Chapter Eighteen — “Suicide, Motive Unknown”
Lines 10768–11025. Jean Tatlock’s death and its personal/security repercussions.
Chapter Nineteen — “Would You Like to Adopt Her?”
Lines 11026–11589. Family life at Los Alamos; children and domestic strain under wartime secrecy.
Chapter Twenty — “Bohr Was God, and Oppie Was His Prophet”
Lines 11590–11964. Niels Bohr’s visits; internationalist open-world vision versus military secrecy; Oppie as Bohr’s prophet.
Chapter Twenty-one — “The Impact of the Gadget on Civilization”
Lines 11965–12527. Interim Committee / target and use debates; scientists’ reckoning with civilization-scale effects.
Chapter Twenty-two — “Now We’re All Sons-of-Bitches”
Lines 12528–13442. Trinity test; Bainbridge’s line; path to Hiroshima and Nagasaki use.
PART FOUR
Lines 13443–13446. Part divider: postwar fame, AEC politics, and approaching doom (Chs. 23–33).
Chapter Twenty-three — “Those Poor Little People”
Lines 13447–13900. Immediate Hiroshima aftermath; Oppenheimer’s reaction to Japanese victims and public celebrity.
Chapter Twenty-four — “I Feel I Have Blood on My Hands”
Lines 13901–14468. Truman encounter and blood-on-hands remark; early postwar guilt and policy voice.
Chapter Twenty-five — “People Could Destroy New York”
Lines 14469–15143. International control, Acheson–Lilienthal lineage, and urban-destruction warnings in the new nuclear order.
Chapter Twenty-six — “Oppie Had a Rash and Is Now Immune”
Lines 15144–15919. Security clearance scrapes and the sense (among allies) that he had survived and was “immune”—a false calm.
Chapter Twenty-seven — “An Intellectual Hotel”
Lines 15920–16867. Directorship of the Institute for Advanced Study; Princeton as intellectual hotel and public platform.
Chapter Twenty-eight — “He Couldn’t Understand Why He Did It”
Lines 16868–17544. Personal contradictions, relationships, and self-sabotaging episodes as political enemies gather.
Chapter Twenty-nine — “I Am Sure That Is Why She Threw Things at Him”
Lines 17545–17985. Kitty, domestic turbulence, and the private costs of public pressure (FBI awareness, wiretap lore).
Chapter Thirty — “He Never Let On What His Opinion Was”
Lines 17986–18659. GAC / Super debates; studied ambiguity and the political price of opposing the hydrogen bomb.
Chapter Thirty-one — “Dark Words About Oppie”
Lines 18660–19662. Campaign of dark words from Strauss, Teller circle, and security bureaucrats; Kennan as intellectual ally after the Super fight.
Chapter Thirty-two — “Scientist X”
Lines 19663–19975. FBI/HUAC/Justice closing in (1950); Weinberg estrangement; “Scientist X” spy-hunt shadow over Oppenheimer.
Chapter Thirty-three — “The Beast in the Jungle”
Lines 19976–21007. Henry James story as personal omen; 1953 “two scorpions in a bottle” image; premonition before Strauss’s letter.
PART FIVE
Lines 21008–21011. Part divider: the 1954 inquisition and after (Chs. 34–40).
Chapter Thirty-four — “It Looks Pretty Bad, Doesn’t It?”
Lines 21012–21493. Refusal to resign; Nichols/Green charges machinery; Kafka Trial epigraph for the American inquisition.
Chapter Thirty-five — “I Fear That This Whole Thing Is a Piece of Idiocy”
Lines 21494–22721. Gray Board proceedings skewed from the outset; Strauss’s fear of defection/passport and McCarthy interference.
Chapter Thirty-six — “A Manifestation of Hysteria”
Lines 22722–23414. Defense witnesses (Bethe, Kennan, McCloy, Bush, Conant, et al.); McCloy to Eisenhower on inquiring into a Newton or Galileo.
Chapter Thirty-seven — “A Black Mark on the Escutcheon of Our Country”
Lines 23415–23970. Waiting for Gray Board judgment; Lilienthal’s verdict on public-service wisdom; FBI wiretaps of Oppenheimer’s despair.
Chapter Thirty-eight — “I Can Still Feel the Warm Blood on My Hands”
Lines 23971–24612. Aftermath letters; Rabi: the hearing achieved opponents’ aim—it destroyed him; public and private wreckage.
Chapter Thirty-nine — “It Was Really Like a Never-Never-Land”
Lines 24613–24979. St. John exile from 1954; separate prison renewed in Virgin Islands beauty; Hiilivirta on his humility.
Chapter Forty — “It Should Have Been Done the Day After Trinity”
Lines 24980–25647. Partial rehabilitation under Kennedy/Johnson; Fermi Award (Dec 1963) and Oppenheimer’s charity/courage remark to LBJ.
Epilogue — “There’s Only One Robert”
Lines 25648–25761. Kitty and Serber; Kitty’s death (1972); Frank’s Exploratorium; Peter in New Mexico; Toni’s clearance denial, depression, and 1977 suicide; Oppenheimer Beach.
Author’s Note and Acknowledgments
Lines 25762–26072. Sherwin’s “Long Ride with Oppie” (1979 Perro Caliente research horseback start); twenty-five-year project; Bird partnership; research thanks.
Notes
Lines 26073–33181. Abbreviations (AEC, AIP, DDEL, etc.) and dense chapter notes; Bird/Sherwin collection disposition note.
Bibliography
Lines 33182–34282. Secondary and primary bibliography.
Illustration Credits / About the Authors / Copyright
Lines 34283–35044. Photo credits; author bios; Also by; First Vintage edition May 2006; © 2005 Bird and Sherwin; LC cataloging; eISBN 978-0-307-42473-0.
Coverage Guide
Formation and Berkeley school (wiki core, 1920s–early 1930s)
Chs. 1–7: childhood frame, Harvard 1922, Cambridge crisis, Göttingen, Caltech/Berkeley “Oppie” and Perro Caliente—core for interwar American physics pages.
Left politics, Tatlock, Kitty, Chevalier (wiki core, 1936–42)
Chs. 8–14: Popular Front / New Deal left, personal life, Rapid Rupture role, Chevalier affair—essential for wartime clearance culture and for pairing with later 1946–89 security-case pages.
Los Alamos and the bomb (wiki core, 1942–45)
Chs. 15–22: lab leadership, secrecy, Bohr, Interim Committee, Trinity, Hiroshima/Nagasaki—primary wartime spine beside Now It Can Be Told and Tuxedo Park.
Postwar AEC, Super, 1954 hearing (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 23–40 + Preface/Prologue/Epilogue: use only as brief forward pointers; full mining belongs in the United States 1946–89 copy of this source.
