sources/foster-henry-j-kaiser.title: [source] Henry J. Kaiser: Builder in the Modern American West (Foster, 1989)
sources/foster-henry-j-kaiser.content:
Henry J. Kaiser: Builder in the Modern American West
Author: Mark S. Foster (foreword by William H. Goetzmann)
Published: 1989 (University of Texas Press, Austin; American Studies Series; 2012 paperback; 2014 ebook packaging)
Working text: MOBI via Anna’s Archive (hash 4513b150e6529d21bdffc83fa33ada19)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/foster-henry-j-kaiser.txt (MOBI via mobi.extract → book.html → pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 19,373 lines · ~160,556 words · 1,046,225 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1866-1919 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters 3–8, plus wartime strands in Chs. 11 and 13, cover Kaiser’s 1920s California road empire, Six Companies Hoover/Boulder and Grand Coulee dams, WWII Liberty-ship yards, Fontana steel, wartime celebrity, postwar-planning speeches, the Hughes cargo-plane collaboration, and Coulee/shipyard medicine through 1945—core western construction and home-front industry for this period. Mine those chapters first. Use Chs. 1–2 only as continuity. Period-gate Chs. 9–10, 12, 14–16 and Conclusion (Kaiser-Frazer, aluminum scale-up, Hawaii, death 1967) to the United States 1946–89 sister page.
Overview
Henry J. Kaiser: Builder in the Modern American West is Mark S. Foster’s narrative biography of Henry J. Kaiser (1882–1967), drawing on the Henry J. Kaiser Papers, Edgar F. Kaiser, Sr., Papers, and Six Companies Papers at the Bancroft Library, presidential libraries, National Archives, oral histories with Kaiser executives and family, and Foster’s own prior articles on Kaiser’s regional industrialization, Detroit automobiles, and consumer/suburban culture. The book traces Kaiser from Steinheim, Germany, immigrant roots and Sprout Brook/Whitesboro childhood through Lake Placid and Florida photography chains, Spokane hardware and Hill Company paving apprenticeship, the 1914 Vancouver road-contract launch, 1920s California highway empire and Six Companies dam consortium, WWII Liberty-ship celebrity, western steel and magnesium, postwar Kaiser-Frazer and aluminum ventures, Kaiser Permanente medical care, Hawaii resort development, and the dispersal of Kaiser Industries after his death.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers Kaiser roads–dams–ships: 1920s California highway empire, Six Companies and Boulder/Grand Coulee, WWII Liberty yards, Fontana steel, wartime “Miracle Man” image, reconversion planning, Hughes cargo-plane collaboration, and Permanente’s Coulee/shipyard origins through 1945. Period-gate Chs. 1–2 to continuity; gate Kaiser-Frazer/Hawaii/death chapters to 1946–89.
Book structure: Foreword; Acknowledgments; Introduction; Chapters 1–16; Conclusion; Notes; Bibliographic Note; Index.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Contents
Lines 1–148. American Studies Series imprint; title page and copyright © 1989 University of Texas Press; Library of Congress and ebook ISBN data; reprint permissions for Foster’s prior Business History Review, Michigan History, and Western Historical Quarterly articles; contents listing Foreword through Conclusion, Notes, Bibliographic Note, and Index.
Foreword (William H. Goetzmann)
Lines 149–254. Goetzmann frames Kaiser for interdisciplinary American Studies: WWII Liberty-ship legend, Horatio Alger camera-marketing origins, dams, steel, labor sympathy, and Kaiser Permanente; compares Kaiser’s Washington navigation and western maverick style to Lyndon Johnson; argues Kaiser continued the federal-aid tradition of western development from Topographical Engineers through reclamation and tourism.
Acknowledgments
Lines 255–416. Foster credits University of Colorado Denver fellowship support, Edgar F. Kaiser, Jr.’s research grant and manuscript reading, Bancroft and National Archives staffs, Hoover/Roosevelt/Truman/Eisenhower libraries, dozens of former Kaiser executives interviewed, Eugene E. Trefethen, Jr., Kaiser family members, and his wife Rickey Lynn Hendricks (whose Kaiser health-plan dissertation informed the project).
Introduction
Lines 417–610. Opens on Kaiser’s July 1942 Portland cargo-plane speech, Oval Office visit, War Production Board “runaround,” and Howard Hughes collaboration as a frame for asking who Kaiser was; surveys his West Coast infrastructure and wartime industries; discusses rival irritation, government partnership, postwar Permanente and labor stances; and states Foster’s biographical method (entrepreneurial “seat-of-the-pants” operator rather than Chandler-style organizational synthesis).
Chapter 1 — Roots
Lines 611–1017. Henry John Kaiser born 9 May 1882 at Sprout Brook, New York; parents Frank and Mary (née Yops/Jobst) as German immigrants from Steinheim; Frank’s cobbler trade, family instability, and 1889 move to Whitesboro on the Erie Canal; Henry’s gregarious childhood, eighth-grade departure from school, Utica dry-goods and photography apprenticeship, mother Mary’s 1899 death, and 1901 departure for Lake Placid.
Chapter 2 — Launching a Career
Lines 1018–1606. Photography partnership with W. W. Brownell at Lake Placid (1901–), Florida chain expansion (Daytona, Jacksonville, St. Augustine, Palm Beach), courtship and 1907 marriage to Bess Fosburgh, Spokane McGowan Brothers hardware sales, Hawkeye Fuel and J. F. Hill paving apprenticeship, 1913 Hill Company management shakeup and Kaiser’s integrity finishing contracts; closes with 1914 firing and readiness to strike out as an independent contractor (Oakland HQ horizon).
Chapter 3 — Taming the Wilderness—Roads
Lines 1607–2318. Kaiser launches general construction in Vancouver, B.C., 1914—$25,000 Commerce Bank loan, Ordway hire, Warren Brothers backing, 1916 Federal Aid Road Act shift to rural Washington/Oregon/Idaho jobs, 1921 Redding–Red Bluff U.S. 99 contract and Oakland headquarters, Le Tourneau earth-moving partnership, Philbrook and Livermore gravel plants, Gas Tax Act lobbying, 1927–1930 Cuba Central Highway subcontract, and transition toward dam bidding as Depression arrives.
Chapter 4 — Taming the Wilderness—Dams
Lines 2319–3459. Depression contraction pushes Kaiser toward federal mega-projects; Colorado River reclamation politics and Black Canyon (Hoover/Boulder Dam) bidding; formation of Six Companies consortium; construction conditions at Boulder City; Grand Coulee and related Columbia Basin work; cement, aggregates, and Washington lobbying through Harold Ickes and New Deal agencies.
Chapter 5 — Patriot in Pinstripes—Shipbuilding
Lines 3460–4513. Kaiser’s lifelong boating interests; 1937–39 entry via Seattle-Tacoma Shipbuilding and Todd partnership on C-1 cargo ships; wartime Richmond, Portland, and Vancouver yards; Liberty-ship prefabrication, labor relations, and record launch times that made Kaiser a national symbol.
Chapter 6 — Man of Steel
Lines 4514–5552. Steel-plate shortages for shipyards drive Kaiser toward a fully integrated western mill; Big Steel resistance, Morgenthau and OPM/Gano Dunn capacity debates; Fontana (Kaiser Steel) authorization, labor, and wartime plate production.
Chapter 7 — Creating an Image
Lines 5553–6242. Kaiser’s rise from obscure contractor to Pearl Harbor–era celebrity; early Elks and AGC service; 1931 Hoover Dam press fights; Washington “point man” role under Hoover and Roosevelt; Corcoran and Ickes connections; wartime press, “Miracle Man” coverage, and 1944 vice-presidential speculation.
Chapter 8 — Planning for a Postwar World
Lines 6243–6935. Kaiser’s future-oriented temperament; December 1942 NAM address urging reconversion planning; housing, health care, industrial diversification, and magnesium/aluminum peacetime visions amid rival executives’ skepticism.
Chapter 9 — Debacle in Detroit
Lines 6936–8001. Kaiser’s wartime automobile interest (Fuller Dymaxion, hobby-lobby tinkering); August 1945 Kaiser-Frazer partnership with Joseph W. Frazer; Willow Run and Detroit production; market reception, dealer network, UAW relations, and decline of the auto venture.
Chapter 10 — Venturing Abroad
Lines 8002–8632. Debunks the “Cuba bribery ended overseas work” myth; Permanente cement Pacific bulk shipments and Panama/Hawaii wartime supply; 1943 Latin America scouting; 1954 Argentina Perón automobile deal and broader postwar international cement, engineering, and assembly investments.
Chapter 11 — Cargo Planes and Government Investigations
Lines 8633–9443. July 1942 five-thousand-plane proposal; Hughes partnership and HK-1/H-4 “Spruce Goose” prototypes; War Production Board politics; postwar C-119/C-123 programs; 1947 congressional investigation of Hughes–Kaiser spending.
Chapter 12 — Light Metals—Heavy Profits
Lines 9444–10119. 1941 western aluminum-fabrication proposals blocked by Alcoa; Ickes support; magnesium plants (Hansgirg carbothermic process, Permanente and Baton Rouge); postwar Kaiser Aluminum expansion and profitability.
Chapter 13 — Kaiser and the Doctors
Lines 10120–11175. Prepaid industrial medicine precedents; workers’ compensation and lodge practice; Dr. Sidney R. Garfield on Colorado River Aqueduct; 1938 Grand Coulee prepaid plan; WWII Richmond and Portland shipyard clinics; 1945 public Permanente launch and AMA “socialized medicine” opposition.
Chapter 14 — Boss
Lines 11176–11877. Kaiser’s consistent hands-on management from 1914; Ordway, Sherwood, and field supervision; loyalty to key men, equipment innovation, long hours, and delegation patterns across construction, dams, shipyards, and later industries.
Chapter 15 — Global Development and a Pacific Paradise
Lines 11878–12869. Kaiser Engineers domestic and overseas work; India Tata Iron contract; Argentina and Brazil automobile plants; 1954 Hawaii “retirement,” tourism, hotels, broadcasting, and planned community development.
Chapter 16 — The Sunset Years
Lines 12870–13324. Kaiser’s sociability and work-centered life; Lake Tahoe Fleur du Lac, powerboating, and rare recreation; Hawaii years; Bess’s death; second marriage to Alyce Chester; declining health; death 24 August 1967 at Honolulu.
Conclusion
Lines 13325–13578. Dispersal of Kaiser Industries after 1967; Edgar Kaiser’s stewardship versus Henry’s inspirational drive; foreign competition, energy crisis, and sale of steel, aluminum, and other lines; Kaiser as last of the personality-driven “captains of industry” and as a government-partnered western developer.
Notes
Lines 13579–17034. Chapter-by-chapter endnotes citing Bancroft Kaiser collections, federal and state records, newspapers, interviews, and Foster’s prior articles.
Bibliographic Note
Lines 17035–17276. Foster’s research narrative: 1981 decision to write the first Kaiser biography; New York Times and periodical-index chronology; Bancroft Papers (~700 linear feet) and gaps in intimate correspondence; presidential libraries, corporate archives, and specialized collections (Reuther UAW papers, Haughey shipyard letters, Weinerman Permanente files, etc.).
Index
Lines 17277–19373. Name and subject index (aircraft, Alcoa, AMA, automobiles/Kaiser-Frazer, Bechtel, dams, Hawaii, labor, Permanente, shipbuilding, steel, and related entries).
Coverage Guide
Origins and apprenticeship — Chs. 1–2 (continuity ← 1866–1919)
Childhood, photography, Spokane—brief background only.
Road-building launch through 1919 (continuity ← 1866–1919)
Early Ch. 3 Vancouver 1914 launch—continuity into the 1920s road empire.
1920s California road empire and Cuba (wiki core)
Late Ch. 3: Redding–Red Bluff, U.S. 99, Le Tourneau, Philbrook/Livermore, Gas Tax, Cuba highway.
Dams and Six Companies (wiki core)
Ch. 4: Hoover/Boulder, Grand Coulee, Boulder City, Ickes politics.
WWII shipbuilding, steel, image, postwar planning (wiki core)
Chs. 5–8: Liberty yards, Fontana steel, celebrity press, December 1942 NAM reconversion speech.
Cargo planes / Hughes wartime strand (wiki core)
Ch. 11 wartime passages: 1942 cargo-plane proposal through wartime prototypes; later investigation spill may continue into 1946–89.
Permanente origins through 1945 (wiki core / hinge)
Ch. 13 through 1945 public launch; later HMO scale-up belongs mainly to 1946–89.
Kaiser-Frazer, abroad, aluminum, boss years (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 9–10, 12, 14: brief forward pointers only.
Hawaii, sunset, empire dispersal (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 15–16 + Conclusion: out of scope except one-line pointers.
Notes, Bibliographic Note, and Index (reference)
Endnotes and Bibliographic Note for archival pointers; Index for subject lookup.

sources/gabler-walt-disney.title: [source] Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination (Gabler, 2006)
sources/gabler-walt-disney.content:
Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination
Author: Neal Gabler
Published: 2006 (Alfred A. Knopf / Borzoi)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 1d4acf64002ec043c355134398547b15)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/gabler-walt-disney.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 41,809 lines · ~382,433 words · 2,337,488 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters One–Eight cover Disney’s post–World War I Kansas City hustle, Hollywood Alice comedies, Mickey Mouse, Depression shorts cult, Snow White, feature Parnassus, the 1941 animators’ strike, and World War II studio films through 1945—core animation and Hollywood material for this period. Mine first from Chs. 2–8 (roughly 1919–1945), with Ch. 1 as childhood continuity. Introduction stats (1966), Chapters Nine–Eleven (postwar drift, Disneyland, EPCOT), and late utopia framing remain primarily for the 1946–89 wiki; use them only as brief forward pointers.
Overview
Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination is Neal Gabler’s biography of Walt Disney (1901–1966), arguing that Disney reshaped American popular culture by turning animation into character-and-emotion art, inventing the theme park as total imaginative environment, and supplying audiences not merely escape but vicarious control over a crafted reality. The life arc runs from hard Elias Disney childhood and midwestern make-believe through Kansas City go-getter years, Hollywood Alice comedies and Mickey Mouse, Depression-era shorts cult and Snow White “folly,” Fantasia/feature Parnassus, the 1941 studio strike and World War II training/propaganda films, postwar creative drift (Song of the South and package features), Disneyland and ABC television as a “city on a hill,” and late EPCOT/utopia projects until death—capped by the cryogenics myth Gabler dismantles in the Introduction.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers how Disney animation and the modern Disney studio were built: go-getter 1920s, Mickey, Depression shorts, Snow White, Burbank features, labor war, and wartime conversion. Period-gate hard after 1945 except where Ch. 9’s immediate postwar reclaim opens stories already under way in 1945.
EPUB structure: Contents; dedication/epigraph (Blake); Chapter Illustrations key; Introduction; Chapters One–Eleven (with photo inserts); Appendix (feature film list); Notes; Selected Bibliography; Acknowledgments; Note About the Author / Also by; Knopf copyright.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–94. TOC; dedication to daughters; Blake epigraph (“I must create a system…”); chapter-illustration key (1915 drawing through 1966 EPCOT map).
Introduction
Lines 95–506. Cryogenics rumor after Disney’s death vs. cremation at Forest Lawn; 1966 audience/merchandising scale; Disney as reshaper of animation, Pop Art adjacency (Fantasia/Stokowski), recreation (Disneyland), and urban design—“Disneyfication” vs. Rouse/Blake praise.
Chapter One — Escape
Lines 507–2227. Elias Disney’s hard, devout temperament; Walt’s childhood need to escape into drawing and make-believe; formative midwestern family pressures.
Chapter Two — Go-Getter
Lines 2228–3600. Post–World War I return from France into booming America; job hunt and Kansas City commercial-art/animation hustle; youthful exuberance of the early 1920s.
Chapter Three — Wonderland
Lines 3601–5074. Move to Hollywood as spiritual destination; Alice comedies with Ub Iwerks; dress-up, attention, and the capital of imagination in the mid-1920s movie boom.
Chapter Four — The Mouse
Lines 5075–7553. Train home after Mintz betrayal; vow never to work for anyone again; creation and rise of Mickey Mouse; Lillian’s fear and Walt’s rage as founding myth of independence.
Chapter Five — The Cult
Lines 7554–9626. Depression immunity of Disney shorts relative to overextended studios; Three Little Pigs and the 1930s cult of Disney character animation.
Chapter Six — Folly
Lines 9627–12472. Restlessness after Three Little Pigs; decision on something big—the feature that becomes Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), long dismissed as folly.
Chapter Seven — Parnassus
Lines 12473–15658. Post–Snow White peak months; grosses and studio triumph; drive toward Pinocchio, Fantasia, Bambi and the Burbank plant as artistic Parnassus—and financial strain beneath.
Chapter Eight — Two Wars
Lines 15659–18443. Belt-tightening under Roy; animators’ strike (1941); World War II takeover of studio capacity (Victory Through Air Power, training films); twin wars of labor and global conflict.
Chapter Nine — Adrift
Lines 18444–21386. Postwar wait to reclaim studio from soldiers and bankers; package features and Song of the South (1946); plans for Alice, Peter Pan, Mickey feature—creative drift and recovery struggle.
Chapter Ten — City on a Hill
Lines 21387–25060. Control thesis: Disney offered empowerment over crafted reality, not mere escape; Leuchtenberg’s “troubled feast” postwar mood; Disneyland planning (Herb Ryman/ABC) and television as new city on a hill.
Chapter Eleven — Slouching Toward Utopia
Lines 25061–28694. Disneyland-driven stock and revenue surge (1952–58); Wall Street formula of wringing value from every property; EPCOT and late utopian schemes; Walt’s final years and death (1966).
Appendix
Lines 28695–28882. Chronological list of feature-length pictures produced by Walt Disney (animation, live action, combination, True-Life).
Notes / Bibliography / Acknowledgments / Copyright
Lines 28883–41809. Dense chapter notes; selected bibliography; acknowledgments; author note / also by Gabler; Knopf 2006 copyright and LC cataloging (eISBN 978-0-307-26596-8).
Coverage Guide
Childhood through Mickey and Depression shorts (wiki core)
Chs. 1–5: Elias household, Kansas City, Hollywood Alice comedies, Mickey, Depression cult—foundation of Disney animation in the 1920s–30s.
Snow White, feature ambition, strike and WWII (wiki core)

sources/gates-dupont-family.title: [source] The du Pont Family (Gates, 1979)
sources/gates-dupont-family.content:
The du Pont Family
Author: John D. Gates
Published: 1979, Doubleday & Company, Garden City, N.Y. (First Edition)
Working text: PDF via pdftotext (Anna’s Archive hash 9130d08d4a9ea53ad5eca33e6890f6a5)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/gates-dupont-family.txt (pdftotext)
Extract stats: 15,031 lines · ~758 KB text
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1866-1919 into the United States 1920–45 wiki for the interwar and mid-century du Pont arc: company reorganization, Pierre S. du Pont and General Motors, Christiana Securities, family politics, and the path toward later antitrust. Mine chapters that treat the 1920s–1940s industrial and corporate story. Early gunpowder / Gilded Age foundation chapters remain primarily for the 1800–65 and 1866–1919 wikis; post-1945 decline and 1960s–70s control fights are trajectory beyond this vault’s core.
Overview
John D. Gates’s The du Pont Family is an insider’s portrait of one of America’s richest and most private industrial dynasties. Gates, a du Pont in-law for many years and a Wilmington newspaper reporter, writes from a position of unusual access: several dozen du Ponts cooperated with the project, granting interviews and opening family perspectives that earlier books had not obtained. The book is explicitly anecdotal and personal rather than strictly scholarly — Gates compares his approach to Marquis James’s biography of Alfred I. du Pont — but it covers the full sweep of the family’s American history from their landing on January 1, 1800, through the 1970s.
The first half of the book is broadly chronological: Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours’s French origins, the family’s migration to America, the founding of the gunpowder mills on Brandywine Creek, expansion into dynamite and explosives, and the transformation of the company under Pierre S. du Pont into the world’s largest chemical corporation, with holdings in General Motors, U.S. Rubber, and other industrial giants. The second half is organized by family branch — Pierre’s relatives, T. C. du Pont, Alfred I. du Pont (the “rebel”), the heirs of “the Boss,” and various other branches — before concluding with chapters on the company itself and “a way of life.”
A central narrative thread is the decline of family control. The book opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s 1972 letter proposing the absorption of Christiana Securities (the family holding company, which held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock) into the Du Pont Company itself — effectively ending the family’s formal control of the enterprise. The antitrust case that forced divestiture of General Motors holdings (63 million shares) and the tax and marketability pressures on Christiana are treated as the terminal phase of a dynastic arc that began with E. I. du Pont’s powder mills in 1802.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki, mine the interwar company, GM, and family-control chapters. For the United States 1866–1919 wiki, the source is valuable for Gilded Age and Progressive Era industrial chemistry, the gunpowder and explosives industry, family-business governance through the holding-company form, the du Pont–GM connection, antitrust policy toward concentrated family wealth, and the social and political power of a single-family industrial empire based in a small state. Material after 1919 covers the later evolution of the company, family succession, and the 1960s–1970s dissolution of control; use those sections mainly for the long-term trajectory and afterlife of du Pont industrial power.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 157–266. Gates explains his personal connection to the du Ponts (debutante party in 1957, marriage to a du Pont descendant, nine years as a Wilmington newspaper reporter). He contrasts his sympathetic perspective with the skeptical or hostile attitudes of fellow reporters. Describes the family’s studied avoidance of publicity and the cooperation of several dozen du Ponts in the project. Notes earlier books: Gerald Colby Zilg’s Behind the Nylon Curtain, Ralph Nader’s The Company State, Alfred Chandler and Stephen Salsbury’s Pierre S. du Pont and the Making of the Modern Corporation, and Marquis James’s Alfred I. du Pont, the Family Rebel.
Chapter 1 — Now and Then: An Overview (lines 369–1500+)
Opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s retirement in 1978 and the 1972 letter proposing Christiana Securities’ absorption into Du Pont. Christiana held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock and was the vehicle of family control; Du Pont once owned 38% of General Motors, and the 1949 antitrust suit (Attorney General Tom Clark: “the largest single concentration of industrial power in the United States”) forced GM divestiture. The chapter frames the book’s central theme: family control as a waning reality, Christiana as an albatross rather than a pendant of power, and the transformation of the du Ponts from a commanding dynasty to a dispersed, divided family.
Chapter 2 — The Move to America (lines ~1500–)
Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours (1739–1817), French physiocrat and politician, his friendship with Thomas Jefferson, the family’s escape from Revolutionary France, their arrival in Rhode Island on January 1, 1800, with one of the largest libraries ever brought to America by an immigrant family. Eleuthère Irénée du Pont’s (E. I. du Pont) decision to enter gunpowder manufacturing, the purchase of land on Brandywine Creek near Wilmington, Delaware, and the founding of the powder mills in 1802.
Chapter 3 — Building the Business (~lines –)
The early decades of the powder works, competition with established powder makers, the War of 1812 and government contracts, expansion through the nineteenth century, the introduction of dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s rise as the dominant American explosives manufacturer.
Chapter 4 — Two Crises (~lines –)
Two critical episodes: the powder-mill explosions that periodically devastated the Brandywine works, and the financial and operational crises that threatened the company’s survival in its early decades.
Chapter 5 — Pierre: Star of the Show (~lines –)
Pierre S. du Pont (1870–1954), the central figure of the family’s modern history. His education at MIT, his reorganization and modernization of the Du Pont Company after the 1902 crisis, the creation of the modern corporate structure, the expansion into chemicals, and the acquisition of a controlling interest in General Motors.
Chapter 6 — Two Brothers (~lines –)
Pierre’s brothers Irénée and Lammot du Pont, their roles in the company and the family, the division of responsibilities, and the dynamics of the fraternal partnership that ran Du Pont for decades.
Chapter 7 — Fathers and Sons (~lines –)
Generational relationships within the family, the pressures on du Pont sons to enter the family business, and the tension between dynastic expectation and individual ambition.
Chapter 8 — Pierre’s Other Relatives (~lines –)
The broader network of du Pont cousins and relations connected to Pierre S. du Pont’s branch, their roles in company and community, and the management of extended-family interests.
Chapter 9 — T.C. and Family (~lines –)
Thomas Coleman du Pont (T.C.), a cousin who was instrumental in the 1902 reorganization and later a U.S. Senator from Delaware. His branch’s history, political ambitions, and the 1920s conflict over family control.
Chapter 10 — The Rebel and His Relations (~lines –)
Alfred I. du Pont, the “family rebel,” who contested control after the death of the senior generation, fought legal battles over the family company, and built his own independent fortune in Florida banking and real estate.
Chapter 11 — Heirs of “the Boss” (~lines –)
The descendants of Eugene du Pont (the “Boss”), who ran the company in the late nineteenth century. Their inheritance, family position, and place in the expanded du Pont network.
Chapter 12 — A Diverse Branch (~lines –)
A lesser-known du Pont branch, their businesses and fortunes outside the main company, and the diversity of paths taken by family members.
Chapter 13 — The Underrated Victors (~lines –)
A branch of the family that built substantial independent success outside the central Du Pont Company narrative — their achievements, their relationship to the main family, and the family’s internal status hierarchies.
Chapter 14 — The In-Laws (~lines –)
The du Ponts who married into the family rather than being born into it — their roles, their acceptance (or lack thereof) in the dynastic structure, and the social dynamics of marriage into a closed wealthy family.
Chapter 15 — The Company (~lines 327–)
The Du Pont Company itself: its corporate structure, research and development, product diversification (explosives, paints, plastics, synthetic fibers — nylon, rayon, cellophane), the shift from a family-managed to a professionally-managed corporation, and the position of the family in the modern company.
Chapter 16 — A Way of Life (~lines 342–)
The social world of the du Ponts: chateaux-country estates, Wilmington society, the Brandywine landscape, charitable foundations, political influence in Delaware, and the texture of daily life in a family defined by inherited wealth and a shared name.
Appendix (~line 359 onwards)
Family charts and genealogical tables.
Coverage Guide
Gunpowder and explosives industry
Chapters 2–4 are the core material on the foundation of the du Pont powder mills, the early American gunpowder market, government contracts (War of 1812, Mexican-American War, Civil War), the transition from black powder to dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s quasi-monopoly position in American explosives by the late nineteenth century. This is the single most important source for the explosives and munitions side of Gilded Age industry.
Corporate reorganization and management
Chapter 5 (Pierre S. du Pont) and Chapter 15 (The Company) cover the 1902 crisis and reorganization, the creation of the modern divisional structure, scientific management, research, and diversification. Pierre S. du Pont’s MIT education and systematic approach transformed a family powder business into a diversified chemical corporation — a case study in Progressive Era corporate modernization.
Family holding company and control mechanisms
The Christiana Securities story runs through Chapters 1, 5, and 15. The family holding company as a vehicle for concentrated control, its tax advantages, the liquidity discount, the intercorporate dividends tax, and the 1972 decision to dissolve it are a unique window into dynastic wealth management in corporate form.
Antitrust, General Motors, and concentrated power
The 1949 antitrust suit (Chapter 1), the forced divestiture of 63 million GM shares, and the earlier acquisition of a 38% GM stake are central to understanding Progressive and mid-century antitrust policy toward family-controlled industrial concentrations. The du Pont–GM case is a major antitrust landmark.
Delaware and political power
The du Pont family’s relationship with Delaware — the “company state” — appears throughout the book: family members in the Senate (T.C. du Pont), governors (Pete du Pont), influence over state politics, the dominance of Wilmington by company employment and family wealth, and the broader question of concentrated private power in a small-state setting.
Family dynamics, intermarriage, and dynastic identity
Chapters 7, 14, and 16, supported by the individual branch chapters, treat the social and psychological dimensions of du Pont family life: cousin marriage (a repeated pattern), the pressure on sons to join the company, the management of reputation and publicity, and the internal status competition between branches.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 268–359: Table of contents — full chapter structure for navigation.
Lines 369–468: Chapter 1 opening — Irenee du Pont Jr.’s 1972 letter, Christiana Securities, the 1949 antitrust suit, the end of family control.
Lines 157–266: Preface — Gates’s access and perspective, the family’s cooperation, the existing literature on the du Ponts.
The Chapter 2–4 material: E. I. du Pont’s arrival, the gunpowder mills, early government contracts, and the nineteenth-century expansion of the powder business.
The Chapter 5–6 material: Pierre S. du Pont’s reorganization, the GM acquisition, and the modernization of the company.
The Chapter 15 material: the Du Pont Company as a professional-managed chemical corporation, the shift from family to management control.

Suggested Future Pages

Du Pont family — entity page on the du Pont dynasty from arrival through the 1970s, the family as an industrial and social institution.
E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company — entity/concept page on the company’s foundation, gunpowder monopoly, chemical diversification, and corporate structure.
Christiana Securities — entity/concept page on the family holding company and its role in maintaining concentrated control.
Pierre S. du Pont — entity page on the central figure of the modern Du Pont Company and his role in General Motors.
Du Pont–General Motors antitrust case — event page on the 1949 suit and forced GM divestiture.
Alfred I. du Pont — entity page on the “family rebel,” his legal battles, and his Florida ventures.

Related Sources

Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. — contrasting model of dynastic industrial wealth: a single-founder oil trust vs. a multi-generational family chemical company.
The House of Morgan — banking and finance-capital dynastic comparison: Morgan’s partnership model vs. du Pont’s family-corporation model.
Andrew Carnegie — steel wealth and philanthropic institutionalization as a contrasting Gilded Age fortune: single founder, no dynastic continuity.
The First Tycoon: The Epic Life of Cornelius Vanderbilt — early nineteenth-century dynastic foundation vs. du Pont’s longer arc from 1800 through the twentieth century.

Notes on Scope
This is a late-twentieth-century popular biography by an insider, not an academic monograph. It is anecdotal and personal in approach and largely sympathetic to the family. Its value lies in the access Gates obtained — interviews with several dozen du Ponts — and in its comprehensive sweep from 1800 to the 1970s. For this 1866–1919 wiki, the core chapters are 2–5 (business foundation and reorganization) and the early portions of 1, 15, and 16 (company structure and family control). Later chapters covering the 1920s–1970s are useful mainly for the long-term arc of dynastic decline and the antitrust aftermath.

sources/groves-now-it-can-be-told.title: [source] Now It Can Be Told: The Story of the Manhattan Project (Groves, 1962)
sources/groves-now-it-can-be-told.content:
Now It Can Be Told: The Story of the Manhattan Project
Author: Leslie R. Groves
Published: Harper & Brothers, 1962 (copyright Leslie R. Groves 1962)
Working text: Da Capo Press paperback, 1983 unabridged republication with new introduction by Edward Teller (ISBN-10 0-306-80189-2 / ISBN-13 978-0-306-80189-1; eBook ISBN 9780786748228; AA hash f6392e8bd36ad6ce1a3139c3e4522c46)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/groves-now-it-can-be-told.txt
Extract stats: 18,218 lines · ~168,426 words · 1,012,543 bytes (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Completeness Assessment
The clean digital EPUB extract is complete for wiki use. Front matter includes Da Capo cataloging, Teller’s 1983 Introduction, dedication, and Groves’s Foreword. Body runs Part I (Chapters 1–17) → Part II (Chapters 18–25) → Part III (Chapters 26–31) → Appendices I–X → About the Author → Index. No missing chapter blocks detected in the pandoc plain text. Image placeholders appear where plates were; text narrative is continuous.
Overview
Groves limits his narrative to what he is “qualified to write about”—his own experiences directing the Manhattan Project from 17 September 1942 through 31 December 1946, when the Atomic Energy Commission took over. He deliberately leaves the pre-1942 scientific milestones to others and treats matters outside his direct cognizance only as needed for the reader’s understanding. He retains wartime vocabulary (“atomic” rather than “nuclear”) because that was the language of the period. Bush and Conant are credited with turning research into a weapons program; Somervell and Styer brought Groves in once the military purpose governed.
For this wiki the book is the Manhattan Project administrative and operational spine: appointment and first steps; uranium ore and Sengier; plutonium and DuPont; Los Alamos and Oppenheimer; Hanford and Oak Ridge production; British negotiations and Combined Development Trust; security and censorship; Alsos in Italy, France, and Germany; 509th training, target selection, Tinian, Trinity, Hiroshima, and Nagasaki; Congress, Japanese cyclotrons, transition, AEC, and postwar Anglo-American friction. It pairs with Tuxedo Park (once added) for pre-Army and radar/science networks, and with Elliott Roosevelt for wartime White House-level diplomacy outside Groves’s remit. Teller’s introduction is a 1983 retrospective frame, not wartime text.
Narrative Source Flow
Introduction (Edward Teller, 1983)
Lines 50–324. ~2,610 words.
Teller praises readers who go to a major participant rather than television dramas (including a seven-hour BBC production he finds inaccurate). Groves was straightforward to a fault; Bush had worried he lacked tact. The assignment seemed minor beside the Pentagon and denied Groves combat command; he retained doubts about feasibility while projecting confidence to DuPont. Teller ranks the Groves–Oppenheimer pairing as the project’s striking human story—Groves clearing Oppenheimer against security opposition. He recounts Los Alamos irritation at military rules, a 4 a.m. gas-diffusion emergency interrogation, and Groves’s humor. Closing plea: rebuild the bridge between those who defend the nation with their lives and those who contribute ideas, or democratic survival is at risk.
Foreword (Groves)
Lines 325–523. ~1,940 words.
Atomic physics is not occult; laymen can grasp its basic laws as they grasp markets or motors. Progress was cumulative across countries and fields; Groves will not retell the scientific milestones. He records only his experiences, 17 September 1942–31 December 1946. Bush (OSRD) and Conant (NDRC) drove Roosevelt’s shift from research to weapon; Somervell and Styer then brought Groves in. He prefers “atomic” over later “nuclear” because that was wartime usage outside specialist circles.
Chapter 1 — The Beginnings of the MED
Lines 530–1115. ~5,630 words.
Mid-September 1942: Groves, Deputy Chief of Construction under Robins, is offered an attractive overseas combat assignment. Somervell blocks it—“The Secretary of War has selected you… the President has approved”—and says if he does the job right it will win the war. Groves’s reply: “Oh, that thing.” Initial disappointment: the uranium-bomb effort seemed under $100 million, small beside weekly Army construction spend, and what little he knew had not impressed him. Full magnitude, reckless wartime risk-taking, and priority over normal diplomatic and pure-science considerations came only later. He sketches the pre-MED organization, DSM designation, early site and heavy-water decisions, and the scale of concurrent construction ignorance.
Chapter 2 — First Steps
Lines 1116–1629. ~5,160 words.
17 September: assignment memorandum to Reybold; delay of open takeover until promotion; brief with Nichols. Groves is “horrified”—the endeavor rests on possibilities more than probabilities; theory abundant, proven knowledge thin; engineering difficulties unprecedented. Ore and priorities are tangible; scientific foundation is not. First call on Bush is a mutual fiasco (Bush not yet informed); Bush then tells Styer Groves is too aggressive and may trouble the scientists, and writes Bundy of his fears. Site work (Tennessee/Clinton), Farrell’s recall from leave, and early organizational moves follow as Groves forces speed and priorities.
Chapter 3 — The Uranium Ore Supply
Lines 1630–1814. ~1,830 words.
Ore is a first concern. But for a chance 1939 meeting of Edgar Sengier (Union Minière) with Sir Henry Tizard—who warned that Congo ore in enemy hands could mean catastrophe—and Sengier’s talks with Joliot-Curie on a Sahara bomb project halted by war, the Allies might not have been first. Shinkolobwe’s exceptional richness (hand-sorted tonnage over 65 percent uranium oxide versus marketable Colorado/Canadian tenths of a percent) becomes strategic. Nichols learns of Sengier stocks in New York days before Groves’s appointment; purchases and stockpiling follow.
Chapter 4 — The Plutonium Project
Lines 1815–2639. ~8,100 words.
Plutonium development is framed as a voyage beyond Columbus: laboratory to commercial plant with almost no time. Chicago’s Metallurgical Laboratory seeks to transmute uranium into plutonium; history’s alchemical precedents are against them. Piles require tens of tons of pure uranium not available until late 1942; even then laboratory output cannot support normal recovery research. When Engineers enter in June 1942, conversion is still only theoretical; experimental proof comes 2 December 1942—after full-speed plant decisions. Groves’s 5 October Chicago visit; military premises (Axis may already be racing; only counter-employment deters use; success shortens war); DuPont recruitment despite chemical engineers’ incredulity; and the Lewis review committee structure the chapter.
Chapter 5 — Los Alamos: I
Lines 2640–2919. ~2,770 words.
Before MED little bomb-design effort existed; mid-1942 feasibility was theoretical only. Compton had put Oppenheimer over bomb physics at Berkeley with a small theoretical group. Groves, with a fresh view, insists on pushing Project Y at once against overoptimistic claims (one extremist: twenty scientists, three months). Directorship is not predetermined; Groves’s first serious meeting with Oppenheimer is 8 October at Berkeley, then Washington planning. He defends the choice: Oppenheimer accomplished the mission; near-universal wartime judgment is that no one would have done better. Site: Los Alamos Ranch School; owners eager to sell, easing condemnation and secrecy risk.
Chapters 6–7 — Hanford: I–II
Lines 2920–3869. ~9,340 words.
Original plan: plutonium semi-works in Argonne, full-scale plant in Tennessee. Hazards force semi-works to Oak Ridge/Clinton; Chicago takes operating responsibility with DuPont loaned supervisors after mutual reluctance. Site team (Matthias, Hall, Church) and power/water/isolation criteria select the Columbia River country; land condemnation fights with Yakima juries and a hostile federal judge complicate acquisition. Hanford II: Clinton air-cooled 1,000 kw pile as rapid semi-works versus water-cooled Hanford production piles; separation chemistry still conjectural while design, procurement, and construction run concurrent; remote handling, periscopes, shielding, and tight tolerances; health of Columbia fish and mundane plant details all matter to the job.
Chapter 8 — Oak Ridge
Lines 3870–5049. ~11,470 words.
Apart from Hanford plutonium, Oak Ridge is the heart of fissionable-material production: electromagnetic and gaseous diffusion authorized late 1942; thermal diffusion added 1944. Groves offers only a sketch of the Clinton Engineer Works and its headaches—Y-12 calutrons, K-25 diffusion plant scale and barrier problems, S-50 thermal plant, power demand, labor and secrecy, accidents, and the race to feed Los Alamos. Largest single chapter on production engineering and site society.
Chapter 9 — Negotiations with the British
Lines 5050–5509. ~4,380 words.
Bush’s White House channel (Roosevelt/Hopkins) is the project’s political spine; no one wants to change it. Chapter traces Quebec and related interchange arrangements, limits on commercial information to Britain, and the friction and repair of Anglo-American atomic collaboration under wartime Combined policy—Groves’s operational view of high diplomacy.
Chapter 10 — Security Arrangements and Press Censorship
Lines 5510–5899. ~3,790 words.
First-year internal security under G-2 Strong; February 1942 Strong–Hoover division of labor. March 1943 friction when Strong asks FBI to drop a scientist investigation. Compartmentalization, press voluntary censorship, cover stories, and the constant tension between scientific talk and military secrecy structure Groves’s security doctrine—including his willingness to clear Oppenheimer against narrower security instincts.
Chapter 11 — Los Alamos: II
Lines 5900–6663. ~7,480 words.
Project Y’s unprecedented collaboration of civilians and officers; scheduling both definite (bomb ready when material arrives) and indefinite (problems unknown until other sites advance). Gun assembly versus implosion, criticality, metallurgy, military detachment, town life, WACs (and Groves’s denial of the pregnant-WAC rumor), water shortages, and Oppenheimer’s laboratory leadership under Army administration fill the second Los Alamos chapter.
Chapter 12 — The Combined Development Trust
Lines 6664–7259. ~5,610 words.
Even with Sengier’s cooperation, Military Policy Committee wants postwar ore security. Belgian government-in-exile is in London; British might gain leverage. Combined Development Trust arrangements, contracts, and Belgian undertakings aim to lock supply beyond immediate military burn-rate—resource geopolitics as extension of the bomb project.
Chapters 13–17 — Alsos and Related Intelligence
Lines 7260–9725. ~22,720 words.
13 Alsos I—Italy: From 1939 until German scientists are taken, Germany may be first; fragmented U.S. intelligence (G-2, ONI, OSS) must be coordinated; Italian mission as first field exploitation.
14 A Serious Military Problem: Fear Germans might use radioactive material to block cross-Channel attack; early 1943 worry about German bombs against England; classified medical/admin memos as cover for fogged film and mysterious illness surveillance in ETO.
15 Alsos II—France: Parallel planning for invasion intelligence; Bush and Groves push Bissell (G-2) for an Italy-style mission; staff-mill delays; French targets and Joliot.
16 French Scientists: Joliot–de Gaulle contacts; dismay at how much Joliot learns of Allied effort; 1939 French patents under Joliot’s group as legal-political tangle.
17 Alsos III—Germany: Operations from 24 February 1945 near Aachen; Goudsmit’s view that German scientists largely did not support the war effort as such; seizure of men, papers, and material; Farm Hall path set up for later chapter.
Chapter 18 — Training the Air Unit
Lines 9728–10101. ~3,580 words.
No weapon improved warfare with comparable suddenness. Groves goes to H. H. Arnold: Air Forces will deliver if the bomb can be airlifted. 509th Composite Group concept—special B-29 squadron, Southwest training base, aircraft modification, Fat Man flight test, field party to forward area—takes shape across late 1944–early 1945 schedules.
Chapter 19 — Choosing the Target
Lines 10102–10599. ~4,930 words.
Pacific strategy still assumes homeland invasion (Kyushu ~1 October 1945, Tokyo ~December) independent of Russia until post-Yalta attrition debate. Target committee work yields a short list: Kokura Arsenal; Hiroshima as embarkation port and military hub; Niigata; Kyoto as large urban industrial area—Stimson’s objections to Kyoto become decisive in the targeting story Groves tells. Criteria stress military significance, blast measurement, and psychological effect.
Chapter 20 — Tinian
Lines 10600–10975. ~3,770 words.
Late 1944 forward-base planning; Nimitz inquiring about the 509th without knowing its purpose. Guam construction and port congestion, distance to Tokyo, existing Tinian airfield and harbor timing, and Army/Navy jurisdiction shape the choice of Tinian. Assembly, storage, and operational security on the island follow.
Chapter 21 — Alamogordo
Lines 10976–11617. ~6,600 words.
Fat Man (implosion) test eyed for mid-July; gun-type never to be full-device tested. Trinity planning from spring 1944; early idea of exploding inside a container to salvage material if yield fails. Weather, Jumbo, observation B-29s, crater and steel-tower effects, and Groves’s own weather calls after forecasters fail structure the narrative. Appendix VIII later prints Groves’s full 18 July 1945 report to Stimson.
Chapter 22 — Operational Plans
Lines 11618–11985. ~3,640 words.
Trinity proves one plutonium implosion device, not the gun-type uranium bomb or production repeatability. Still, indications suffice to proceed. Directives to the 509th/20th Air Force on first and follow-on bombs, information control, and chain of authority (issued with Marshall/Stimson/Truman weight) set the combat rules of engagement.
Chapter 23 — Hiroshima
Lines 11986–12673. ~6,430 words.
1 August weather holds the mission; 4 August briefing—Parsons’s twenty-thousand-tons-TNT equivalent stuns crews who knew only that the bomb was “special.” Air-sea rescue, Enola Gay flight, strike, and Washington/Tinian reporting chains; Groves’s management of notification to the President and War Department. Operational payoff of Chapters 18–22.
Chapter 24 — The Germans Hear the News
Lines 12674–12972. ~2,750 words.
6 August at Farm Hall: Rittner tells Otto Hahn; Hahn is shattered, speaks of personal responsibility and earlier suicidal thoughts when he saw the discovery’s potential. Intercepted/recorded German scientists’ reactions and their retrospective account of the failed German program (Hahn’s fission, heavy water at Rjukan, Freiburg/Celle experiments) close the Alsos intellectual story.
Chapter 25 — Nagasaki
Lines 12973–13511. ~5,430 words.
While Tinian holds center stage through first use, Los Alamos accelerates the second implosion core; missing nonnuclear assembly parts cut tests. Kokura primary socked in; secondary Nagasaki struck. Surrender politics sit at the edge of Groves’s operational frame; the chapter is delivery, yield, and project completion under combat conditions.
Chapter 26 — The MED and Congress
Lines 13514–13780. ~2,640 words.
Stimson resigns; Patterson becomes Secretary—already generally familiar, having controlled much expediting money. Post–V-J congressional awakening to the secret billions; Groves’s testimony posture and the problem of explaining a project designed not to be explained. Bridge into legislative fight for domestic control.
Chapter 27 — The Destruction of the Japanese Cyclotrons
Lines 13781–13983. ~1,870 words.
Late November 1945 news: five cyclotrons destroyed (Tokyo Institute for Physical and Chemical Research; Osaka; Kyoto). Scientific and civic protest; heavy correspondence for Groves’s office and the Secretary of War; Staff papers. Groves’s defense of the order within occupation disarmament logic versus pure-science outrage.
Chapter 28 — Transition Period
Lines 13984–14548. ~5,720 words.
V-J Day threatens loss of the nonregular officers who ran almost the entire military side (regular contingent long reduced to a handful). How fast can work fall to peacetime needs without losing a going concern? Retention, demobilization, laboratory morale, and holding production/knowledge until a civilian agency exists.
Chapter 29 — The AEC
Lines 14549–14957. ~4,180 words.
Interim Committee (civilian), appointed April to advise on bomb-raised problems, drafts domestic control legislation. Groves, Marshall, Stimson all want prompt statute once MED’s war job is done. Legislative path toward the Atomic Energy Commission and the 31 December 1946 handoff that ends Groves’s stated period of charge.
Chapter 30 — Postwar Developments
Lines 14958–15413. ~4,130 words.
British push for postwar collaboration agreement from spring 1945; after Roosevelt’s death they produce the Hyde Park aide-mémoire (claimed Roosevelt–Churchill conversation, 18 September 1944)—first U.S. principals have heard of it in this telling. Combined Policy Committee friction, limits of wartime Quebec framework, and early Cold War atomic diplomacy from the American project director’s desk.
Chapter 31 — A Final Word
Lines 15414–15520. ~1,000 words.
As war memories fade, some question whether atomic energy should have been developed; a few call the United States morally corrupt for the effort. Groves will not ignore the charges if free men are to appraise the project fairly—he restates the wartime case: Axis race, no defense but deterrence, shortening the war, and the responsibilities of those who had to decide under incomplete knowledge.
Appendices I–X
Lines 15521–16793. ~11,530 words.
Key documents: I assignment of Groves to DSM/MED (17 September 1942); further organizational and policy papers (II–VII); VIII Groves’s long 18 July 1945 memorandum to the Secretary of War on the Trinity test (crater, steel tower, cloud, weather, Farrell, press cover stories); IX–X additional official texts. Primary-source backbone for cross-check against narrative chapters.
Index
Lines 16837–18218. ~4,330 words.
Dense name and subject index (Agencies, persons, sites, bomb types, 509th, MED, DSM, OSRD, etc.) supporting point retrieval across the memoir.
Coverage Guide
Mine first as the 1942–46 Manhattan Project operational spine. Chapters 1–2 for appointment and shock of thin knowledge; 3–8 for materials and production geography (Congo ore, Chicago plutonium, Hanford, Oak Ridge); 5 and 11 for Los Alamos and Oppenheimer; 9–10 and 12 for British, security, and ore trust diplomacy; 13–17 for German atomic intelligence and cross-Channel radiological fear; 18–25 for delivery sequence through Nagasaki; 26–31 for Congress, occupation science policy, AEC transition, and postwar Anglo-American strain. Use Appendix VIII with Chapter 21 for Trinity. Teller’s introduction is reception history (1983), not a wartime source.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 325–523: Groves’s scope statement (17 Sept 1942–31 Dec 1946) and Bush/Conant framing.
Lines 530–1115: “Oh, that thing”; Somervell; underestimation of scale.
Lines 1116–1629: “horrified”; Bush’s “too aggressive” note.
Lines 1630–1814: Sengier, Tizard warning, Shinkolobwe richness.
Lines 1815–2639: plutonium as beyond Columbus; 2 Dec 1942 proof after plant go-ahead.
Lines 2640–2919: Oppenheimer selection and Los Alamos site.
Lines 3870–5049: Oak Ridge processes and production headaches.
Lines 7260–8091: Alsos Italy; radioactive barrier fear for Overlord.
Lines 8890–9725: Alsos Germany; Goudsmit judgment on German scientists.
Lines 10102–10599: target list and Kyoto issue.
Lines 10976–11617 and Appendix VIII: Trinity.
Lines 11986–13511: Hiroshima and Nagasaki operations.
Lines 12674–12972: Farm Hall / Hahn on 6 August.
Lines 14549–15413: AEC legislation and Hyde Park aide-mémoire.
Lines 15414–15520: Groves’s moral-defense close.

Suggested Future Pages

Manhattan Engineer District (MED) — entity page on organization under Groves.
J. Robert Oppenheimer and Project Y — entity/event cluster for Los Alamos bomb design.
Hanford Engineer Works — entity page on plutonium production.
Clinton Engineer Works / Oak Ridge — entity page on isotope separation.
Alsos Mission — event page (Italy–France–Germany).
Trinity Test (16 July 1945) — event page.
Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki — event pages (operational thread).
Combined Development Trust and Congo Uranium — concept/event on ore geopolitics.
Atomic Energy Commission Transition (1946) — event page on MED to AEC.

Related Sources

Only Yesterday / Since Yesterday — public-mind spines for 1919–39; not technical precursors.
Jennet Conant, Tuxedo Park (to be added) — Loomis, radar, and scientific mobilization networks adjacent to atomic work.
Elliott Roosevelt, As He Saw It (to be added) — wartime conference diplomacy from a different seat.
Nevins & Hill Ford volumes (to be added) — industrial mass production parallel, not atomic.

Notes on Scope
First-person command memoir (1962) by the project’s military head, not a multi-archival synthesis. Exceptionally strong on decision sequence, contracting, site choice, security doctrine, delivery operations, and Groves’s judgments of persons; scientific priority disputes, Tokyo casualty ethics debates, and later historiography should be cross-checked when building contested event pages. Dates and document texts in appendices are high-value anchors; anecdotal dialogue is Groves’s recollection.

sources/kroc-grinding-it-out.title: [source] Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s (Kroc with Anderson, 1977)
sources/kroc-grinding-it-out.content:
Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s
Author: Ray Kroc with Robert Anderson (Preface by Paul D. Paganucci)
Published: 1977 (Contemporary Books); St. Martin’s Griffin ebook edition August 2016; Afterword © 1987 Robert Anderson
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 5e2271eadd452dd8a590286782db4dde)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/kroc-grinding-it-out.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 6,899 lines · ~70,549 words · 396,704 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters 3–5 cover Kroc’s interwar sales apprenticeship—Florida boom selling, Lily Tulip / Sanitary Cup years (1927–37), and Multimixer / Prince Castle entrepreneurship from 1938—core traveling-salesman and small-equipment material for this period. Mine first from Chs. 3–5 (plus Ch. 2’s early Lily Tulip/marriage close and Ch. 6’s brief 1930s drive-in opening). Chapters 1–2 hinge and 6–16 (1954 San Bernardino contract through McDonald’s empire, Padres, 1976 stats) belong primarily to 1946–89; use them only as brief forward pointers.
Overview
Grinding It Out is Ray A. Kroc’s first-person account of building McDonald’s, written with Robert Anderson. For this United States 1920–45 wiki the usable core is the long apprenticeship before McDonald’s: Bohemian-ancestry salesman philosophy, paper-cup routes and Florida winters, John Clark’s paper-cup decade, and the Multimixer gamble that made Kroc a national soda-fountain equipment man by mid-century. Period-gate hard after the 1954 San Bernardino visit except as forward continuity.
EPUB structure: Macmillan front matter; dedication and jacket blurb; Preface (Paganucci, June 1976); Chapters 1–16; Afterword; About the Author; Copyright.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / dedication / blurb
Lines 1–65. Cover; St. Martin’s ebook notices; dedication with wife Joni to the McDonald’s family; jacket line on Kroc as hamburger salesman, moneymaker, and storyteller (including San Diego Padres P.A. scolding).
Preface (Paul D. Paganucci)
Lines 66–172. Tuck School entrepreneurship frame; Kroc’s 1974 and 1976 Dartmouth visits with Fred Turner; “grinding it out” as thirty-year sales apprenticeship before the 1954 opportunity at age fifty-two; 1976 as McDonald’s first billion-dollar revenue year compared with IBM/Xerox timelines; industry impact on speed, price, fries, and cleanliness expectations. Dated Hanover, N.H., 29 June 1976.
Chapter 1
Lines 173–432. Philosophy of personal responsibility; Lily Tulip and Multimixer flashbacks; news of a San Bernardino stand running eight Multimixers; flight west; meeting Dick and Mac McDonald; Speedee Service System, limited menu, and assembly-line kitchen; Kroc’s offer to franchise additional units—“Well, what about me?”
Chapter 2
Lines 433–778. 1954 return to Chicago with signed contract at age fifty-two (diabetes, arthritis, prior surgeries); gray Chicago landing as omen; early life sketch closing the chapter—piano work, Ethel, Lily Tulip paper cups as America’s direction, father’s assent to marriage.
Chapter 3
Lines 779–1250. Early-1920s Florida underwater-lot boom as winter escape from seasonal cup selling; Kroc as salesman defending honest operators against “alligator lot” folklore; nightclub/piano work; Palm Island; Capone and later Latin Quarter notes; departure before the boom’s collapse.
Chapter 4
Lines 1251–1951. 1927–37 “decade of destiny” in paper cups; John Clark / Sanitary Cup and Service; full-time selling vow; disillusionment and the bargain that pushed Kroc toward Multimixer independence; formation of Prince Castle Sales with corporate capital terms that became an “anchor.”
Chapter 5
Lines 1952–2264. Entrepreneurship credo (Dartmouth 1976 aside); early Multimixer road years from 1938; Frejlack / capital squeeze and Arlington Heights mortgage; sleep discipline as “grinding it out”; stories of the McDonald brothers’ eight-mixer volume pull him west at fifty-two.
Chapter 6
Lines 2265–2653. 1930s Southern California drive-in context; McDonald brothers’ innovation; Kroc’s first Des Plaines store and obsessive standards (fries, cleanliness, detail fights with partner Ed); perfection as non-negotiable.
Chapter 7 — Harry Sonneborn
Lines 2654–2994. May 1955: Tastee-Freeze veteran Harry Sonneborn offers himself after watching Des Plaines; Franchise Realty / site-control logic; June Martino; funding strain while Prince Castle still bankrolls the franchise launch.
Chapter 8 — Fred Turner
Lines 2995–3401. February 1956: twenty-three-year-old Fred Turner answers a franchise ad with Joe Post; $1/hour Des Plaines apprenticeship; rise into corporate operations; seed of the later president/chairman path and operator training culture.
Chapter 9
Lines 3402–3812. Clem Bohr mechanic’s-lien crisis on East Coast sites; Sonneborn’s scramble; Milton Goldstandt path to a $1.5 million loan from three insurance companies for ~22½ percent of stock—financial bridge for expansion.
Chapter 10
Lines 3813–4249. Art Trygg as companion; meeting organist Joni Smith in St. Paul; divorce settlement with Ethel; McDonald brothers’ buyout demand (~$2.7 million / “a million apiece after taxes”); struggle to finance the purchase of name and rights.
Chapter 11
Lines 4250–4577. 1959: Sonneborn named president/CEO after the insurance loan; Kroc as chairman focused on retail/operations; California move and marriage to Jane; brief, jarring call from Joni.
Chapter 12
Lines 4578–4897. Beverly Hills years and 1963–64 construction/earnings surge (110 stores in 1963; 2.1 million net on 129.6 million sales cited for the following year); commuting to Chicago; Sonneborn studying a public offering; coming fight over building redesign.
Chapter 13
Lines 4898–5260. Final confrontation and Sonneborn’s resignation; loneliness at the top; operators’ convention and renewed interest in Roland and Joni Smith of Winnipeg / Rapid City.
Chapter 14
Lines 5261–5883. Reunion with Joni at San Diego Western Region Operators Convention; divorce from Jane and marriage to Joni; impulse to buy the San Diego Padres (“What on earth is that, a monastery?”).
Chapter 15
Lines 5884–6217. 1974 Padres ownership; P.A. microphone blast at opening home game; press and Joni’s reaction; defense of McDonald’s against cheap shots; Truman kitchen line—still not hanging up the spatula.
Chapter 16
Lines 6218–6623. Reincarnation joke about the 1929 Cubs; Kroc Foundation (medical science, not tax shelter); free-enterprise / pioneer-risk closing creed.
Afterword
Lines 6624–6814. Omissions apology; end-1976 snapshot—4,177 stores in the U.S. and 21 other countries; system-wide sales over 3 billion; corporate revenue over 1 billion; net earnings over 100 million; net worth 500 million; still “green and growing”; review blurbs.
About the Author / Copyright
Lines 6815–6899. Author note and Macmillan copyright block (© 1977 Ray A. Kroc; Afterword © 1987 Robert Anderson; Griffin 2016; eISBN 9781250127518). Publisher “About the Author” date line is garbled in this EPUB packaging—use Chronology from the narrative (1902 birth; career through mid-1970s; death 1984 outside this text’s close).
Coverage Guide
Lily Tulip / Multimixer apprenticeship (wiki core)
Chs. 3–5 (+ Ch. 2 close; Ch. 6 drive-in opening): Florida boom, paper-cup decade, Multimixer independence.
McDonald’s empire (forward → 1946–89)
Chs. 1–2 hinge and 6–16 + Afterword: San Bernardino, Des Plaines, Sonneborn/Turner, buyout, public growth, Padres—brief forward pointers only.
High-value passages to mine





















































































TopicWhereSan Bernardino Multimixer buzz; brothers’ Speedee SystemCh. 1“What about me?” franchise offerCh. 1Age-52 Chicago return with signed contractCh. 2Lily Tulip / early marriage flashbackCh. 2 (close)Florida winter selling; Silent Night / Palm IslandCh. 3John Clark bargain; Prince Castle Sales launchCh. 4Multimixer road grind; Frejlack cash squeezeCh. 5Des Plaines store; fries/cleanliness obsessionCh. 6Harry Sonneborn; Franchise Realty logicCh. 7Fred Turner $1/hour Des Plaines apprenticeshipCh. 8Clem Bohr liens; $1.5M insurance loan / stockCh. 9Joni Smith; Ethel divorce; $2.7M brother buyoutCh. 10Sonneborn as president; Jane marriageCh. 111963–64 store/earnings surge; public-offering studyCh. 12Sonneborn resignationCh. 13Joni reunion; Padres impulseCh. 141974 Padres P.A. scoldingCh. 15Kroc Foundation; pioneer-risk creedCh. 161976: 4,177 stores; $1B+ corporate revenueAfterword
Sources

Kroc, Ray, with Robert Anderson. Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s. Originally Contemporary Books, 1977; St. Martin’s Griffin ebook, 2016. ISBN 978-1-250-12751-8.
