sources/lansing-peace-negotiations.title: [source] The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative (Lansing, 1921)
sources/lansing-peace-negotiations.content:
The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative
Author: Robert Lansing
Published: Houghton Mifflin, Boston and New York, 1921 (Riverside Press, Cambridge)
Working text: Hathi/IA-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 395570, hash 9aa101984caf7f993208f1401cb494ff)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lansing-peace-negotiations.txt
Extract stats: 360 OCR page files · 11,672 lines · ~89,625 words · 536,579 bytes
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1866-1919 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because the book’s occasion is Wilson’s 11–12 February 1920 demand for Lansing’s resignation, the 1921 publication, and the Versailles/League settlement as the founding condition of the interwar decade. Mine first Chapter I and the Conclusion (resignation correspondence), Chapter XIX (Bullitt’s September 1919 Senate testimony during Wilson’s western tour), Chapters XIV–XVIII (Article 10, French assistance treaty, secret diplomacy, Shantung as Far Eastern inheritance), and the Covenant/Fourteen Points appendices as working texts. Paris conference mechanics (Chapters II–XIII: Wilson’s presence, substitute articles, 10 January Crillon episode, mandates drafting) remain primarily for the 1866–1919 wiki.
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as a single-volume 1921 Houghton Mifflin printing. Pages 00000001.txt through 00000360.txt are present with no gaps. The joined raw text includes Harvard library stamps and blank plate pages, title/copyright, Contents, Illustrations list, Chapters I–XIX, Conclusion, Appendices I–VI (Wilson’s original Covenant draft, Cecil plan, Versailles Covenant, Fourteen Points, Wilson’s 11 February 1918 principles, Shantung articles), and Index (imprint pp. 321–end). OCR shows typical hyphenation across lines and garbled facsimile/plate pages; chapter blocks are continuous and narrative-readable. Confidence high is a quoting-readability cue for this working text: check nearby context before long quotes from hyphenated lines or plate OCR.
Overview
Lansing, Wilson’s Secretary of State and a Commissioner Plenipotentiary to Negotiate Peace, writes after Wilson’s letter of 11 February 1920 asked him to resign for “reluctance and divergence of judgment.” He tenders the office the next day. The book is not a full history of the Paris Conference. It is a brief of the subjects on which the two men differed from the October 1918 armistice talks through delivery of the German treaty on 7 May 1919, with a coda on William C. Bullitt’s September 1919 Senate testimony.
For this wiki the source is the American interior of the peace that the 1920s inherited: Article 10 as the Senate’s target, the unratified French assistance treaty, Shantung as a Far Eastern grievance, secret Councils of Ten and Four as the method later blamed for the treaty’s reception, and Lansing’s February 1920 fall as the last official act of the Wilson peace. Pair it with Recent History of the United States Chapters XXV–XXVII for demobilization and normalcy, and with Only Yesterday for the public League fight, Red Scare onset, and the Post-war Decade’s opening. The Economic Pinch (1923) is a different postwar brief—domestic deflation and privilege—against which Lansing’s diplomatic narrative can be set.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter
Lines 1–273. Cover and title pages identify The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative by Robert Lansing, Houghton Mifflin, 1921. Copyright is reserved under the 1914 convention for named Latin American states. Contents lists nineteen chapters, a Conclusion, and six appendices. Illustrations include the American delegation at Paris (House, Lansing, Wilson, White, Bliss), Lansing’s commission, Wilson’s arrival on the Rue Royale, 14 December 1918, the delegation and staff, a Quai d’Orsay meeting after Wilson’s departure, Lansing’s “full powers” for the French assistance treaty, and the daily conference of the American Peace Commission.
Chapter I — Reasons for Writing a Personal Narrative
Lines 275–623. Opens with Wilson’s 11 February 1920 letter asking Lansing to give up the office because he accepted presidential guidance only with increasing reluctance, and with Lansing’s 12 February resignation letter dating the breach from January 1919. Lansing states that propriety kept him silent until a new administration was in power; the American people are entitled to know the subjects of disagreement over the Treaty of Versailles. He limits the narrative to those differences, not to a complete conference diary.
Chapter II — Mr. Wilson’s Presence at the Peace Conference
Lines 624–1069. October 1918: Austria-Hungary’s peace overtures, the Bulgarian armistice, Turkish collapse, and the German armistice of 11 November. Wilson sends Colonel Edward M. House as Special Commissioner to the Supreme War Council (Clemenceau, Lloyd George, Orlando). House tells Lansing that both will be plenipotentiaries and that Wilson is considering attending in person. Lansing argues against a sitting President at the conference: it mixes the office with delegate bargaining, weakens the Secretary of State, and exposes the President to European pressure. Wilson sails 4 December 1918. The American Commission is Wilson, Lansing, House, Henry White, and General Tasker H. Bliss.
Chapter III — General Plan for a League of Nations
Lines 1070–1762. Lansing holds that Wilson went to Paris chiefly to put a League into the treaty. From American entry in April 1917 Wilson treated a strong international agency as the condition of a lasting peace. Lansing supports a League in principle but opposes an affirmative military/economic guaranty of territory and independence, a primacy of the Great Powers, and haste in drafting. He prefers a “self-denying covenant” (negative undertaking not to violate independence and integrity) and equality of nations. The chapter includes the facsimile of Lansing’s commission as plenipotentiary.
Chapter IV — Substitute Articles Proposed
Lines 1763–2764. The President, White, and Lansing arrive in Paris 14 December 1918; House and Bliss are already there. On 23 December Lansing sends Wilson a “Secret and Urgent” letter from the Hôtel de Crillon warning that the proposed mutual guaranty will split other governments and raise constitutional, Monroe Doctrine, and congressional objections at home. He drafts substitute articles based on equality of nations and a self-denying rather than affirmative obligation. Wilson does not adopt them. This is the longest chapter and the core documentary brief on Lansing’s alternative Covenant language.
Chapter V — The Affirmative Guaranty and Balance of Power
Lines 2765–2868. Clemenceau’s Chamber speech of 30 December 1918 defends the balance of power and a concert of the four allied Great Powers. Wilson had just denounced the balance of power at Manchester. Lansing and House agree the doctrine must not be revived; Lansing argues that Wilson’s affirmative guaranty would in practice rest on the Great Powers and thus continue the same system under a new name.
Chapter VI — The President’s Plan and the Cecil Plan
Lines 2869–3237. Lansing examines Wilson’s draft Covenant (Appendix I). He finds loose drafting curable, but the use of force to make good the guaranty, Great-Power primacy, weak arbitration, no permanent international judiciary, and the mandatory system to be contrary to American ideals and traditions. He compares the draft with the published Smuts plan and with Lord Robert Cecil’s British plan (Appendix II), which he prefers on several points, including the absence of Wilson’s affirmative guaranty.
Chapter VII — Self-Determination
Lines 3238–3655. Tracks the mutual guaranty from Article III of Wilson’s original draft (territorial integrity plus future “self-determination” readjustments) through Article 7 of the revised draft to Article 10 of the Versailles Covenant. Lansing treats self-determination as a phrase dangerous in application: it invites irredentism, cannot be applied consistently (Ireland, India, American subject peoples), and was stripped from the final Article 10, which kept the guaranty without the safety-valve.
Chapter VIII — The Conference of January 10, 1919
Lines 3656–3748. At the Hôtel Crillon Wilson reviews his typewritten Covenant with the American Commissioners. Lansing raises objections of principle and policy; Wilson, as Lansing reads words and manner, will not receive them. Lansing then decides to take no further part in preparing or revising the Covenant text, lest subsequent silence be read as neglect or disloyalty. This episode is his explanation of later ignorance of League drafting.
Chapter IX — A Resolution Instead of the Covenant
Lines 3749–4154. After 10 January, Lansing tries delay: put only general principles in a preliminary treaty, then draft a detailed League later, preferably in a separate treaty or a world congress including neutrals. He prepares a resolution of declarations on the creation, nature, and purposes of a League. Wilson proceeds with a complete Covenant in the peace treaty.
Chapter X — The Guaranty in the Revised Covenant
Lines 4155–4279. In the three weeks before the League Commission meets, Wilson and House revise the draft with British and French statesmen; Gordon Auchincloss and David Hunter Miller produce a memorandum later published through Bullitt’s Senate hearing. The affirmative guaranty survives into the revised text.
Chapter XI — International Arbitration
Lines 4280–4531. On 3 February 1919, the day the League Commission first meets, Lansing writes Wilson from the Crillon on arbitral procedure: litigants’ national “judges” act as advocates; a permanent international court is needed. He treats this as a legal subject on which he may still speak without re-entering general Covenant drafting.
Chapter XII — Report of Commission on League of Nations
Lines 4532–5015. The Commission, Wilson presiding, holds ten meetings between 3 and 14 February 1919 and reports to a plenary of the Conference on the Preliminaries of Peace. Lansing praises Wilson’s presentation as literary oratory. The reported Covenant improves expression and drops some objectionable features of the first draft; if one accepts Wilson’s theory of organization, little remains to criticize except remaining inexactness. Lansing does not accept the theory.
Chapter XIII — The System of Mandates
Lines 5016–5431. Lansing objects to mandates on legal grounds and on policy: American guardianship of Near Eastern peoples aspiring to independence would break the tradition of aloofness from European political quarrels. The Council of Ten discusses mandates for German colonies and the Ottoman inheritance. Wilson rejects condominium and treats mandates as a duty of the new order. Lansing records the legal puzzle of sovereignty under a League mandate.
Chapter XIV — Differences as to the League Recapitulated
Lines 5432–5936. The differences are called irreconcilable. As a commissioned representative Lansing follows instructions rather than resign at Paris. He holds that Wilson endangered American and presidential prestige to obtain a defective League plan worked out with Smuts and Cecil, and that making the Covenant the principal feature of the German treaty was both wrong in principle and bad policy for Senate acceptance.
Chapter XV — The Proposed Treaty with France
Lines 5937–6345. Parallel American and British treaties of assistance to France in case of unprovoked German attack form, with France, a triple defensive alliance with the same object as Article 10 and even stronger affirmative force. Lansing’s 20 March note on “Impressions as to the Present Situation” records House circulating the proposal; White, Bliss, and Lansing agree that such an alliance would destroy the chief reason for the League as planned. Facsimile of Lansing’s full powers to negotiate the French treaty is among the plates.
Chapter XVI — Lack of an American Programme
Lines 6346–7128. A central charge: Wilson gave the Commissioners no detailed programme beyond the Fourteen Points and later addresses. The first five Points are principles; the next eight name territorial adjustments without boundaries; the Fourteenth is the League. Without authoritative interpretation the Commissioners lacked instructions “to negotiate peace.” Inquiry commissions and experts existed, but the President did not convert their work into a brief the delegation could use with other delegations.
Chapter XVII — Secret Diplomacy
Lines 7129–8104. Lansing attacks closed negotiations among the principal statesmen as a breach of “open covenants…openly arrived at.” Directing bodies—the Council of Ten (identical in membership with the Supreme War Council) and, from late March 1919, the Council of Four—never received a mandate from the full Conference. Wilson’s daily conversations with European leaders were seldom reported to the American Commission, except possibly to House. Smaller nations and even the American Commissioners were left in uncertainty.
Chapter XVIII — The Shantung Settlement
Lines 8105–8992. Near the last moment, with Orlando absent in Rome, Wilson, Clemenceau, and Lloyd George order Shantung articles granting former German rights in the peninsula to Japan. Japan, in return, drops a racial-equality amendment to the Covenant, agrees to sign the German treaty, and orally promises later restoration of Chinese sovereignty—a promise Lansing says was not confirmed in writing. He holds that an impartial commission would have decided otherwise, and that the American Commissioners considered resignation over the settlement.
Chapter XIX — The Bullitt Affair
Lines 8993–9311. William C. Bullitt, formerly of the American Commission, tells the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on 12 September 1919 that Lansing called many parts of the treaty thoroughly bad, especially Shantung and the League, and predicted the Senate would reject the treaty if it understood what it meant. The statement is published while Wilson is in the West appealing for the League. Lansing makes no comment on Bullitt’s disclosure of a confidential conversation; he includes it because Wilson later treated it as proof that Lansing’s mind had not gone along with his.
Conclusion
Lines 9312–9388. Recapitulation: from before Wilson’s 4 December 1918 departure through delivery of the German treaty on 7 May 1919, disagreements were many; Wilson rejected or ignored volunteered advice; Lansing followed unwillingly. Personal frictions were minor. The February 1920 letters are explained by these official differences (Wilson also cited Lansing’s calling Cabinet meetings during the President’s illness—mentioned as the cause Wilson specifically stated).
Appendices I–VI
Lines 9389–10750. I: Wilson’s original Covenant draft laid before the American Commission 10 January 1919. II: Cecil’s League plan. III: Covenant as in the Treaty of Versailles. IV: Fourteen Points (8 January 1918 address). V: Principles of 11 February 1918. VI: Versailles Articles 156–158 on Shantung (Kiaochow, Tsingtao–Tsinanfu Railway, cables to Shanghai and Chefoo).
Index
Lines 10751–11672. Useful entries: affirmative guaranty, American Commission, Article 10, Bliss, Bullitt, Cecil, Clemenceau, Council of Four/Ten, equality of nations, House, mandates, Monroe Doctrine, self-denying covenant, self-determination, Shantung, Wilson.
Coverage Guide
Use this source for the 1920 rupture and the Versailles inheritance: why Article 10 and the affirmative guaranty became the Senate’s target, how Shantung and the French alliance entered American postwar politics, and how Lansing narrated February 1920 as the delayed invoice of January–May 1919. It is not a military history of 1917–18 and not a substitute for the treaty text or the Senate record. Mine first the resignation letters, Bullitt/Senate coda, Article 10, French treaty, Shantung, and secret diplomacy; use paxson-recent-history-united-states and allen-only-yesterday for the public League fight and 1919–20 aftermath. Paris drafting mechanics remain primarily for the 1866–1919 sister page.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 275–314: Wilson’s 11 February 1920 letter and Lansing’s 12 February resignation; the January 1919 dating of the breach.
Lines 624–680: House’s appointment to the Supreme War Council; Wilson’s decision to sit at Paris.
Lines 1763–1850: 23 December 1918 Crillon letter against the affirmative guaranty; constitutional and Monroe Doctrine objections.
Lines 2765–2820: Clemenceau on the balance of power versus Wilson at Manchester.
Lines 3238–3300: Article III → Article 7 → Article 10; self-determination dropped, guaranty retained.
Lines 3656–3748: 10 January 1919 Crillon conference; Lansing withdraws from Covenant drafting.
Lines 4280–4330: 3 February 1919 letter on international courts.
Lines 5016–5060: mandates versus American aloofness; Near East guardianship.
Lines 5937–5980: French assistance treaty as a Great-Power alliance duplicating Article 10.
Lines 6346–6400: no detailed American programme beyond the Fourteen Points.
Lines 7129–7180: Council of Ten and Council of Four as unauthorized secret directorates.
Lines 8105–8160: Shantung bargain with Japan; racial-equality amendment withdrawn; oral restoration promise.
Lines 8993–9100: Bullitt testimony of 12 September 1919 during Wilson’s western tour.
Appendices IV–VI: working texts of the Fourteen Points, February 1918 principles, and Shantung articles.

Suggested Future Pages

Robert Lansing — entity page: Secretary of State through the peace, February 1920 resignation, 1921 narrative.
League of Nations / Article 10 in American politics — concept page: Senate target, reservations, 1920 election aftertaste.
Treaty of Versailles (American non-ratification) — event page pairing this interior narrative with Allen’s League fight and Paxson’s normalcy chapters.
Shantung Settlement — event page: Kiaochow, Japanese succession to German rights, China, racial-equality amendment; Far Eastern inheritance into the 1920s.
Treaty of Assistance to France — event page: unratified American–French–British defensive arrangement of 1919.

Related Sources

Recent History of the United States — postwar / normalcy chapters as near-contemporary spine beside this insider brief.
Only Yesterday — public mind of the League fight, demobilization, and the Post-war Decade.
The Economic Pinch — 1923 domestic-political-economy brief on the same postwar years.
The House of Morgan — Diplomatic Age finance through the peace and the 1920s.

Notes on Scope
This is an interested party’s brief, published in 1921 to explain a forced resignation. Use it as direct evidence of Lansing’s positions, of documents he quotes, and of how the American Commission experienced Wilson’s method. Do not treat it as a complete or impartial history of the Conference or of Allied motives. The February 1920 Cabinet-meeting charge Wilson named in the correspondence is acknowledged in the Conclusion and not litigated in the body.

sources/lindbergh-economic-pinch.title: [source] The Economic Pinch (Lindbergh, 1923)
sources/lindbergh-economic-pinch.content:
The Economic Pinch
Author: C. A. Lindbergh (Charles August Lindbergh, 1859–1924), former U.S. Representative from Minnesota
Published: Dorrance & Company, Inc., Philadelphia, 1923 (copyright 1923 Dorrance & Company, Inc.; all rights reserved; manufactured in the United States of America)
Working text: Page-image OCR zip (HathiTrust-style sequential .txt pages) via Anna’s Archive hash c2340875a51675bde5067726234e0a71 (OCLC 3260455)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lindbergh-economic-pinch.txt
Extract stats: 7,058 lines · ~46,494 words · 263,283 bytes (260 page files concatenated in order)
Completeness Assessment
The working text is a full-volume OCR assembly of 260 page images (library stamps and blank leaves included). Body is complete for wiki use: title and copyright → Contents → Book I (Ch. I–XXII) → Book II (Ch. I–V) → General Index. Printed book pagination in the OCR runs roughly 9–247 for main text; file pages 1–14 are library/title/contents front matter; Book I body begins file page 15; Book II half-title is file page 203; Index begins about file page 253. OCR noise is continuous (broken words, running headers, hyphenation, occasional garble) but chapter openings and argument structure are recoverable throughout. This is the elder Lindbergh (Congressman), not Charles A. Lindbergh the aviator.
Overview
Writing in 1923 amid the postwar agricultural and industrial deflation, Lindbergh offers a populist–progressive indictment of “profiteers” as a fourth, useless group above farmers, wage workers, and legitimate business. Book I diagnoses concentration of wealth, capital–labor conflict, kept press and Congress, the Federal Reserve Act as a private profit system, “scientifically created” panics, the war boom and 1920–22 deflation, the Esch-Cummins railway guarantee spirit, congressional investigations and rules, legislative blocs, and “progressive” inadequacy. Book II shifts to program: business and politics as a game whose rules must be rewritten by united farmer–labor–useful-business federations, team-work, American associations on common ground, world relations, and government “by the people—for the people.”
For this wiki the tract is a near-contemporary primary voice of Midwestern agrarian–anti-monopoly politics in the early Coolidge years—Federal Reserve and railway legislation, Liberty Bond transfers, farm distress, and bloc politics—set against Allen’s more middle-class Only Yesterday narrative of the same decade.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter (title, copyright, contents)
File pages 7–12. Title The Economic Pinch by C. A. Lindbergh; Dorrance, Philadelphia; copyright 1923. Contents list Book I chapters I–XXII (printed pp. 9–191) and Book II chapters I–V (printed pp. 199–236) plus General Index (247).
Book I — Chapter I — A Key to the Good Things
File pages 15–22. ~1,570 words.
The key to the world’s good things is the mind; failure of honest thought leaves most people under the influence of a few who control the things that control others. Lindbergh sketches farmer, wage worker, and small business man as groups whose futures are gambles, then names a fourth group that has “taken possession.” Politics still fails to give the public satisfaction because office-holding, not condition-bettering, is most politicians’ object. Protest votes and rosy candidates do not yield industrial independence; business interests must first be understood in relation to each other before political agreement is possible.
Book I — Chapter II — Three Useful Groups; One Useless Group
File pages 23–26. ~720 words.
Economically the nation divides into three useful groups—farmers, wage workers, and business managing exchange and distribution—plus a fourth, the profiteers, not classed as useful though some individuals do useful work. The three useful groups have been half antagonistic, especially politically, and lose by it. They should establish a common field and conference committees, then present united concrete demands so officials of any party cannot dodge. The United States Chamber of Commerce is cited as a private model of how interests put measures in form and force action; profiteers draft bills whose titles promise relief while the body takes it away. Existing conditions are intolerable and leading to chaos.
Book I — Chapter III — The American Nobility
File pages 27–30. ~705 words.
European kings could not make the nobility bear taxes, so burdens fell on peasants and produced revolutions. American profiteers ape that nobility but are better fortified: they shift taxes and burdens, rob by authority of law, and secure trust-made statutes through subservient officials. Whichever party the people elect, officials betray them; exceptions are never enough. The country nears a state of anarchy; the super-wealthy drive toward destruction; hope lies in popular action that may even save the profiteers from their own race for stolen wealth—not as profiteers.
Book I — Chapter IV — The Capital and Labor Conflict
File pages 31–41. ~2,010 words.
Government and business administration have created capital–labor conflict that harms farmer, wage worker, and useful business and will wreck the capitalist too if continued. Capital presently has the best of it. Workers do not deny property rights but deny owners’ right to use property to subject industry to toll. War and postwar inflation made thousands of new millionaires; then farmers were pressed to expand and sell below cost while wage workers were deflated by idleness and wage cuts. Centralized wealth bought Liberty Bonds and other assets at discount and became a compounding liability charged against producing energy. When capital “strikes,” the press calls it hard times or panic; when labor strikes, labor is condemned. Railway Labor Board language equating labor’s lot with capital’s “earnings” (profits) is read as the keynote of official bias. Machinery’s gains partly delay the penalty but also swell capital that workers must again pay profits upon.
Book I — Chapter V — The Capitalistic Aim
File pages 42–50. ~1,820 words.
Railroad capital already approximates twenty billions including water; with other trusts and wealth controllers the total approaches or reaches two hundred billions, whose compounded profits under present law will take all workers’ earnings above bare subsistence. Capital will not destroy the worker any more than a farmer destroys his team, but will make labor the slave on bare keep. Minimum wage and minimum farm price are not fundamental remedies though temporarily favor-able; the fallacy of legal “reasonable profit” is the main trouble and a seed of future wars. Lindbergh does not condemn all profit—human beings still need inducement—but insists much better rules are already within reach.
Book I — Chapter VI — Classification of Property Relations
File pages 51–59. ~1,310 words.
Exaggerated profit to the few unsettles the world and amounts to industrial slave service. Readjustment of business relations to present intelligence is required. A small percentage group can double wealth by cutting farm prices and wages, raising living costs, or forcing more hours and output. Permanent peace is impossible while labor is forced to guarantee profit as under Esch-Cummins practice and Federal Reserve sanction. Strikes are usually rebellions against wrong conditions; correction points to Washington, where important laws are made.
Book I — Chapter VII — The Press, and Others
File pages 60–71. ~2,375 words.
A sample capitalist-paper editorial on the railroad shopmen’s strike and the Railway Labor Board’s outlawing of the organization illustrates kept-press framing. Unlike the Revolutionary generation, the people have means of correction short of force, yet they still petition while measures are pigeonholed or worsened. Profiteers exploit through the Federal Reserve Bank Act and Esch-Cummins Railway Act and through gifts of water-powers, minerals, and forests; the bank and railway acts are the greatest public gifts to wealth.
Book I — Chapter VIII — Believing + Voting — Thinking
File pages 72–82. ~2,135 words.
National catastrophe follows from accepting kept-press falsehoods, adroit schemes of the wealthy, and Congressmen who sacrifice constituents for press support and committee place. The Federal Reserve Act’s title implies public good and government ownership; Lindbergh calls that promise a deliberate lie—the government owns no stock; “IT IS A SNAKE.” Subsidiary chambers of commerce and dominated associations secure what wealth demands. Note on W. P. G. Harding of the Federal Reserve Board and missions such as Cuban financial reorganization during inflation and early deflation years.
Book I — Chapter IX — Banks and the People
File pages 83–88. ~1,150 words.
Everyone is interested in banks; bankers direct the course of business more than the press molds opinion. Bigger is not always stronger; borrowers determine standing. Finance in big bankers’ hands practically controls business interests; Europe in 1923 is stranded on finance. Banks are organized to use other people’s money; deposits—often credit, not real money—are what they want. The Civil War National Bank System served profiteers but grew too limited; people wanted fairness, profiteers a bigger profit scheme—“Let us see who won.”
Book I — Chapter X — The Federal Reserve Act
File pages 89–100. ~2,380 words.
Before 1907, trust combination and boom strained the old financial system; big interests needed a finance system of their own and control of most banks. Popular dissatisfaction was real but inarticulate. The Act, in Lindbergh’s reading, corners gold and gold certificates, puts finances under big banks, and is a private system for maximum profit from other people’s money—inconsistent with free government. Panics recur (1890–91, 1893–94, 1897, 1903, 1907, 1913, 1921–23); under the new act they can be scientifically created rather than bungled combinations of circumstance.
Book I — Chapter XI — Panics Now Scientifically Created
File pages 101–104. ~790 words.
The present panic is the first scientifically created one, worked as a mathematical problem. At the tail of a panic everything bottoms except money, which booms. Emergency currency legislation furnished banks controlled by speculators until the Reserve could operate fully. For gold plus eligible paper pledged, the Treasury issued multiple paper dollars at a trivial charge; Reserve banks accumulated more than three billion in gold and could end stringency at once if Wall Street profit lay that way.
Book I — Chapter XII — The War Boom
File pages 105–108. ~650 words.
Speculators bought American commodities for European shipment and resold at enormous profit, taking American securities held abroad at bargain prices. War destruction and Allied demand pushed high wages and farm prices; almost everyone expanded. Reserve mechanics—gold pledged for paper at half of one per cent to the government, member rates as the Board directs—concentrated power; at one time over $3.5 billion of such money, more than half the country’s money stock, was in that channel. Farmers, workers, small business, and country banks ran at high speed, little expecting Wall Street to “ring up” the 1920–22 panic.
Book I — Chapter XIII — War Deflation
File pages 109–113. ~970 words.
Before the new panic Wall Street aimed to hit farmers especially hard and to deflate before the costly crop was marketed. Billions made in the boom would be worth less if money stayed cheap. Under Reserve and Esch-Cummins powers the controllers could drive the panic as hard as they wished. People held billions in Liberty Bonds that profiteers had been too busy to buy heavily at issue; panic prices delivered those bonds. Future public and private indebtedness was made to command higher interest for long periods—mortgage on the backs of the living and their children.
Book I — Chapter XIV — Ultimate Breakdown, or Radical Change
File pages 114–125. ~2,400 words.
Boom then collapse of commodity prices (except trust-controlled lines) and the swing in money’s purchasing power set up a future boom for profiteers unless “the radicals” scare it away. The last eight years have doubly mortgaged the future. Mid-argument Lindbergh notes that since earlier chapters were written, bankers and big business find they have nearly killed “the goose that laid the golden egg”—the farmer—and now call conferences. Farmers and wage workers are still exploited; acts such as Lenroot-Anderson are claimed as claims to re-election while parasites take the substance and honest industry the crumbs.
Book I — Chapter XV — The Esch-Cummins Railway Act
File pages 126–130. ~910 words.
No full railway treatise is attempted. Congressmen who voted for Esch-Cummins deny a profit guarantee; Lindbergh answers that after an express six-month guarantee the act in substance charges the Interstate Commerce Commission to fix rates to yield return, and that common ownership links railroads with other great trusts. House and Senate majorities of lawyers and bankers understand the language. The 1922 shopmen’s strike costs could be folded into “cost of maintenance and operation” and recovered in rates—one purpose of the act being to subordinate labor, right or wrong.
Book I — Chapter XVI — “Congressional Investigations”
File pages 131–138. ~1,510 words.
Important acts leave doors open for profiteering; general “stupidity” always favoring wealth is unreasonable as accident. Delayed investigations after damage (loyalty badges to be removed, billions already lost) educate little compared with personal investigation. Speakers and press seek to make others think as they wish them to act; anyone who would know the truth must weigh arguments himself.
Book I — Chapter XVII — The Rules of Congress
File pages 139–148. ~1,900 words.
People need not master every parliamentary trick, but should know that introduction is easy and passage runs a gauntlet. Calendars and leadership fritter time so that bills important to the people and opposed by profiteers never reach consideration. Rules are mainly bad because leaders have served special privilege; the same rules could serve the people under different leaders. A people’s organization removed from party prejudice can check manipulation.
Book I — Chapter XVIII — The Legislative Bloc
File pages 149–155. ~1,400 words.
A bloc or balance of power groups enough votes to force compromise when two larger sides are nearly equal. It may join either side or block action. Special privilege’s luxury leads some to dream the government can make a living for all—an impossibility without briefly exploiting the exploiters. The bloc is a “dog in the manger”: useful if “our” dog, but affirmative action is required to stop serfdom; over-reliance on blocs wastes time and money.
Book I — Chapter XIX — From Lowest to Highest
File pages 156–174. ~3,890 words.
Man’s distinction is intellect over brute force. Nations go to war over disputes smaller than many home problems while neglecting industrial justice. Great individual achievements have not produced a satisfactory plan of justice among persons. Education, schools, and what teachers may say are constrained; children deserve facts at home and in school so the next generation can correct what parents fail to correct—and worse times will come first unless parents learn and force teaching of the truth.
Book I — Chapter XX — Economic Evil, and “Progressives”
File pages 175–186. ~2,400 words.
Those who dominate have no moral right to rule by exploitation; expediency lasts only while the public lacks a remedy. Returning all stolen wealth overnight would not itself found a system. Concrete example: petroleum waste and Standard Oil of New Jersey’s 400 per cent dividend (1922) and another Standard company’s 900 per cent. “Progressive” officeholders drown in small demands, speeches, and constituent errands and cannot do constructive work without risking defeat by constituents who do not understand priorities.
Book I — Chapter XXI — Government; Nation; People
File pages 187–196. ~1,900 words.
Nation and people differ from “government” as administration of political and industrial affairs. True citizenship supports common welfare even while criticizing administration and laws. Arbitrary class lines by wealth and work put a small non-working upper class first; workers alone can reverse enjoyment of the fruits of labor. Mr. and Mrs. Voter must rise above monopolists’ cunning and follow natural law so monopoly serves instead of enslaves.
Book I — Chapter XXII — The Way Out
File pages 197–202. ~840 words.
Abstract subjects and concrete acts have been treated in a human way; readers should draw their own conclusions. Individual action based on truth, not blind following of leaders, is required. Latent powers exist to deal aright; steam and photography show how fast technique moves within living memory. People must create their own conditions and relations with each other and the world rather than let others create conditions that control them.
Book II — Chapter I — The Greatest Game
File pages 205–215. ~2,210 words.
Book I covered general conditions; Book II takes up rules and moves by which workers—including legitimate business—may improve living and approach constitutional individual rights. Business and life advantages are a game: capital confuses and splits workers while exploiting them all; politics writes the rules, so politics matters. Civilized requirements create mutual need; understanding of respective rights is required to break capital’s stranglehold.
Book II — Chapter II — Team-Work for Victory
File pages 216–222. ~1,220 words.
Farmer, wage worker, and legitimate business must stand as one force against separate defeat by capital; relative rights must be adjusted even if not perfect. Organization of all useful elements is required. Federal Reserve and Esch-Cummins showed on their faces how profiteers would use them. Not all is bad; the Constitution still belongs to the people, who may interpret it toward the Preamble’s spirit and use its amending resources through knowledge and united support.
Book II — Chapter III — The American Federations
File pages 223–226. ~650 words.
Existing farm, labor, professional, and business organizations lack common ground to coordinate and adjust differences. Association purposes should be educational and protective against exploitation, waste, and selfish corporate purpose. Present unfair business–politics partnership is again “taxation without representation.” Escape is economic knowledge and honest political control of business while leaving individual initiative that does not trespass the common welfare. Independence of blind political leadership is essential.
Book II — Chapter IV — World Relations
File pages 227–241. ~words in extract band ~2,500+.
Extends the domestic argument to international finance, war settlements, and examples of popular force against governments abroad (Germany, Austria, Italy, Turkey, Hungary, Portugal, Greece, Mexico, and others appear in the OCR). American policy and foreign debts/commerce are treated as continuous with the profiteer problem at home; the useful groups’ federation logic is applied beyond national borders. (OCR density and running headers are heavier in this band; use raw pages 227–241 for quotation.)
Book II — Chapter V — By the People—For the People
File pages 242–252. Closes the program with the claim that government must be made to execute the people’s will, not merely voice it weakly. Direct popular energy, informed federation, and refusal of machine rule are restated as the path from Book I’s diagnosis to durable self-rule under the Constitution’s spirit.
General Index
File pages ~253–260. Topical index (banks and Federal Reserve, farmer and wage worker, gold, Esch-Cummins, panics, Liberty Bonds, Congress, etc.) pointing to printed pages.
Coverage Guide









































TopicBest chaptersThree useful groups vs profiteersI–III, XXI; Book II I–IIICapital–labor, war inflation/deflationIV–V, XII–XIVFederal Reserve, gold, panicsVIII–XI, XII–XIIIEsch-Cummins / railways / 1922 shopmenVI–VII, XVCongress: investigations, rules, blocsXVI–XVIII, XXProgram: federation, Constitution, team-workXXII; Book II I–V1920–23 farm crisis, Liberty BondsIV, XIII–XIVPress and “kept” opinionVII–VIII, XVI
High-Value Passages (for entity/concept work)

Opening “key is the mind” and four-group setup (Ch. I–II)
“American nobility” / profiteers as fortified nobility (Ch. III)
Liberty Bonds bought at discount after deflation (Ch. IV, XIII)
$200 billion capital and “reasonable profit” critique (Ch. V)
Federal Reserve title as deception; “IT IS A SNAKE” (Ch. VIII)
Scientifically created panics; gold multiple and $3+ billion hoard (Ch. X–XI)
War boom mechanics and $3.5 billion Reserve paper (Ch. XII)
Esch-Cummins rate-of-return and strike-cost pass-through (Ch. XV)
Bloc as “dog in the manger” (Ch. XVIII)
Book II game metaphor and farmer–labor–business team-work (Book II I–II)

Limitations and Caveats

Partisan primary tract, not neutral economic history; claims about Reserve ownership, panic design, and congressional motive are advocacy framed as exposé.
OCR quality requires checking wiki/raw/lindbergh-economic-pinch.txt (or original page images) before long quotation; hyphens and headers break many lines.
Person disambiguation: author is Charles August Lindbergh (1859–1924), Minnesota congressman and father of the aviator; do not merge with 1927 flight or 1930s–40s America First material without a separate source.
Dated statistics (rail capital, gold stocks, dividend percentages) are 1922–23 polemical figures as printed, not modern revised series.

Source
Lindbergh, C. A. The Economic Pinch. Philadelphia: Dorrance & Company, Inc., 1923. Working text: sequential page OCR from Anna’s Archive zip hash c2340875a51675bde5067726234e0a71 (OCLC 3260455) → wiki/raw/lindbergh-economic-pinch.txt.

sources/lyons-david-sarnoff.title: [source] David Sarnoff: A Biography (Lyons, 1966)
sources/lyons-david-sarnoff.content:
David Sarnoff: A Biography
Author: Eugene Lyons
Published: 1966 (Harper & Row, New York; first edition)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash e30c54dd944dfea91261cdfdaf2d8e20)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lyons-david-sarnoff.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 15,099 lines · ~159,840 words · 1,028,553 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
OCR note: Scan OCR (pdftotext -layout); frequent hyphenation and name garbling (Samoff for Sarnoff, Bom for Born).
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters 6–19 cover RCA’s birth and “Sarnoff’s Folly,” radio networks and talkies, the RCA presidency, Depression research policy, the struggle for television, and World War II electronics/European theatre service through 1945—core broadcasting-and-electronics material for this period. Mine first from Chs. 6–19. Chapters 1–5 (immigrant/Marconi/Titanic) also support continuity and are shared with 1866–1919; Chapters 20–26 (postwar TV/color) belong primarily to 1946–89.
Overview
David Sarnoff is Eugene Lyons’s life of the RCA chief—immigrant childhood through electronics leadership: ghetto childhood in Russia; New York slums and Marconi messenger/operator years (including Titanic survivor traffic); commercial manager and “radio music box” prophecy; creation of the Radio Corporation of America; NBC networks and talkie/phonograph alliances; Depression research stubbornness and the fight for television; World War II mobilization and European theatre service; postwar “father of television,” color-TV triumph, setbacks, public-figure roles, and still-active eighth decade as of the mid-1960s.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers how American radio broadcasting and RCA power were built between the early 1920s and V-E/V-J: networks, Depression R&D, prewar television struggle, and wartime electronics. Period-gate hard on color-TV succession chapters except as brief forward pointers.
PDF structure: jacket/title/copyright; dedication; Contents (Chs. 1–26 + Index); Chapters 1–26; Index; residual jacket blurbs.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–301. Jacket copy; title; books by Lyons; Harper & Row 1966 copyright (LC 66-10632); dedication to grandchildren; Contents.
Chapter 1 — Success Story
Lines 302–766. Frames Sarnoff as rags-to-riches classic of the electronic age—radio, TV, satellites, gadgetry—rather than merely another fortune tale.
Chapter 2 — Twin of the Electron
Lines 767–1286. Birth of wireless as long scientific arc; Sarnoff’s life paired with the electron’s industrial coming-of-age.
Chapter 3 — Boyhood in the Promised Land
Lines 1287–1901. Immigrant arrival; New York “promised land” boyhood and early American weeks.
Chapter 4 — The Formative Years
Lines 1902–2497. Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company apprenticeship; formative wireless-operator years.
Chapter 5 — The Titanic and the Music Box
Lines 2498–3191. 1912 voting-age year; Titanic wireless traffic fame; early “radio music box” vision for broadcasting.
Chapter 6 — The Radio Corporation Is Born
Lines 3192–3774. Commercial manager role; RCA’s birth from Marconi/GE wartime communications complex.
Chapter 7 — “Sarnoff’s Folly”
Lines 3775–4380. Early RCA push for broadcasting dismissed as folly; Sarnoff’s energy inside the new corporation.
Chapter 8 — The Self-Appointed Leader
Lines 4381–4875. After age thirty (May 1921), self-assertion as industry leader.
Chapter 9 — Prophet with Honor
Lines 4876–5517. Forecasts of industry growth; forums with Hoover-era figures; prophet reputation.
Chapter 10 — Networks and Talkies
Lines 5518–5995. Private life (Lizette; sons Robert, Edward, Thomas) beside network building and phonograph/talkie alliances.
Chapter 11 — A New President Is Born
Lines 5996–6593. Phonograph–radio “marriage”; path to RCA presidency.
Chapter 12 — Double Trouble
Lines 6594–7119. Presidency amid Depression dual crises for radio industry and company.
Chapter 13 — The Roosevelt Years
Lines 7120–7908. Depression research as first ballast to cut—Sarnoff refuses to jettison R&D under bookkeeping pressure.
Chapter 14 — Quest for Quality
Lines 7909–8535. September 1937 board/quality drive; programming and technical standards agenda.
Chapter 15 — Struggle for Television
Lines 8536–9219. Prewar and wartime TV development fight; antenna forest as postwar symbol introduced retrospectively.
Chapter 16 — At the Half-Century Mark
Lines 9220–9648. WWII decorations and half-century career mark framing.
Chapter 17 — Another World War
Lines 9649–10037. 7 Dec 1941 offer of RCA facilities to FDR; electronics switch to military radio, radar, tubes, navigation.
Chapter 18 — In the European Theatre
Lines 10038–10528. Near age fifty-one; wartime service in the European theatre.
Chapter 19 — D Day and After
Lines 10529–11031. Allied invasion and Sarnoff’s wartime communications role through war’s end.
Chapter 20 — Father of Television
Lines 11032–11646. Dec 1944 Television Broadcasters Association award of the title “Father of Television”; postwar TV push—wiki core begins.
Chapter 21 — Roster of Setbacks
Lines 11647–12291. Late-1940s setbacks (Newsweek Dec 1949 cover era); competitive and regulatory bruises.
Chapter 22 — Triumph for Color
Lines 12292–12716. Color television hammered out at Princeton labs; 1951 forty-five-year association celebration.
Chapter 23 — Tribute in Gold
Lines 12717–13230. Dec 1955: Robert Sarnoff named RCA president/CEO; succession tribute.
Chapter 24 — The Crusade That Failed
Lines 13231–13575. Firm opinions on domestic/world problems; a public crusade that fails.
Chapter 25 — The “Public Figure”
Lines 13576–14173. FDR-era request beginnings of public-service persona; postwar public-figure stature.
Chapter 26 — In the Eighth Decade
Lines 14174–14638. 1961 Capitol Hill luncheon honor (55th anniversary with radio); still-active eighth decade as Lyons writes.
Index
Lines 14639–end. Index and residual jacket blurbs.
Coverage Guide
Immigrant wireless years (bridge / shared with 1866–1919)
Chs. 1–5: boyhood, Marconi, Titanic, music-box prophecy—continuity into RCA era.
RCA, networks, Depression, TV fight, WWII (wiki core)
Chs. 6–19: RCA birth through D-Day electronics—primary mining for this wiki.
Postwar TV and color (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 20–26: forward pointers only.
High-value passages to mine

sources/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.title: [source] Vision: A Saga of the Sky (Mansfield, 1956)
sources/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.content:
Vision: A Saga of the Sky
Author: Harold Mansfield
Published: 1956 (Duell, Sloan and Pearce, New York; First Edition; Library of Congress 56-9591; copyright © 1956 by Harold Mansfield)
Working text: Scanned PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash 519b658d106d9c0ea1aa2c7341cff4c2; OCLC 1151666232)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.txt (pdftotext -layout from scanned PDF)
Extract stats: 14,780 lines · ~130,567 words · 794,842 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
HOME = United States 1920–45. Mine Book One (especially 1920s–30s road from mail/pursuits into commercial aviation) + Book Two (all-metal Monomail/247, Flying Fortress, Clipper/Stratoliner) + Book Three (WWII B-17/B-29 production, 8th Air Force raids, Battle of Kansas, Pacific Superfortress campaigns, Victory)—core Boeing for this period.
Also copy to United States 1866–1919: Book One early chapters on William E. Boeing, Pacific Aero Products / Boeing Airplane Co. founding ~1916–1919, Model C and WWI production—period-gate later 1920s+ material.
Also copy to United States 1946–89: Books Four–Five (swept-wing jet bomber studies, Stratocruiser, B-47/B-52, KC-135 tankers, 707 board decision, Bomarc missiles, Cold War outlook)—postwar jet age.
Do not claim 1866–1919 as primary home for Fortress/Superfortress; do not claim 1946–89 as primary for WWI–WWII airframe story.
Overview
Vision: A Saga of the Sky is Harold Mansfield’s thematic company saga of Boeing—not a formal corporate history but a narrative built on scores of interviews, records, and rechecks with participants (research assisted by Reynolds Phillips of Boeing Magazine). Mansfield centers engineering progress and individual vision (Egtvedt, Johnson, Allen, Wells, Schairer, Beall, Eddie Allen) rather than manufacturing detail. The frame is engineer John Haberlin preparing a speech at a 1950s thirty-year-awards banquet, looking back forty years from fabric-covered machines to the 707 jet and pilotless-aircraft work.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers Boeing’s rise from post-WWI survival through mail-plane contracts, pursuit fighters, the all-metal transport revolution, Flying Fortress procurement politics, and WWII mass production of B-17s and B-29s—including Eddie Allen’s flight-test philosophy, 8th Air Force deep penetrations, and the Kansas/Salina Superfortress crisis. Period-gate Books Four–Five to the 1946–89 sister page except brief forward pointers.
Book structure: Foreword; Book One — THE CHALLENGE (10 chs.); Book Two — THE INSPIRATION (10 chs.); Book Three — THE TEST (8 chs.); Book Four — THE REALIZATION (11 chs.); Book Five — THE OUTLOOK (5 chs.); airplane timeline plates; illustrations lists.
OCR caveat: Raw text is pdftotext -layout from a scanned first edition. Expect hyphenation noise (¬), form-feeds, running headers (“VISION”), garbled chapter numerals/titles, and medium confidence on fine orthography; high confidence on overall structure and line-range anchors below.

sources/nasaw-the-chief-hearst.content:
The Chief
Author: David Nasaw
Published: 2000 (Houghton Mifflin; 2nd printing packaging in working file)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash abf8a051a2a9c556b27154729d695ce7)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nasaw-the-chief-hearst.txt (pdftotext -layout)

Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
OCR note: Clean digital PDF extract; occasional ligature glyphs (ﬁ/ﬂ) in plain text.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Parts V–IX (and the close of Part IV) cover Hearst’s 1920s studio/collecting/Marion Davies Hollywood court, San Simeon, Depression finance, 1932 Roosevelt choice, anti–New Deal crusades, Hearst–Hitler contacts, the late-1930s fall, and Citizen Kane (1941)—core media/politics material for this period. Mine first from Chs. 16–35. Parts I–III (Examiner through Progressive politics) belong primarily to the 1866–1919 sister; Ch. 36/Epilogue (1946–51 old age) belong primarily to 1946–89.
Overview
The Chief is David Nasaw’s full-life biography of William Randolph Hearst, built with new access to Hearst Corporation materials, San Simeon oral histories, and Joseph P. Kennedy papers among many archives. Nasaw tracks the making of a self-fashioned media sovereign: mining-heir childhood; Harvard dropout turned Examiner proprietor; New York Journal spectacle and the Spanish-American War; Progressive-era candidacies and Congress; World War I neutrality/treason fights; 1920s studio, collecting, and Marion Davies Hollywood court; Depression finance crisis; Roosevelt support then anti–New Deal/anti-Communist crusades; European contacts including Hitler; the late-1930s fall; Citizen Kane; and managed old age until death in 1951.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book is a media-and-politics spine of the interwar Chief: Hollywood kingship, dream houses, Crash flattening, New Deal break, Hitler trip, empire collapse, and Kane. Period-gate hard on Gilded Age/yellow-press origins (→ 1866–1919) and 1946–51 coda (→ 1946–89) except for continuity.
PDF structure: TOC; copyright/LC; Acknowledgments; Preface; Parts I–IX with Chapters 1–36; Epilogue; Notes; Index; About the Author.

sources/nevins-hill-ford-decline-1933-19.content:
Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962
Author: Allan Nevins and Frank Ernest Hill
Research associates: Mira Wilkins, George B. Heliker, and William Greenleaf
Published: Charles Scribner’s Sons, New York; © 1962, 1963 Columbia University
Working text: Internet Archive / History e-book project PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash bd4f2991244f7c0aadb472f19eb3ac65; OCLC 26741539; IA forddeclinerebirOOnevi)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nevins-hill-ford-decline-1933-1962.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 23,563 lines · ~219,454 words · 1,435,209 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The source appears complete as a usable OCR text of the full third volume. Front matter includes title (Decline and Rebirth 1933–1962), Scribner’s / Columbia copyright block, research-associate credits, preface (signed F.E.H., Columbia University, March 1963), full Contents (chs. I–XVIII plus Appendices and Illustrations), and illustration lists. Body opens at Chapter I “Crisis of 1933” (line ~598) with Roosevelt’s inaugural and runs through Chapter XVIII “Present and Future”; chapter-keyed Notes begin near line 19,872; Appendix I (production report 1903–) and Index close the file. OCR is generally cleaner at the front than Volume II’s cover noise; hyphenation breaks and occasional character errors remain. Structure is intact through index.
This is Volume III of the trilogy. Volume I ends near mass production and rising autocracy; Volume II ends with depression impact, V-8, and the symbol/legend/reality balance. This volume carries the firm through New Deal labor conflict, World War II, dynastic crisis, and managerial rebirth into the early 1960s.
Overview
The March 1963 preface (F.E.H.) frames an aging genius who fails to recover automotive supremacy and the tragedy of Edsel’s under-use; wartime chapters draw special help; picture sources include Ford Motor Company, UPI, and Wide World. The narrative contrasts Roosevelt’s experimental state with Henry Ford’s industrial individualism, then follows the company’s depression weakness relative to General Motors, the bitter labor decade culminating in the 1941 UAW contract, Bennett’s security empire, Willow Run and arsenal production, Edsel’s death and the succession struggle, Henry Ford II’s ouster of Bennett, Breech and the “Whiz Kids,” Ferguson litigation, automation and Korean War work, overseas postwar realignment, the Ford Foundation’s public stock sales, and a closing contrast between the 1896 shed and the 1950s Research and Engineering Center under shareholder and union constraints.
For this wiki the source is central for Ford in the New Deal and World War II, UAW organization in auto, Willow Run, Harry Bennett, Edsel’s last years, Henry Ford II, Ernest Breech, postwar corporate modernization, and the Ford Foundation as tax-and-philanthropy transformer of the family firm. It continues Expansion and Challenge and pairs with Since Yesterday, Now It Can Be Told (wartime production state), and As He Saw It (Roosevelt-era political frame).
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines ~200–259. Frank Ernest Hill at Columbia, March 1963. Frames the volume around the aging Henry Ford’s failure to regain supremacy and the tragedy of Edsel’s insufficient authority; notes wartime-chapter assistance; credits research associates Mira Wilkins, George B. Heliker, and William Greenleaf; picture acknowledgments (Ford, UPI, Wide World). Continues the Columbia–Ford Fund scholarly arrangement of the trilogy.
Chapter I — Crisis of 1933
Lines 598–1767. Noonday 4 March 1933: Roosevelt inaugurated on “bold, persistent experimentation” and fear itself; contrast with Henry Ford. Depression effects on the automotive industry and nation; the Big Three; Detroit banking crisis and new banks; NIRA/NRA and the automobile code. Ford refuses to sign; persuasion efforts and public reaction; Roosevelt’s attempts at a harmonious relationship. Flashback on Model A’s 1929 lead (1,710,734 units) and the industry’s climb from twenty-first to first in dollar value since 1909.
Chapter II — The Troubled March of Labor
Lines 1768–2921. NRA storm weathered; larger labor tempest gathers. Mid-depression plant conditions via Richard Frankensteen at Chrysler (49¢/hour; Works Council rebuff: “We don’t control the price of butter”). Workers take heart from New Deal and Section 7A; AFL under William Green of little help; Communist partial success. Battle at the Rouge gate and funerals for the dead; Briggs strike fails but pushes organization. Automotive code and Section 7A; Ford maintains independence. Threatened upheaval and Roosevelt settlement’s unsatisfactory features. Ford’s firm anti-union stand. NRA invalidated; CIO born; UAW joins; Bendix and Chrysler successes; Fisher Body next.
Chapter III — Challenge of the Future
Lines 2922–3858. Poor 1936 financial showing versus General Motors; Ford responsible through confused engineering, fetishes and taboos. Dealer and credit comparison across the Big Three; sales obstacles including former anti-Semitism, cigarette opposition, New Deal hostility. 1934 V-8: good car, advertising, Chicago World’s Fair exhibit; lower prices help; used-car market. Outside activities: Greenfield Village, soy beans, village industries. Partial success in 1937.
Chapter IV — Overseas Domain
Lines 3859–5229. Dagenham and European plans; Perry’s empery and Dearborn’s role; 1932 “baby Ford” essential and successful. Continental companies find Dagenham costs high; separate French and German manufacture. Mathis union produces Matford under Dollfus; Ford-France in 1936 strike; Mathis bought out; Dollfus defense-manufacturing plans. Weak then improving German Ford; Nazi control increases; Dearborn export help. Ford serves both sides in the Spanish Civil War. Hitler launches European war; world Ford companies add stability to the parent.
Chapter V — A Company in the Doldrums
Lines 5230–6283. J. R. Davis’s Used Car Week. Harry Bennett’s position, Ford Security force, increasing operational control, friends and supporters. Edsel’s role and Bennett’s attitude; Henry’s efforts to remake his son. Davis sales policies; Lincoln Zephyr and Mercury; New York World’s Fair exhibit. Davis–Harry Mack incident and Davis’s demotion; Doss becomes sales manager. Ford, Harry Ferguson, and the Ford-Ferguson tractor system. 1939 sales; improved national auto position; organization morale.
Chapter VI — A New Deal for Labor
Lines 6284–7899. GM–UAW conflict; sitdown brings GM surrender; Chrysler and U.S. Steel recognize unions. Ford and other employers still defiant; Bennett as Ford’s union agent; Edsel resentful. Determination to obstruct the Wagner Act. Battle of the Overpass: unfavorable publicity and firm NLRB opposition; cease-and-desist order; Ford appeals. Dallas and Kansas City strikes fail. UAW dissension: Homer Martin ousted, R. J. Thomas elected. Terror at the Rouge; Martin’s AFL dual union; April 1941 strike and plant election won by UAW. Ford signs a contract highly favorable to the union.
Chapter VII — Shadow of War
Lines 7900–9134. Ford belittles European war danger; liking for Germans; accepts decoration from German vice-consul. Oxford Group; relations with Lindbergh, who opposes American involvement after war starts. Defense preparations: Rolls-Royce engine contract accepted then cancelled; later Pratt & Whitney aircraft engines—plant and manufacturing improvements. Jeep overall design accepted. Lindbergh and Ford continue non-intervention stance. Liberator bomber contract via Sorensen; Willow Run planned; Ford versus Consolidated methods; M-4 tank and tank engine; M-7 aircraft director.
Chapter VIII — Arsenal of Democracy
Lines 9135–10543. Pearl Harbor; automotive industry’s defense preeminence as “high priests of production.” Edsel’s telegrams and 24-hour 7-day week; raised quotas for engines, M-7 directors, tanks. Aircraft-engine output; medium tank engines continue after tank production ceases; glider program. Willow Run as public symbol: construction difficulties, hangars, field; labor and transportation troubles; disappointing bomber pace; Truman Committee; work farmed out; production rises until Ford is chief bomber source. Summary of Ford war production.
Chapter IX — Power Is the Prize
Lines 10544–11569. Early 1944 press image of an empire with “acute indigestion”; Byzantine metaphor—aging sultan, vizier Sorensen versus janissary chief Bennett. Henry near eighty; Edsel’s ulcer operation and dubious health; succession vacuum. Intrigue and apprehension. Sorensen’s long service (“Sorensen period” 1925–1944); Bennett’s challenge; both rise by instant obedience to Henry. Henry’s conviction Edsel lacks steel; Sorensen later claims regent aims for Edsel’s heirs; Bennett wants power to keep. Labor-legend blame split; “Cast-Iron Charlie.” Bennett’s pay, appearance, followers; Ford’s further health decline; antagonism to Edsel’s sons. Edsel’s death; Henry assumes presidency; secret codicil to his will; situation precarious.
Chapter X — End of a Legend
Lines 11570–12471. Henry Ford II released from Navy (Secretary Knox, August 1943); Detroit bets he will share Edsel’s frustrations. Power triangle: sick Henry, clinging Sorensen, Bennett. Board meetings farcical when Henry attends (“Come on, Harry, let’s get the hell out of here”). Young Henry’s prior attention to production cards and plant news from the Navy. High officials discharged through Bennett; Sorensen’s difficult exit and past achievements. Henry II versus Bennett; Doss leaves; Bugas procured, Davis returned. Mysterious will destroyed. Mead Bricker takes Rouge charge for Henry II. Henry II becomes president and discharges Bennett. Henry Ford’s notable achievements recalled at the legend’s end.
Chapter XI — Outer Empire: War and Peace
Lines 12472–13379. Able chiefs: Perry (England), Albert (Germany), Dollfus (France); war divides control. Dollfus bows to Nazi invaders but wins independence from Schmidt of Ford-Werke over conquered territories. Schmidt and Albert protect properties manufacturing for Nazis; Dollfus serves Hitler independently. Camouflaged Dagenham: tractors, engines, carriers; Rolls-Royce Merlin and other war materials. French plants hit by Allied bombers; Cologne little injured. Americans arrive; postwar continental conditions; Ford of England in best shape.
Chapter XII — Reaching for Answers
Lines 13380–14380. Company condition September 1945; Henry II’s personality and persistent courage. Bennett followers purged; Policy Committee created. Postwar car production permitted but hedged; unresolved OPA conflict. Labor negotiation demands end of unauthorized strikes; early 1946 agreement. Search for a right-hand man; Thornton group (Whiz Kids) hired. Ernest R. Breech targeted; refuses while Bendix president; Ford persists; Breech finally: “My answer is Yes.”
Chapter XIII — To Rebuild a Company
Lines 14381–15704. Breech brings Lewis D. Crusoe (finance) and Harold T. Youngren (engineering); Delmar S. Harder sought for manufacturing; Albert J. Browning for purchasing. Crusoe’s GM/Fisher Body cost discipline; Youngren from Borg-Warner. Plans for new company, construction, curbing of old “drivers.” Disposal of money-losing properties (Brazilian rubber, soy factories, much of Ford Fleet). GM-style decentralized organization; Thornton group with Crusoe and Breech. Finances reformed. Henry Ford’s death. Foremen’s strike fails; improved foremen status planned. New UAW contract; Engineering Center plans; Dykstra plants. 1949 Ford shown; Ford Division created.
Chapter XIV — Lions in the Path
Lines 15705–16780. Ferguson’s 250 million suit after failed compromise; Dearborn Motors for Ford’s own tractor; Ferguson’s difficulties. Case and company reply. Ford Division progress under Crusoe. New facilities at Buffalo, Cleveland, and elsewhere; more assembly plants. Harder and automation adapted to Ford factories. Korean War production; quotas Ford calls unjust. Ferguson suit settled: Dearborn Motors pays 9,250,000; company profits and market share.
Chapter XV — Ford Becomes a Challenge
Lines 16781–17546. Fiftieth anniversary: Ford Archives; Engineering Center dedication. Henry II’s public activities. New plants; wider car range; Davis Committee. Power race among Chevrolet, Plymouth, and Ford; new divisions and personnel shifts. Tractors versus competitors. Reith’s program including the E-car (later Edsel)—fully approved.
Chapter XVI — Foreign Scene: The Postwar World
Lines 17547–18281. Henry II and Graeme K. Howard tour Europe; material, manpower, credit handicaps. English company sells European interests to Ford-US. Howard heads International Division; New York offices and large plans; Breech and Henry II curb him; Howard leaves but leaves a sound base. English prosperity; Sir Patrick Hennessy’s diesel; large UK construction. Ford-France difficulties; F. C. Reith restores efficiency; Ford-US sells French holdings to Simca. German Ford-Werke grows but Volkswagen leads. Canada and Australia. Rising volume and Ford-US ownership/control overseas.
Chapter XVII — The Great Transformer
Lines 18282–19194. Henry Ford’s individualism and rejection of organized charity; productive philanthropy and self-help; opposition to New Deal wealth-sharing; jobs and goods as true sharing. Personal aid, Greenfield Village, schools, Ford Hospital, Martha Berry. Ford Foundation created 15 January 1936 to avoid federal taxation of the Ford fortune. Through deaths of Edsel, Henry, and Clara, Foundation receives 95 percent of company stock (non-voting); 5 percent voting to Edsel’s children. 1948 program committee and Funds. By 1955, after ~$875 million granted or appropriated, sale with heirs of 3,600,000 shares to the public; further sales leave public stockholders with more than 60 percent of voting rights.
Chapter XVIII — Present and Future
Lines 19195–19871. Contrast: 1896 brick shed (Rockwell image of Henry and Clara with the quadricycle, now in Greenfield Village) versus 1956 Ford Research and Engineering Center campus—ten thousand white-shirted development staff, plant and equipment valued above $2.5 billion, ~180,000 average workers prior year. Stockholders’ meetings: 1903 twelve owners and tight control versus 1960 public meeting after share distribution—end of czarist non-meetings. Labor then and now: five-dollar day versus UAW negotiation. Laissez-faire original company versus social fabric of organized labor, stockholders, and government. 1955 labor settlement. Present character: size, growth, individuality; major loss on the Edsel; character of current Ford cars.
Notes, Appendices, and Index
Lines 19872–end. Chapter-keyed notes (I–XVIII). Appendix I: Ford Motor Company production report, 1903 through later years. Index runs to final pages (~507 book pages). Illustrations clusters document V-8s, Rotunda, Overpass, UAW contract signing, M-4, Willow Run, glider, Perry/Sorensen/Albert, Breech/Crusoe/McNamara “Team,” three Ford brothers, and 1950s–60s models.
Coverage Guide
New Deal, NRA, and depression auto politics
Chapters I–III place Ford against Roosevelt’s experimental state, the auto code refusal, Detroit banks, V-8 recovery efforts, and non-automotive side projects.
Labor organization and the UAW
Chapters II and VI are the core labor arc: Frankensteen exemplar, Rouge gate violence, Section 7A, CIO/UAW rise, Battle of the Overpass, NLRB, April 1941 strike and election, favorable union contract.
Bennett, Edsel, and succession
Chapters V, IX, and X cover Security force power, Edsel’s erosion, Sorensen–Bennett duel, Edsel’s death, secret will, Henry II’s return, and Bennett’s discharge.
World War II production
Chapters VII–VIII and XI cover non-intervention stigma, Pratt & Whitney, jeep, Willow Run Liberators, tanks, gliders, Truman Committee, and European Ford under occupation versus Dagenham’s Allied output.
Managerial rebirth
Chapters XII–XV cover Policy Committee, Whiz Kids, Breech–Crusoe–Youngren–Harder rebuild, GM decentralization model, 1949 Ford, Ferguson suit and automation, fiftieth anniversary and Edsel-car approval.
Foundation, public ownership, overseas
Chapters XVI–XVIII cover Howard’s International Division, Simca and Volkswagen contexts, Foundation stock and 1955 public sale, and the shed-to-Research-Center / autocrat-to-shareholder closing meditation.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 200–259: Preface on aging Ford, Edsel tragedy, wartime help, March 1963.
Lines 598–680: Roosevelt inaugural versus Ford; depression and industry rank.
Lines 1768–1820: Frankensteen and the turn to organization under 7A.
Lines 6284–6400 and Overpass narrative through ~7800: UAW campaign to 1941 contract.
Lines 9135–9200: Pearl Harbor arsenal mobilization and Edsel’s all-out wire.
Lines 10544–10600: Sorensen versus Bennett power prize; Edsel’s lack of “steel.”
Lines 11570–11630: Henry II from Navy; farcical board; path to Bennett’s fall.
Lines 14381–14450: Breech team assembly—Crusoe, Youngren, Harder, Browning.
Lines 15705–15800: Ferguson suit opening and Dearborn Motors.
Lines 18282–18350: Ford on philanthropy versus the Foundation’s origin.
Lines 19195–19280: 1896 shed versus 1956 Research Center; stockholders’ revolution.

Notes on Scope
Columbia-administered trilogy finale (© 1962/1963), archival and oral-history rich, carrying the firm past Henry Ford’s death into the managerial and shareholder order of the 1950s–early 1960s. Chronological center of gravity for this wiki is 1933–45 (NRA, UAW, Willow Run, succession crisis); postwar chapters remain valuable for completion of the Ford arc and for concepts (Foundation, public ownership, automation) that begin in the period. OCR requires caution on short verbatim quotes; chapter architecture and factual spine are reliable. Volume is complete as the third book, not as an endless corporate update beyond ~1962.
