Ford: Expansion and Challenge, 1915–1933
Author: Allan Nevins and Frank Ernest Hill
Research associates: William Greenleaf and George B. Heliker
Published: Charles Scribner’s Sons, New York, 1957
Working text: Internet Archive PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash bfcc9c354be4fc003f49da999c3c9d28; IA fordexpansionchaOOalla)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nevins-hill-ford-expansion-1915-1933.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 30,920 lines · ~312,489 words · 1,982,917 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The source appears complete as a usable OCR text of the full second volume. Front matter includes the Internet Archive digitize stamp, title page (Expansion and Challenge 1915–1933), Scribner’s imprint, 1957 copyright (Allan Nevins; A-7-57[V]), LC card 57-9695, Preface, Contents (chs. I–XXIII plus Notes, Appendices, Bibliographical Note, Index), and Illustrations list. Body text runs from Chapter I through XXIII; notes begin near line 26,244 with chapter-keyed citations; appendices and index follow through the final pages. OCR is noisy on early cover/scan pages (roughly lines 1–68) and shows hyphenation, character substitution, and occasional running-header garble, but chapter structure and continuous narrative are intact.
This is Volume II of the Columbia University / Ford Motor Company Fund trilogy. Volume I (Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company, 1954) ends near the five-dollar day and the rise of personal power (covered in the United States 1866–1919 wiki). Volume III (Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962) continues from the New Deal crisis through Henry Ford II and corporate rebirth.
Overview
The preface frames 1915–1933 as the years when Ford Motor Company released “powerful new forces in American life”: mass production perfected at Highland Park, Model T as the most widely used vehicle in human history, the River Rouge as vertical integration (mines, forests, foundries, steel, glass, railroad, fleets), airplane and tractor ventures, overseas plants, and the socio-economic experimentation of high wages and inexpensive goods even as Henry Ford became an industrial autocrat. The volume is the product of the same Columbia–Ford Fund arrangement as Volume I: written under university auspices, university employees and salaries, royalties to Columbia, authors’ independence guaranteed; Columbia takes no responsibility for content.
For this wiki the source is central for Henry Ford and Edsel Ford in war, boom, and depression; Ford Motor Company organization and one-man rule; Rouge construction; Model T’s climax and death; Model A and the V-8 transition; the Peace Ship; wartime production and the unreturned war-profits pledge; the Dodge minority suit and buy-out; the Dearborn Independent and anti-Semitism; Muscle Shoals; labor after the Sociological Department’s idealistic phase; Harry Bennett’s rise; and Ford overseas in the expansive and nationalist years. It pairs with Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company (vol. 1) and Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962 (vol. 3), and with contemporary narrative sources such as Only Yesterday and Since Yesterday.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 130–240 approx. Nevins and Hill date the story from Woodrow Wilson’s reelection through war, boom, and into the Great Depression. Ford by 1915 already ranked among major world industrials and was making Americans an automobile-using people. Expansion includes mass production’s full instrument at Highland Park, Model T’s ubiquity, Rouge vertical integration, airplanes and tractors, overseas plants, and the challenge that ends Model T. Socio-economic experimentation in wages and sales advances and retreats; Ford believes in high wages and abundant cheap goods while becoming an autocrat. Volume I covered beginnings through the Five Dollar Day and dawn of mass production (1913–14); this volume covers war, boom, and incipient depression under the Columbia–Ford Fund independence arrangement. Acknowledgment of Ford Archives (Dr. Henry Edmunds), Owen Bombard’s oral-history interviews, and research associates Greenleaf and Heliker.
Chapter I — Scene and Actors: 1915
Lines 639–1654. Opens at the Panama-Pacific Exposition, 20 February 1915: Ford’s Highland Park assembly-line replica draws crowds until rails fail and the line is shut to restore order. Mass production is unveiled; the line later turns out twenty cars a day for nine months. Context: Panama Canal (August 1914), world war mechanization, continental telephone and wireless, skyscraper height debate. Survey of the United States as industrial power; the automotive industry’s social and technological influence; Highland Park as mass-production exemplar; Henry Ford’s associates, friends, and interests—world peace, the tractor, and a projected manufacturing center on the River Rouge.
Chapter II — Peace Crusade
Lines 1655–2856. Ford’s peace activity from November 1915: Rosika Schwimmer and Louis P. Lochner; continuous mediation; interview with Wilson; Clara Ford won to the cause; telegram barrage. The Oscar II peace ship, sensationalism, haste, poor planning, ridicule and defenders; quarrel among pilgrims; Ford leaves the cruise in Norway but supports a European commission until American entry into the war ends the effort.
Chapter III — Producing for War
Lines 2857–4184. Ford’s shift from peace advocate to war supporter after the break with Germany (February 1917) and declaration of war: plants offered without profit; tractors for Britain then America; ambulances, helmets, shells, armor plate; Liberty engine work; Eagle boat submarine chasers on the Rouge; tank experiments. Attacks on personnel including Edsel and Carl Emde. Promise to return war profits, controversy, and eventual failure to repay.
Chapter IV — Drive for Power
Lines 4185–5362. Edsel’s marriage (November 1916) and the Dodge brothers’ suit the next day to stop expansion spending and force a large special dividend. Trial: Ford as colorful witness; court-ordered dividend over $19,000,000. Ford holds 58½ percent yet is not free to direct policy; threat of a new car depresses stock; secret purchase of all minority holdings. Immense personal power and plans for using it.
Chapter V — Forays in Politics
Lines 5363–6542. Support for Wilson in 1916 (perhaps crucial). 1918 Michigan senatorial race as Democrat; defeat by Newberry and investigations. Dearborn Independent launched 1920 as liberal weekly. Chicago Tribune suit over “anarchist” / “ignorant idealist” editorial; Ford’s humiliation as witness; press comment and public standing.
Chapter VI — Postwar Crisis
Lines 6543–7698. Industry’s war-to-peace transition; retooling; loss of Wills, Lee, and Hawkins. Boom production slowed by strikes then collapsed with the postwar bust. September 1920 price cut fails to hold demand; plant shutdowns; surplus equipment sold; organization simplified. Need for funds to repay the minority-stock loan; defiance of bankers; plant reopening and shipment of cars to dealers (February–March 1921). Crisis met; production mounts; discharge of officials including Knudsen and Klingensmith.
Chapter VII — The Lincoln Story
Lines 7699–8926. Lincoln Motor Company crisis, fall 1921; Henry M. and Wilfred Leland; receivership; Edsel’s interest; Ford acquisition at receiver’s sale; clash with Lelands and their departure; payment of old creditors; 1927 Leland suit for former stockholders lost; appraisal of Ford’s role.
Chapter VIII — The Rouge: Concept and Growth
Lines 8927–9565. Ford’s new efficiency conception, 1918–1924: control of raw materials, concentration of related units, “flow” in manufacture and shipping. Site advantages (water, rail, labor, space). First supplementary to Highland Park, later meant to displace it. Slip, coke ovens, blast furnaces, power house, foundry; Sorensen’s arrival 1921 and control; Rouge River improvement for water transport.
Chapter IX — Projects in Expansion
Lines 9566–10881. Peripheral ideas: timber, iron, silica, coal; glass process; Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Railroad purchase, reconditioning, profit; “village industries” bringing factory to country; Ford fleet; Brazilian rubber adventure; Ford aircraft 1926–1934 as commercial-aviation pioneer. Ford as social and industrial experimenter.
Chapter X — The Greater Company
Lines 10882–12128. Early-1920s organization: research facilities and limits; branch assembly and marketing. Administration and sales under Edsel and E. C. Kanzler; shipment, used cars, price cuts, advertising. Ford’s distrust of formal administration; fluid one-man rule; rise of Liebold (office) and Sorensen (production). Edsel’s difficult position and refusal to oppose his father. Efficiency despite lack of central organization.
Chapter XI — The Rouge: Industrial Colossus
Lines 12129–12953. Rouge’s rising importance versus Highland Park; Sorensen’s drive; mechanization; transfer of units from Highland Park. Experimental steel plant 1923–1926; moving assembly line at Rouge 1927; large-scale discharge of officials. Mature plant: size, modernity, cleanliness; industrial limitations; branch and outside units; essential values surviving later.
Chapter XII — From Muscle Shoals to Anti-Semitism
Lines 12954–13951. Presidential boom 1922–1924; equivocal attitude and final repudiation. Muscle Shoals offer, wide support, Norris opposition, withdrawal. Dearborn Independent anti-Semitic campaign; possible sources of Ford’s attitude; public reaction. Sapiro articles and suit 1924–1927; Ford’s apology to the Jews; harmfulness of the attacks; indulgent public attitude toward Ford’s public-life errors.
Chapter XIII — Labor: A Bright Dawn Pales
Lines 13952–15259. Five-dollar day (1914) and employee-service program; wartime wage effects. Sociological Department standards and activity: investment certificates, liberal employment (Negroes, ex-convicts, handicapped), English and Americanization classes, Ford Trade School, grocery and housing. Dean Marquis’s departure 1921 and end of the idealistic era; retention of some benefits; anti-union attitude and realistic wage policy.
Chapter XIV — Ford Overseas: The Expansive Years
Lines 15260–16335. Model T reputation abroad during and after the war; early-1920s expansion plans; Knudsen’s European survey; Ford and General Motors abroad; Sir Percival Perry and his departure. Plants under Edsel and Sorensen in France, Denmark, Germany, Spain, Italy; prosperous Canadian company work in Australasia and South Africa; Latin American expansion.
Chapter XV — Winds of Challenge
Lines 16336–17536. Early-1920s motor-car effect on American life: highways, motels, buses, truck freight. Model T improvements 1914–1920 and defects; Ford’s resistance to alteration. Competitors—Chevrolet, Overland, Dodge—appearance and comfort versus utility; women’s role in car selection. Price cuts preserve leadership while Chevrolet gains. “X” car as hoped-for T successor; Edsel and Kanzler advocate a new car.
Chapter XVI — The End of Model T
Lines 17537–18628. Kanzler’s January 1926 memorandum proposing a new car; Ford’s hostile response; Kanzler’s departure. Pride, residual T support, hope for a revolutionary successor. Price cuts lose effectiveness; dealer pressure fails; “X” car experiments fail. Hints then announcement of a new model; Model T closes an extraordinary career.
Chapter XVII — Throes of New Birth
Lines 18629–19522. National interest in the unborn car; Ford’s plans; engineers with Laurence Sheldrick as chief designer. Research shortcomings; Ford’s unusual methods. Hicks’s engine work; Model A completed late 1927. Advances over T in design, comfort, appearance; durability and low price; cost in time and money of development.
Chapter XVIII — Model A: A New Era
Lines 19523–20329. Public excitement and order backlog; limping production from quality insistence, unforeseen changes, prior discharges of able officials. Dealer desperation; Universal Credit Corporation for time-payment sales. Chevrolet’s new model; Chrysler’s background, Dodge purchase, Plymouth as cheap car. Model A’s great year 1929.
Chapter XIX — Projects and Personalities
Lines 20330–21529. Fair Lane: Clara’s gardens, Henry’s trees, birds, farm experiments. Edsel at Gaukler Pointe. Friends and camping with Edison, Burroughs, Firestone; Fort Myers winters near the Edisons; Georgia estate beginnings; Edsel’s Seal Harbor and Haven Hill. Diet and health ideas; ban on smoking and drinking; soy beans; old-fashioned dances. Opposition to “philanthropy” and praise of self-help; Henry Ford Hospital, Berry Schools, Greenfield Village; educational contributions.
Chapter XX — How the Workers Fared
Lines 21530–22898. 1920s auto labor: unions not a factor in worker gains. Ford plant goods: cleanliness, light, air, safety, liberal hiring. Contrasts: silence, exact rules, no smoking or chewing; “drive” and conflicting testimony on pace. Five-day week and wage effects; seven-dollar day 1929–1931; low-wage supplier accusation; case for Ford’s policy. Anti-union stance; increasing reliance on Harry Bennett; plant espionage; use of Negro workers.
Chapter XXI — Ford Overseas: The Years of Storm
Lines 22899–24093. 1928 overseas reorganization; Perry’s return supervising European plants; Dagenham on the Thames; sale of British and other Ford companies’ stock. Growing European industrial nationalism hurts France, Germany, Italy; better conditions in Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, Spain, Britain. German pressure; China impracticable; Japan activity. Depression and nationalism squeeze overseas business.
Chapter XXII — Impact of Depression
Lines 24094–25209. Relative Ford prosperity early in the depression; other firms’ failures. 1931 losses; branch construction, price cuts. Chrysler as competitive factor; gift of a Plymouth to the Fords. Dealer feud over low discounts—dealers win. Workforce sharply reduced; grievances; Bennett’s enlarged power. V-8 planned and introduced March 1932 after Model A; eventual success.
Chapter XXIII — Ford: Symbol, Legend, Reality
Lines 25210–26243. Moving Forward (1931) and Ford’s ideas. Ford as symbol of the mass-production era; appearance, manner, accomplishments. Controversy; popularity in Russia; mixed reception in Ireland, Germany, England, Italy, the United States. Legend fostered by pithy utterance; books by Merz, Marquis, Crowther. Actual Ford: social vision of industrialism’s effects, mechanical genius, faith in experiment; many-faceted personality; rural youth; unhappy attitude toward Edsel. Balance of accomplishments (including associates’) against defects.
Notes, Appendices, Bibliographical Note, and Index
Lines 26244–end. Chapter-keyed notes; appendices including “The Russian Adventure” and related documentary matter; bibliographical note on Ford Archives and related collections; index through final OCR pages. Illustrations list (Rouge diagrams, Liberty engine, Eagle boat, tractor with Northcliffe, Fair Lane, Firestone/Wills/Ford, Coolidge telegram, etc.) appears before the body in the raw extract.
Coverage Guide
War, peace, and public politics
Chapters II, III, V, and XII cover the Peace Ship, war production and the profits pledge, Wilson support and the Newberry race, Tribune trial, Muscle Shoals, and the Dearborn Independent’s anti-Semitic campaign through the Sapiro suit and apology.
Corporate power and organization
Chapters IV, VI, VII, X, and XXIII cover the Dodge suit and minority buy-out, postwar financial crisis and banker defiance, Lincoln acquisition, one-man rule under Liebold and Sorensen, Edsel’s constrained role, and the interpretive balance of symbol, legend, and reality.
Rouge, vertical integration, and experiments
Chapters I, VIII, IX, and XI cover Highland Park’s 1915 showcase, Rouge concept and colossus, raw materials, DT&I railroad, village industries, Brazilian rubber, and aircraft.
Model T to Model A and depression competition
Chapters XV–XVIII and XXII cover competitive challenge, end of Model T, birth and boom of Model A, Chrysler/Plymouth, early depression losses, and the V-8.
Labor
Chapters XIII and XX cover the fading Sociological ideal, Marquis’s exit, five-day and seven-dollar policies, plant discipline, Bennett, espionage, and Negro employment.
Overseas Ford
Chapters XIV and XXI cover expansive interwar planting of factories and the later storm of nationalism, Dagenham, and depression pressure.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 130–200: Preface on 1915–33 forces, Rouge and Model T expansion, Columbia independence, Ford Archives.
Lines 639–720: Panama-Pacific assembly-line exhibit and 1915 world context.
Lines 1655–1720: Schwimmer, Lochner, continuous mediation, and launch of the peace effort.
Lines 2857–2920: Conversion from pacifism to war production behind Wilson.
Lines 4185–4300 region: Dodge suit, dividend, and drive for absolute stock control (open at Drive for Power).
Lines 12954–13200 region: Muscle Shoals and Independent anti-Semitism cluster.

Suggested Future Pages

Related Sources

Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962 — Volume III: NRA, UAW, Willow Run, Bennett vs. Henry II, Breech, Ford Foundation.
Only Yesterday — contemporary 1920s public mind against which Ford’s celebrity and Independent episode sit.
Since Yesterday — 1929–39 depression and New Deal frame for late chapters and the handoff to Volume III.

Notes on Scope
Columbia-administered, company-archives-rich modern secondary history (1957). Mine as the major narrative bridge for Ford and the American automobile industry from Wilson’s second term through the onset of the Depression and the V-8. Treat Volume II as complete for 1915–1933, not as the full Ford story; labor violence climax, UAW recognition, World War II production, and postwar managerial revolution belong to Volume III. OCR artifacts require caution on exact wording of short quotations; chapter arguments and factual scaffolding are solid.

sources/paxson-recent-history-united-sta.title: [source] Recent History of the United States, 1865–1927 (Paxson, 1928/1929)
sources/paxson-recent-history-united-sta.content:
Recent History of the United States, 1865–1927
Author: Frederic L. Paxson
Published: Houghton Mifflin, revised and enlarged edition, copyright 1928/1929
Working text: Hathi/IA-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 816137, hash c9f117629c6ba1aee0f51a53dc7e84da)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/paxson-recent-history-united-states-1865-1927.txt
Extract stats: 712 OCR page files · 32,026 lines · ~253,868 words · 1,571,589 bytes
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1866-1919 into the United States 1920–45 wiki for Paxson’s postwar and normalcy chapters (especially Chapters XXV–XXVII): demobilization, 1919 strikes, Prohibition, Klan, motor cars and roads, Versailles aftermath, Harding–Coolidge politics, immigration restriction, debts, and the 1920s environment through the book’s 1927 horizon. Mine those chapters as a near-contemporary synthetic spine beside Only Yesterday. Reconstruction through Wilson/war chapters remain primarily for the 1866–1919 wiki.
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as a single-volume revised and enlarged edition. The joined raw text includes title/copyright pages, preface, full contents, list of maps, Chapters I–XXVII, and index. The title page gives the scope as 1865–1927, although the file name says 1865–1929; the text should therefore be treated as Paxson’s 1865–1927 narrative in a 1928/1929 printing.
Overview
Paxson describes the United States after the Civil War as a transition from agricultural civilization to industrial society, from isolation to world eminence, and from European debtor to international creditor and power. The book is an especially useful backbone source because it connects the whole period of this wiki: Reconstruction, the railroad and frontier economy, money and tariff politics, Populism, the 1890s crisis, McKinley, Spanish-American War, Roosevelt, Progressive regulation, Wilson, World War I, the peace settlement, and the first postwar political settlement.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki, mine first the postwar / normalcy chapters (XXV–XXVII and selective 1919 spillover). For the United States 1866–1919 wiki, its strongest value is the 1900–1919 narrative core: Roosevelt, imperialism, trusts, muckraking, federal control, Taft, insurgency, Wilson, neutrality, preparedness, World War I, the American war government, peace, and the League. It pairs with The Life of William McKinley, Volume II for McKinley-era diplomacy, Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company for industrial mass production, The House of Morgan for finance and world power, and Andrew Carnegie for anti-imperial and peace politics.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface and Framing
Lines 58–79. Paxson frames the book as a history of a new industrial, post-frontier, world-facing United States. The stated theme is not merely political chronology but the structural transformation of American society after the Civil War.
Chapters I–IV — Union, Reconstruction, Readjustment, and Postwar Politics
Lines 770–4862. These chapters cover the control of the Union, Reconstruction, the Fourteenth Amendment, Johnson, Grant, the Far West, railroads, Indian wars, greenbacks, panic, Liberal Republicans, education, literature, postwar thought, Hayes, Garfield, Arthur, patronage, strikes, labor, and factional Republican politics.
Chapters V–VIII — Material Basis, Cleveland, Frontier Aftermath, and Protection
Lines 4863–9308. Paxson turns to economic realities: silver, specie resumption, railroads, Standard Oil, inventions, New South, tariff reform, Cleveland, public lands, cattle, Interstate Commerce, sport, urbanization, labor parties, ballot reform, Harrison, the McKinley tariff, silver legislation, pensions, and the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.
Chapters IX–XII — Farmers’ West, Panic, Gold Standard, and War with Spain
Lines 9309–13808. This cluster covers Populism, statehood, free silver, the Panic of 1893, Homestead, Debs, Cleveland’s bond issues, the Wilson tariff, Venezuela, the new navy, McKinley, Hanna, Bryan, gold, the Dingley tariff, Cuba, yellow journalism, the Maine, Manila, Santiago, Hawaii, the Philippines, and Theodore Roosevelt’s rise.
Chapter XIII — The Age of Roosevelt
Lines 13809–14564. Paxson opens the twentieth-century section with McKinley, the Currency Act of 1900, prosperity, trusts, the 1900 campaign, imperialism, McKinley’s assassination, Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency, political reform, letters and sport, Booker T. Washington, labor unrest, and the enlarged presidential office.
Chapter XIV — The New Imperialism
Lines 14565–15482. The chapter treats Roosevelt, Hay, Root, Panama, the Hay-Pauncefote and Hay-Herrán treaties, the Panama secession, Goethals, Venezuela, the Monroe Doctrine, Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Philippines, War Department reorganization, the General Staff, the fleet’s world cruise, Portsmouth, Algeciras, the Hague, and the Declaration of London.
Chapters XV–XVII — Business, Muckraking, and Federal Control
Lines 15483–17542. Paxson follows railroads, mergers, United States Steel, Northern Securities, antitrust legislation, the Department of Commerce and Labor, Cuban reciprocity, the anthracite strike, campaign contributions, muckraking, Ida Tarbell, new journalism, universities, expert government, immigration, the Hepburn law, Pure Food Act, Roosevelt Panic of 1907, Aldrich-Vreeland Act, and conservation.
Chapters XVIII–XX — Taft, Insurgency, and Wilson
Lines 17543–20728. These chapters cover Taft’s election and cabinet, Payne-Aldrich tariff, income tax amendment, insurgent Republicans, Ballinger, Cannon, direct election of senators, postal savings, Panama Canal, Canadian reciprocity, arbitration treaties, Carnegie and peace, Roosevelt’s return, New Nationalism, the Progressive Party, Wilson’s election, tariff revision, Federal Reserve, Federal Trade Commission, labor legislation, the Philippines, woman suffrage, socialism, syndicalism, and the I.W.W.
Chapters XXI–XXIV — Neutrality, World War I, War Government, and Peace
Lines 20729–26206. Paxson covers Bryan, Mexico, Vera Cruz, canal diplomacy, Caribbean policy, neutrality, propaganda, submarine warfare, Lusitania, preparedness, the 1916 election, the German peace overture, unrestricted submarine warfare, the war session of Congress, Council of National Defense, Committee on Public Information, Hoover, munitions, finance, selective service, Pershing and the A.E.F., War Trade Board, Alien Property Custodian, Food and Fuel control, War Industries Board, labor policy, Fourteen Points, the 1918 battles, armistice, Wilson in Europe, the Big Four, League covenant, American Legion, and economic demobilization.
Chapters XXV–XXVII — Postwar Environment and Normalcy
Lines 26207–29757. The final chapters move beyond this wiki’s endpoint into postwar society, aviation, wireless, motor cars, highways, movies, Prohibition, Ku Klux Klan, fundamentalism, Versailles, Wilson’s collapse, strikes of 1919, radicalism, woman suffrage, railroad legislation, Harding, Coolidge, immigration restriction, foreign debts, World Court, Panama, Nicaragua, Mexico, China, naval limitation, and the politics of the 1920s.
Index
Lines 29758–32026. The index is extensive and useful for locating names and subjects across the full 1865–1927 narrative.
Coverage Guide
The book should be mined first as the period’s synthetic spine. Chapters I–XII support Reconstruction, Gilded Age politics, economic change, Populism, the 1890s, McKinley, and the Spanish-American War. Chapters XIII–XXIV are the strongest fit for 1900–1919: Roosevelt, Progressivism, empire, trust regulation, Taft, Wilson, neutrality, war mobilization, and peace. Chapters XXV–XXVII should be used selectively for immediate postwar spillover, especially 1919 strikes, demobilization, normalcy politics, and the postwar social environment.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 58–79: Paxson’s thesis on industrial society, world eminence, and the post-frontier United States.
Lines 13809–15482: McKinley/Roosevelt transition and the New Imperialism.
Lines 15483–17542: trusts, business politics, muckraking, federal regulation, and conservation.
Lines 17543–20728: Taft, insurgency, Progressive Party, Wilson’s domestic program, and labor/social reform.
Lines 20729–26206: neutrality, preparedness, World War I, war government, armistice, peace, and League of Nations.
Lines 26207–27207: postwar society, Prohibition, Klan, motor cars, roads, communications, and cultural change.

Suggested Future Pages

Progressive Era — concept page linking Roosevelt, Taft, Wilson, regulation, muckraking, conservation, and labor.
New Imperialism — concept/event cluster on Panama, Caribbean, Philippines, Roosevelt diplomacy, and naval power.
World War I Mobilization in the United States — concept page on war boards, finance, food, fuel, labor, and selective service.
Election of 1912 — event page on Taft, Roosevelt, Wilson, New Nationalism, and Progressive Party.
League of Nations Debate — concept/event page on Wilson, peace, Senate reaction, and domestic politics.

Related Sources

The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — McKinley, Spanish-American War, Philippines, China, and the 1900 election.
Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company — industrial production, labor, automobiles, and the commercial modernity of the 1900s.
The First Tycoon — post-Civil War railroad consolidation, the Erie War, New York Central system, corporate securities, and Vanderbilt’s 1877 endpoint.
The House of Morgan — finance, empire, war loans, and the international power of American capital.
Andrew Carnegie — anti-imperialism, peace activism, philanthropy, and elite public politics.
Titan — trust politics, Standard Oil, antitrust, philanthropy, and Progressive public opinion.

Notes on Scope
This is a broad synthetic textbook-style history written close to the period it describes. It is valuable for period structure and near-contemporary interpretation, but individual claims should be cross-checked against specialized source pages when creating detailed entity or event pages.

sources/roosevelt-as-he-saw-it.title: [source] As He Saw It (Elliott Roosevelt, 1946)
sources/roosevelt-as-he-saw-it.content:
As He Saw It
Author: Elliott Roosevelt
Published: Duell, Sloan and Pearce, New York, 1946 (copyright Elliott Roosevelt 1946; second printing in working PDF)
Foreword: Eleanor Roosevelt
Working text: Scan PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash ff49fcc7a186c071bab875e2299959f2)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/roosevelt-as-he-saw-it.txt
Extract stats: 8,776 lines · ~75,015 words · 445,503 bytes (pdftotext -layout)
Completeness Assessment
The PDF extract is complete enough for wiki use. Front matter: title, copyright, dedication, Eleanor Roosevelt’s Foreword (pp. vii–ix), Contents, Introduction. Body: eleven chapters (1 Texas to Argentia through 11 Conclusion) matching the imprint Contents, then Index. OCR shows typical scan artifacts (hyphenation across lines, occasional garbled characters such as \\V for W, mixed running heads), but chapter blocks are continuous and narrative-readable. Elliott was not at Yalta; Chapter 10 reconstructs from Anna Boettiger, Harry Hopkins, letters from FDR, and the official trip log—stated in the text.
Overview
Elliott Roosevelt frames the book as only incidentally about the war and primarily about the peace. He writes in 1946 under the spur of Churchill’s Fulton, Missouri speech, Security Council sessions at Hunter College, the American atom-bomb stockpile, and what he calls renascent power politics and broken promises. His qualifications are biological (FDR’s son) and situational: he was most often available as wartime presidential aide—Argentia while based at Gander; Casablanca while operating from Algeria; Cairo–Teheran while headquarters remained in Tunisia—and sat in on formal and informal conferences, then compared notes with his father at night. He draws on official conference logs plus his own contemporaneous notes more than unaided memory.
For this wiki the book is the wartime high-diplomacy spine from a family aide’s seat: Atlantic Charter and Lend-Lease priorities; Casablanca strategy, French politics, and “unconditional surrender”; Chiang at Cairo; Teheran and OVERLORD versus Mediterranean/Turkish diversions; Anzio as Churchill’s “end run”; Yalta as fleshing out Teheran after Dumbarton Oaks friction; and a 1946 Conclusion blaming U.S./British departure from Big Three unity (Greece, Turkey/Dardanelles, Iran oil, atom secrecy, military diplomacy). It pairs with Groves for the atomic-production/operations track, with Allen’s Since Yesterday for the 1930s approach to war, and later with Conant for scientific mobilization. Treat as partisan contemporary memoir, not multi-archival synthesis—cross-check contested dialogue and Soviet policy claims when building event pages.
Narrative Source Flow
Foreword (Eleanor Roosevelt)
Lines 42–125. ~690 words.
FDR wanted individual impressions of the war and peace-planning recorded for better understanding among peoples. He sought family companionship on trips when duty allowed; James as secretary is recalled as comfort despite political cost. Eleanor was not on the conference trips; she heard first-night reunion accounts. She presents Elliott’s book as one observer’s firsthand material for future historians, while noting that each personality colors the same facts differently.
Introduction
Lines 146–323. ~1,490 words.
Incidentally a war book, designed more importantly to shed light on the peace. Span: roughly war’s outbreak through shortly after Yalta. Decision to write is recent—Fulton, Hunter College Security Council, atom stockpile, disunity, broken promises, “renascent power politics.” Trust or distrust of Russia is molded by scare headlines rather than Russia’s contribution to victory. Elliott stakes an individual space among the postwar flood of generals’ and correspondents’ books: as son he could hear FDR talk “as though he were talking out loud to himself”; as aide he ushered Churchill, Stalin, the Chiangs, Combined Chiefs, de Gaulle, Giraud, Hopkins, Molotov, and others, then heard FDR’s impressions. Only Yalta found him unable to be at FDR’s side. He claims knowledge of bargains and promises for postwar peace structure—and writes because he has seen them violated. Audience: those who hold FDR the wartime architect of United Nations unity and believe that path has been deliberately forsaken.
Chapter 1 — Texas to Argentia
Lines 324–828. ~4,310 words.
Opens with Munich weekend 1938: Elliott about to launch Texas radio stations, pumps FDR on whether war will wreck business. FDR will not guarantee no war; sooner or later Britain and France will decide Hitler has gone too far; U.S. working hard to stay out; advises Elliott to go ahead with the radio project. Path from civilian enterprise through service entry to Newfoundland reconnaissance duty. Summons to Argentia: at first thought a naval maneuver; Friday before lunch finds FDR aboard for a multi-day stay; neck size matches father’s shirts for the Atlantic Charter signing. Sets family and military positioning for Chapter 2.
Chapter 2 — The Atlantic Charter
Lines 829–1724. ~7,520 words.
Franklin Jr. and Elliott receive temporary aide aiguillettes. FDR delights in throwing White House correspondents off the scent (supposed fishing off Fundy/Potomac to Augusta) under agreement with Churchill for no press coverage—then Churchill arrives with a press retinue “not very well disguised as Ministry of Information officials,” the first of several such surprises. Meeting at sea suits two naval men who had last met in that capacity in 1919; security and rumor control keep it out of Washington. Substance: Lend-Lease allocation fights in afternoon military sessions—British pressure for more to the United Kingdom and less to the Soviet Union; Marshall, King, and Arnold insist on keeping both warrior nations supplied. Time and production still a gamble; American destiny framed as in firm hands striving to keep the country at peace while protecting long-range interests. Charter text and public announcement close the conference arc as Elliott returns to duty.
Chapter 3 — From Argentia to Casablanca
Lines 1725–2175. ~3,760 words.
Post-Argentia: squadron ordered home; Elliott seeks navigation school (Kelly Field) against stateside complacency he blames on a section of the press (Chicago Tribune, Hearst, New York Daily News, Washington Times-Herald, Scripps-Howard). Pearl Harbor weekend at the Fort Worth ranch; wartime acceleration; overseas to North Africa after TORCH. Hard operational grind at Maison Blanche near Algiers. 11 January 1943: ordered to report to Eisenhower’s Chief of Staff—bridge into Casablanca as presidential aide while still a serving air officer.
Chapter 4 — Casablanca Conference
Lines 2176–4204. ~16,600 words.
Largest chapter. Arrival after TORCH: Jean Bart in harbor, Patton’s traffic, Anfa Camp security under Mike Reilly amid residual enemy agents, Spanish Morocco proximity, and a recent Nazi air raid. French political tangle: Giraud, de Gaulle’s delayed appearance, FDR’s pointed pressure on Churchill over de Gaulle. Military strategy debates (ROUNDUP/Mediterranean weight, production, timing). FDR’s jeep inspection with Patton. Extended father–son evening talk: Empire, Atlantic Charter obligations, Asia and Europe after victory—“not senior partner”; Britain must not hang on to “archaic, medieval Empire ideas.” Birth of the public phrase “unconditional surrender” in FDR’s press-handling (no exclamation point in Elliott’s telling)—with FDR in “fine fettle” over the formula. Operational and political Casablanca as hinge between Argentia idealism and later Cairo–Teheran command decisions.
Chapter 5 — From Casablanca to Cairo
Lines 4205–4755. ~4,600 words.
Stalingrad as tonic; photographic reconnaissance for HUSKY (Sicily) at extreme cost—stripped unarmed aircraft, ~20 percent monthly plane loss; within ninety days fewer than ten percent of original ninety-four pilots answer roll call. Occasional bridge with Eisenhower, Butcher, “Tex” Lee; Pantelleria surrender to air forces. Sicily and Italian mainland work; summons toward the Cairo meetings as FDR’s party enters the Near East theater.
Chapter 6 — Cairo I
Lines 4756–5701. ~8,020 words.
Flight Tunis–Egypt; Nile green against desert; Mena House and Kirk villa; Chiangs and Churchill already present; Reilly’s barbed wire and assassination worry in a crowded political city. FDR breakfasting in bed; Combined Chiefs and political sessions with Generalissimo and Madame Chiang; China theater supply, Burma, and postwar Asia threads. Military planning for Europe continues in parallel with Pacific/China agenda. Sets personnel and issues for the flight to Teheran.
Chapter 7 — Teheran Conference
Lines 5702–6653. ~8,040 words.
Seventy-seven Americans view Teheran from the air—compromise site forced by Stalin’s one-day-from-Moscow requirement; former Axis espionage HQ; open-ditch water/sewage and disease risk. Security shared with Soviet services. Core military issue: OVERLORD—timing, weight, command—versus further Mediterranean exploitation and bringing Turkey into the war. Stalin sides with the American cross-Channel emphasis against diversions Elliott associates with Churchill. Gift symbolism (Stalingrad sword), plenary and dinner diplomacy, and FDR’s effort to mediate British–Soviet tension. Elliott treats Teheran as projecting the overall postwar and strategic picture later only detailed at Yalta.
Chapter 8 — Cairo II
Lines 6654–7106. ~3,940 words.
Brief return to Tunis to close La Marsa rear HQ and move north to Italy; word to Eisenhower that OVERLORD is definitely scheduled and that Russians opposed further Mediterranean exploitation and Turkish entry—command of OVERLORD still unsettled in Eisenhower’s hearing. Back to Cairo: contest over whose plane brings Turkey’s İsmet İnönü from Adana (John Boettiger wins for the American side). İnönü conversations; further Combined Chiefs work; detective-story downtime for FDR between plenaries. Closes the November–December 1943 conference cycle.
Chapter 9 — From Cairo–Teheran to Yalta
Lines 7107–7713. ~5,240 words.
Italy scuttlebutt; skepticism toward Anzio (“end run” near Rome) after Combined Chiefs strategy in Egypt/Iran; orders to Spaatz in England to reorganize Eighth/Ninth Air Force reconnaissance for invasion support. Later learns Churchill personally insisted on SHINGLE. January 1944 arrival in Britain; praise for RAF opposite numbers despite earlier criticisms of some British warmakers. Build-up to OVERLORD operations; stateside leaves and White House nights as available. Bridge to Yalta chapter without Elliott’s physical presence at the Crimea.
Chapter 10 — Yalta Conference
Lines 7714–8159. ~3,790 words.
Explicitly reconstructed: not present at Malta, Yalta, or Great Bitter Lake; sources are sister Anna, Harry Hopkins, FDR’s letters, and official trip log—accounts said to tally on major particulars. Longest trip in time (~five weeks away); eight formal Big Three meetings plus many informal talks in eight Crimean days; more advisers than ever. Elliott’s thesis: not the war’s most important high-level conference because principal decisions had already been taken in Washington, Cairo, and Teheran—Yalta filled in specifics after Dumbarton Oaks showed lower levels not seeing eye to eye. Unanimity again put “flesh on the skeleton” of Teheran. Counterfactual: had FDR lived, further Big Three meetings beyond Potsdam would have followed. Personal reactions and health notes filtered through family and Hopkins.
Chapter 11 — Conclusion
Lines 8160–8574. ~3,540 words.
Job of forging global peace was begun under FDR and since his death has been prejudiced or is “fast being lost.” Evidence: no peace (Lippmann); advanced U.S. air bases and rocket planes in Germany; jealous refusal to share the atom “secret” that Manhattan scientists say is no secret; cocktail-party talk of war with the Soviet Union “preferably before 1948.” Elliott’s causal claim: the United States and Britain first shook the mailed fist and abrogated collective decisions; the U.S. vacated mediator role between Britain and the USSR and lined up behind Britain—Greece (British shooting of Greek anti-fascists; election recognized as democratic), Turkey/Dardanelles, Iran oil and Security Council theater. Blames “a small group of willful men”: State Department career men FDR never trusted, reactionaries of both parties, irresponsible press attacking the veto, and officers shrinking foreign policy to the atom bomb. Favors large forces only as UN security instrument under Big Three unity. Closes with democratic lesson: great Presidents respond to articulated popular will; citizens must push government back onto FDR’s charted path.
Index
Lines 8575–9059. ~3,350 words.
Name and subject index (persons, conferences, OVERLORD, unconditional surrender, production, theaters) supporting point retrieval across the memoir.
Coverage Guide
Mine first as 1941–45 conference diplomacy and 1946 peace polemic from an aide-son. Chapters 2, 4, 6–8, and 10 for Argentia, Casablanca, Cairo, Teheran, and Yalta event pages; Chapter 4 for unconditional surrender and French leadership; Chapter 7 for OVERLORD decision politics; Chapter 9 for Anzio/SHINGLE as Churchill initiative in this telling; Chapter 11 for early Cold War contest over FDR’s legacy (Fulton, Iran, Greece, atom). Cross-check all quoted FDR/Churchill/Stalin dialogue and anti-imperial / pro-unity theses against official FRUS minutes and other memoirs before locking narrative wiki claims. Eleanor’s Foreword is framing, not conference evidence. Yalta chapter is second-hand by admission.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 146–323: purpose, Fulton spur, aide-son method, notes over memory, Yalta absence.
Lines 324–400: Munich/radio-business interview with FDR (1938).
Lines 829–1000: aiguillettes, press decoy, Churchill’s MOI “press retinue.”
Lines ~1500–1700: Lend-Lease to Britain vs. USSR at Argentia military sessions.
Lines 2176–2500: Anfa security, Jean Bart, French agents.
Lines ~4000–4150: birth of “unconditional surrender” phrase.
Lines ~4100–4200: FDR on Empire and Atlantic Charter after victory.
Lines 4205–4500: recon losses; Pantelleria; Ike.
Lines 4756–5200: Cairo I setting; Chiangs; Mena.
Lines 5702–6200: Teheran site drawbacks; OVERLORD vs. Mediterranean/Turkey.
Lines 6654–6900: OVERLORD word to Eisenhower; İnönü plane contest.
Lines 7107–7400: Anzio/SHINGLE as Churchill’s end run; England recon mission.
Lines 7714–8000: Yalta as detailing Teheran; sources Anna/Hopkins/letters/log.
Lines 8160–8572: 1946 indictment—atom secrecy, Greece, Turkey, Iran, willful men, citizen duty.

Suggested Future Pages

Atlantic Charter Conference (Argentia, August 1941) — event page.
Casablanca Conference (January 1943) — event page (strategy + unconditional surrender + French).
Cairo Conferences (1943) and Chiang Kai-shek — event/entity cluster.
Teheran Conference — event page (OVERLORD commitment).
Yalta Conference — event page (with explicit second-hand caveat for this source).
Unconditional Surrender doctrine — concept page.
Big Three unity / early Cold War break (1945–46) — concept page from Chapter 11 lens.
Elliott Roosevelt (wartime aide) — entity page if multi-source.

Related Sources

Now It Can Be Told — Manhattan Project operations; atom “secret” debate in Elliott’s Conclusion is the diplomatic/political counter-voice.
Since Yesterday — 1930s public mind and approach to war before Elliott’s conference narrative.
Only Yesterday — 1920s prelude only.
Jennet Conant, Tuxedo Park (to be added) — scientific mobilization adjacent to high policy.
Nevins & Hill Ford volumes (to be added) — industrial production parallel, not diplomacy.

Notes on Scope
1946 contemporary memoir and political argument by a participant-observer with unmatched informal access and clear advocacy (preserve FDR’s Big Three peace architecture; criticize Churchillian empire, State careerists, and early Cold War alignment against the USSR). Strong on atmosphere, seating, security logistics, and remembered private talk; weak as sole authority on formal agreed texts, military staff detail, or Soviet motives. OCR noise requires care when quoting; prefer paraphrase with line anchors or verify against a cleaner edition when precision matters. Second printing statement appears on the copyright page of the working PDF.

sources/schroeder-snowball-warren-buffet.title: [source] The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life (Schroeder, 2008)
sources/schroeder-snowball-warren-buffet.content:
The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life
Author: Alice Schroeder
Published: 2008 (Bantam Books; authorized biography)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash d5a26ea03a5c1840ea27adcc0eb2d8d8)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/schroeder-snowball-warren-buffett.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 46,431 lines · ~412,288 words · 2,478,937 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters 5–14 cover Buffett family lineage, Omaha Depression childhood, Pearl Harbor and Howard Buffett’s isolationism, Washington wartime paper routes and sales, racetrack handicapping habits, and Philadelphia college years through 1949—core interwar/WWII youth material. Mine those chapters first. Chapters 15–46 (Graham through 1980s Berkshire) belong primarily to 1946–89; Chapters 1–4 and 47–62 to 1990–present.
Overview
The Snowball is Alice Schroeder’s authorized life of Warren Buffett. For this United States 1920–45 wiki the usable core is the making of the young money mind: Nebraska preaching inheritance, bathtub-steeplechase Omaha childhood, inky-fingered wartime Washington, and the Elephant years in Philadelphia before Columbia. Period-gate hard after ~1950 except as forward pointers.
Book structure: Parts One–Six / Chs. 1–62; Afterword; Notes; Acknowledgments.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / prologue
Lines 1–55. forexebooks.co.in packaging; title/dedication “To David”; childhood snowball vignette; PART ONE — The Bubble.
Chapter 1 — The Less Flattering Version
Lines 56–137. Omaha, June 2003: Kiewit Plaza office ethnography; Schroeder’s commission; “use the less flattering version.”
Chapter 2 — Sun Valley
Lines 138–987. July 1999 Allen & Co. conference; tech-bubble exuberance vs. Buffett’s caution—gate → 1990–present.
Chapter 3 — Creatures of Habit
Lines 988–1280. Pasadena / habit and circle around the 1999 moment.
Chapter 4 — Warren, What’s Wrong?
Lines 1281–1406. Late-1999 pressure as Berkshire lags the bubble—gate → 1990–present.
Chapter 5 — The Urge to Preach
Lines 1407–1695. Buffett lineage from Huguenot John Buffett; Nebraska preaching/political inheritance through Howard Buffett—1920–45 continuity.
Chapter 6 — The Bathtub Steeplechase
Lines 1696–2090. Omaha 1930s childhood play, family tension, early money mind.
Chapter 7 — Armistice Day
Lines 2091–2367. Mid-1930s household and Depression-era Omaha.
Chapter 8 — A Thousand Ways
Lines 2368–2707. 1939–42 hustles and inventiveness before wartime move.
Chapter 9 — Inky Fingers
Lines 2708–3645. Pearl Harbor; Howard’s isolationist politics; move toward Washington; early newspapering.
Chapter 10 — True Crime Stories
Lines 3646–3756. Washington, D.C., 1943–45; papers and pulp crime reading.

sources/sloan-my-years-with-general-moto.title: [source] My Years with General Motors (Sloan, 1964)
sources/sloan-my-years-with-general-moto.content:
My Years with General Motors
Author: Alfred P. Sloan, Jr. (edited by John McDonald with Catharine Stevens)
Published: 1964 (Doubleday & Company, Garden City, NY)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 92f790472362294573bf9ee84eeb4730)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/sloan-my-years-with-general-motors.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 17,902 lines · ~174,986 words · 1,064,902 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because Chapters 1–15 and much of 16–17, 20–21 cover Durant vs. Ford, the 1920 collapse, decentralized organization, product policy, copper-cooled failure, financial controls, 1920s market transformation, annual model/styling/GMAC origins, World War II defense production, and the 1945–46 strike—core Detroit material beside Ford: Expansion and Challenge, Ford: Decline and Rebirth, and The du Pont Family. Mine first from Chs. 1–15 plus wartime/labor passages in Chs. 20–21. Mid-1960s overseas tallies, Cold War defense-as-permanent-fact framing, and “seventeen years without a national strike” retrospectives (Chs. 18–24) remain primarily for the 1946–89 wiki; use them only as brief forward pointers.
Overview
My Years with General Motors is Alfred P. Sloan, Jr.’s first-person corporate history of GM, written from the vantage of twenty-three years as chief executive and forty-five years on the board and its committees. With Fortune editor John McDonald and Catharine Stevens—and consulting historian Alfred D. Chandler—Sloan reconstructs policy documents and managerial reasoning rather than a private life memoir. The book’s spine is organization and strategy: Durant’s opportunity versus Ford’s Model T philosophy; the 1920 collapse and Pierre S. du Pont rescue; the concept of decentralized divisions with coordinated control; product policy (a car for every purse and purpose); the copper-cooled engine failure as organizational lesson; committee coordination and financial controls; transformation of the mass market in the 1920s; annual model change, styling, dealers, and GMAC; overseas and nonautomotive lines; World War II and Cold War defense production; personnel, the UAW, and incentive compensation; and a closing statement on change and progress.
For this United States 1920–45 wiki the book covers how modern GM was built between the Model T era and World War II’s end: 1920 crisis, du Pont–Sloan succession, committee and financial-control inventions, 1920s competitive triumph over Ford’s single-model concept, annual model/styling/dealer/GMAC machinery, and wartime/national-defense conversion through the 1945–46 strike. Period-gate hard on early-1960s statistical updates and permanent Cold War defense language except where needed to complete a wartime story.
EPUB structure: Table of Contents; title/editor/Doubleday 1964; Preface; Introduction; Chapters 1–24; Illustrations captions; Footnotes.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–77. TOC; title page (Sloan; edited by John McDonald with Catharine Stevens; Doubleday, Garden City, 1964).
Preface
Lines 78–192. Justifies GM story from Sloan’s policy focal point; credits McDonald (Fortune), Catharine Stevens, Alfred D. Chandler (MIT consulting historian), and Fortune/research collaborators (Seligman, Parker, Silberman, Walker Evans as picture editor, et al.).
Introduction
Lines 193–461. Progress of the world’s largest private industrial enterprise across the century and the earth; Chevrolet, Pontiac, Oldsmobile, Buick, Cadillac, GMC as roughly half U.S. passenger cars and trucks; frames engineering arts and modern corporation as the book’s subject.
Chapter 1 — The Great Opportunity—I
Lines 462–952. 1908 dual founding moment: Durant forms General Motors from Buick base; Ford announces Model T—two philosophies that will dominate successive industry periods.
Chapter 2 — The Great Opportunity—II
Lines 953–1868. Sloan’s entry path: born New Haven, 23 May 1875; father’s Bennett-Sloan wholesale move to New York/Brooklyn; Hyatt Roller Bearing and route into GM via United Motors / Durant orbit—personal bridge into the corporation.
Chapter 3 — Concept of the Organization
Lines 1869–2467. End-1920 crisis: vanished market, shut plants, high-priced inventory, cash shortage, confused product line; simultaneous external slump and internal management crisis demanding reorganization.
Chapter 4 — Product Policy and Its Origins
Lines 2468–2947. Need for a concept of the automobile business after 1908–10 and 1918–20 expansions; logical industry concept as competitive force; origins of GM’s graded product ladder.
Chapter 5 — The “Copper-Cooled” Engine
Lines 2948–3936. Painful departure from first principles for ~2½ years; copper-cooled engine program as organizational failure and lesson despite Executive Committee push and divisional resistance.
Chapter 6 — Stabilization
Lines 3937–4079. Spring 1923: Pierre S. du Pont resigns presidency; Sloan succeeds; end of first modern-corporation period; credit to du Pont for rescue and return of general stability after 1920–21.
Chapter 7 — Co-Ordination by Committee
Lines 4080–4726. Fall 1923 boom atmosphere (first four-million vehicle year prospect); reconciliation after copper-cooled conflict; committee coordination as discipline for the 1920s boom.
Chapter 8 — The Development of Financial Controls
Lines 4727–6036. Financial control coevolving with committee coordination from 1920 ruins; modern financial policies as major advance alongside organization and product policy.
Chapter 9 — Transformation of the Automobile Market
Lines 6037–6849. Mid-1920s: strategy known in the mind but little reflected in market results by end-1924; then transformation of demand and competitive structure through the decade.
Chapter 10 — Policy Creation
Lines 6850–7685. By 1929 market transformation essentially complete; Ford’s Model A as stubborn old concept vs. Chrysler’s GM-like policy; Ford’s nearly two million of five million 1929 units as splurge not trend.
Chapter 11 — Financial Growth
Lines 7686–8624. GM as growth company; after 1918 and especially under modern administration, faster than industry to number-one producer; stakeholders—employees, shareholders, dealers, consumers, suppliers, government.
Chapter 12 — Evolution of the Automobile
Lines 8625–9399. Early reliability goal; motorists as risk-capital source; engineering evolution from buggy-like machines to modern cars.
Chapter 13 — The Annual Model Change
Lines 9400–9772. Annual models as accepted American life; vast management effort behind them; contrast with foreign/special cars; competitive advanced engineering and styling each year.
Chapter 14 — The Technical Staffs
Lines 9773–10424. GM as engineering organization (~19,000 engineers/scientists; 17,000 in divisions, 2,000 on general technical staffs); continuous technological progress as policy.
Chapter 15 — Styling
Lines 10425–11030. Styling as organized staff activity pioneered by GM in late 1920s; continuous interaction with engineering since 1928 producing modern GM style.
Chapter 16 — Distribution and the Dealers
Lines 11031–11955. Turbulence when markets shift buyers’/sellers’; novelty in each cycle; evolution of the dealer distribution system; postwar dealer facility and training-center expansion into the 1950s–60s.
Chapter 17 — GMAC
Lines 11956–12368. Why GM owns a major consumer-finance institution; GMAC’s share of U.S. car-credit; business sought only through GM dealers.
Chapter 18 — The Corporation Overseas
Lines 12369–13480. Free-world vehicle absorption and GM overseas position circa 1962–63; Overseas Operations Division assets/employees; manufacturing/assembly in twenty-two countries.
Chapter 19 — Nonautomotive: Diesel Electric Locomotives, Appliances, Aviation
Lines 13481–14872. Diversification limits: durables connected with motors (~10% civilian sales); diesel locomotives, appliances, aviation engines, earth-moving; Durant-era expansion contrasted with later discipline.
Chapter 20 — Contributions to National Defense
Lines 14873–15435. Permanent defense establishment as fact of corporate life; GM defense sales $350–500 million/year (1959–62), ~3% of sales; wartime and Cold War production role.
Chapter 21 — Personnel and Labor Relations
Lines 15436–16097. More than seventeen years without extended national-issue strike as of writing; contrast with mid-1930s violence and 1945–46 postwar strike; labor peace without surrendering basic management responsibilities; inflation critique of contracts.
Chapter 22 — Incentive Compensation
Lines 16098–16986. Bonus Plan since 1918 as integral management philosophy; 1942 annual-report statement placing executives as if running their own businesses; incentive as progress and stability tool.
Chapter 23 — The Management: How It Works
Lines 16987–17239. Motivation (incentive) and opportunity (decentralization); thesis that good management reconciles centralization and decentralization.
Chapter 24 — Change and Progress
Lines 17240–17567. Unique historical opportunity of Sloan’s generation: new product (automobile) and new organization type (large-scale corporation); transformation of United States and world economy.
Illustrations / Footnotes
Lines 17568–17902. Picture captions (early roads, Mercedes, Flint, etc.); numbered footnotes supporting chapters (e.g., early GM presidents; Ethyl sale 1962; dealer training centers).
Coverage Guide
Founding rivalry and Sloan’s entry (wiki core)
Chs. 1–2: Durant vs. Ford Model T philosophies; Hyatt/United Motors path into GM.
1920 crisis, organization, product policy (wiki core)
Chs. 3–7: reorganization, product ladder, copper-cooled failure, du Pont→Sloan succession, committee coordination—how modern GM was built in the early 1920s.
Financial controls, 1920s market, growth (wiki core)
Chs. 8–11: control systems, market transformation, 1929 Ford/Chrysler map, financial growth to industry leadership.
Product, styling, distribution machine (wiki core through WWII)
Chs. 12–17: engineering evolution, annual model, technical staffs, styling, dealers, GMAC—operating system of interwar and wartime Detroit.
Defense and labor through 1945–46 (wiki core / hinge)
Chs. 20–21 wartime and strike passages: national defense conversion and the great postwar strike as period close; later “seventeen years of peace” framing belongs mainly to 1946–89.
Overseas tallies, Cold War defense permanence, management coda (period gate → 1946–89)
Chs. 18–19 and forward-looking parts of 20–24: use only as brief pointers; full mining in the United States 1946–89 sister page.

Overnight Success: Federal Express and Frederick Smith
Author: Vance H. Trimble
Published: 1993 (Crown Publishers, New York; first edition)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash c12b4305840178217a4cf0367184a665)

OCR note: Scanned book (confidence: medium). Running headers, broken words, and garbling are common; verify names/dates against nearby context before long quotes.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1920–45 wiki because the early chapters cover the Smith transportation fortune—river steamboat ancestry, father’s Dixie Greyhound / Toddle House rise (“How to Make $17,000,000”), 1930s Memphis courtship, and East Parkway childhood through the 1940s. Mine those first. Yale, Vietnam, and Federal Express founding (1970s–80s) belong primarily to 1946–89.
Overview
Overnight Success is Vance Trimble’s biography of FedEx founder Frederick W. Smith. For this United States 1920–45 wiki the usable core is the Memphis “transportation Smiths”: Cap’n Jim Buck’s river world, how Fred Smith Sr. made seventeen million, Charlotte Clark and the Perfect Baby birth of Freddie (1944), and life in the East Parkway mansion. Period-gate hard after childhood flying except as forward pointers to overnight air cargo.
Book structure: jacket/title; 21 narrative chapters (+ father-fortune section); Notes and Acknowledgments; Index. OCR from scan (confidence: medium).
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Contents
Lines 1–215. Jacket flap (six packages on day one; hub concept; forgery to save company; July 1975 first profit); title page; © 1993; LC catalog; dedication; Contents listing chapter titles through Notes/Index.
An Hour Most Desperate
Lines 216–475. May 15, 1974 Little Rock frame: age-thirty Smith fired as CEO, forged $2M Union National loan papers, FBI threat, suicidal visit to banker Herbert Hall McAdams II; compassion and Scripture; sets the crisis that the founding narrative will explain.
Cap’n Jim Buck’s Steamboat Life
Lines 476–872. Mississippi River steamboat world and Smith family transportation ancestry—wiki core.
How to Make $17,000,000
Lines 873–1420. Father Fred Smith’s rise: Fisher’s trucks, Dixie Greyhound, Toddle House, Memphis fortune—wiki core.
A Perfect Baby!
Lines 1421–2005. Charlotte Clark meets Fred Smith (Peabody Skyways, 1934); marriage politics; birth of Frederick Wallace Smith (1944)—wiki core.
The House on East Parkway South
Lines 2006–2482. Memphis mansion childhood among siblings/stepsiblings; household chaos and privilege—wiki core.
If I Die Flying…
Lines 2483–3054. Calvé-Perthes hip disease; childhood aviation obsession; early flying and “if I die flying” temperament—wiki core close; later flying → forward.
Yale—And Scars of Guilt
Lines 3055–3564. Yale fall 1962; friend’s death and hospital guilt; path toward Marine Corps/Vietnam as expiation—forward → 1946–89.
War and Love
Lines 3565–4332. Marine lieutenant in Vietnam (1967 jungle firefight); combat leadership; wartime marriage/love strand—forward → 1946–89.
Little Rock Brainstorms
Lines 4333–4993. Home from Vietnam to rescue Arkansas Aviation / Adams Field fixed-base operation; stepfather Col. Fred Hook’s bad investment; seedbed for overnight air-freight idea—forward → 1946–89.
That Damned Purple Airplane
Lines 4994–5793. Art Bass meeting; feasibility studies (A. T. Kearney / AAPG dual hire); Falcon fleet; designer Rick Runyon’s purple/plum livery—forward → 1946–89.
Put in All the Fruit Salad
Lines 5794–6593. 1972–76 operational grind; financing and early network build—forward → 1946–89.
The Wooing of Colonel Crown
Lines 6594–7335. April–May 1973 New Court / Charles Lea; pitch to Henry Crown—forward → 1946–89.
When Soul-Mates Split
Lines 7336–8090. March 12, 1974 Icarus Room investor revolt; lenders’ dread; Smith’s ouster politics—forward → 1946–89.
We, the Jury, Find…
Lines 8091–8920. Memphis criminal defense via Lucius E. Burch, Jr.; trial over forged trust documents—forward → 1946–89.
Falling in Love Again
Lines 8921–9725. Post-crisis private-life shatter; CAB denial of DC-9s; Falcon inefficiency—forward → 1946–89.
Backwater Town Critic
Lines 9726–10328. Late-1970s–early-1980s wealth and public-company rise; Smith as Memphis civic critic—forward → 1946–89.
Drama at Midnight
Lines 10329–10792. Late 1980 midnight hub visits; package-night volumes—forward → 1946–89.
Out of a High-Tech Brain
Lines 10793–11715. Bold/failed side ventures; keeping FedEx reins—forward → 1946–89.
Esprit de Corps
Lines 11716–12238. Fear that scale would kill start-up spirit—forward → 1946–89.
In Search of Adventure
Lines 12239–12725. 1978 Rhodesia/Zimbabwe bush observation—forward → 1946–89.
The Naked Madonna
Lines 12726–13239. Diane Smith’s nude Madonna-and-child portraits; Memphis gossip—forward → 1946–89.
The Flying Tiger Crisis
Lines 13240–14001. 1980s global ambition; Flying Tigers approach; Gelco Express—forward → 1946–89.
Notes and Acknowledgments
Lines 14002–14541. Smith’s refusal to authorize a biography; Trimble’s 1990 turn from Walton to the “transportation Smiths”; source notes and thanks.

Cap’n Jim Buck; How to Make $17,000,000; Perfect Baby; East Parkway; early If I Die Flying childhood.
